speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
1. The Government has received the following information from the officers of the Canadian Peace Centenary Association.
An International Conference took place in New York from~May 5 to May 9, between delegations representing the American Committee for the celebration of the One Hundredth Anniversary of Peace between the United States and the British Empire; the British Committee for the celebration of the One Hundredth Anniversary of Peace between the British Empire and the United States; and the Canadian Peace Centenary Association. In addition, it was attended by representatives of Australia, of Newfoundland and of the city of Ghent.
Mr. PROULX.
The delegates from the British Committee included: The Right Hon. Baron Wear-dale; the Right Hon. Earl Stanhope; the Hon. Sir Arthur Lawley, G.C.S.I., G.C.I.E., K.C.M.G.; the Right Hon. Sir Herbert Maxrwell, P.C.; Hon. Neil Primrose, M.P., Mr. Moreton Frewen; Mr. Henry Vivian and Mr. H. S. Perris.
The delegates from the Canadian Peace Centenary Association were:	Sir Edmund
Walker, C.V.O., LL.D.; Senator R. Dandu-rand; Mr. Travers Lewis, K.C., Mr. C. A. Magrath, Mr. C. F. Hamilton.
The delegates from the American Committee, who were more numerous, included Hon. Joseph H. Choate, Judge Alton B. Parker, Hon. Chauncey M. Depew, Mr. Nicholas Murray Butler, Mr. John D. Crim-mins, Dr. Thomas Nelson Page, Mr. Andrew Carnegie, Mr. Cornelius Vanderbilt, Mr. H. P. Judson, Mr. John A. Stewart, Mr. William Church Osborn, Mr. George Burleigh, Mr. George T, Wilson and Mr. W. B. Howland.
Australia was represented by Sir George H. Reid, G.C.M.G., High Commissioner for Australia; Newfoundland by Mr. Eugene H. Outerbridge; and the municipality of Ghent by M. C. deBruyen and M. Alphonse Van Werveke.
The delegates were given a cordial and sympathetic reception by the President of the United States, Mr. Wilson, by the VicePresident of the United States, Mr. Marshall; by the Secretary of State of the United States, Mr. Bryan; by Mr. Theodore Roosevelt, formerly President of the United States; by Mr. Clark, Speaker of the House of Representatives; and by Mr. Underwood, leader of the majority in the House of Representatives. The American Committee showed a zeal and interest in the movement which created a most favourable impression on all who came in contact with them.
The British and Canadian delegates received many courtesies and attentions from the United States Committee as well as from other prominent and representative citizens.
The Government understands that the proceedings of the conference, which were entirely harmonious, resulted in the passing of resolutions recommending a definite scheme of commemoration, partly by the erection of visible monuments, possibly of identical design; partly by the ceremonies attending the laying of the corner stone of these monuments, and partly by the establishment of lectureships scholarships and similar methods of diffusing correct information upon international relations.
The Canadian delegation has communicated full information with regard to the conference in a letter which is herewith laid on the table for the information of the House.

2. While the Canadian Peace Centenary Association is an unofficial body, the Government strongly sympathizes with and approves o! its object and purpose of promoting good will and peace between the nations of the world. The Government is disposed to give favourable consideration to a grant such as that mentioned in the question in case similar action should be taken in other countries.

Canadian Peace Centenary Association.
Ottawa, May 24, 1913.
Sir,-The Canadian delegates have the honour to lay before you a statement of the events associated with the International Conference recently held in New York for the purpose of adopting a definite programme ifor the celebration oif the centenary of the sign-in s of the treaty of Ghent.
The delegation from the Canadian Peace Centenary Association was headed by Sir Edmund Walker, C.V.O., the president of tlie association. At the conclusion of the deliberations Sir Edmund Walker was obliged to proceed to Europe, having indeed, more than once postponed his sailing and dislocated his personal arrangements in order to discharge his duties as a member of the conference. In his absence the duty of making this report devolves upon the remaining members of the delegation.
The conference did not regard itself as a body authorized to determine with finality the questions before it, but rather as a meeting of delegations from parent bodies to which report must be made and to which all recommendations must be submitted. Ail business transacted and resolutions passed are conceived upon that basis.
The British delegation consisted of:- The Rt. Hon. Baron Weardale; the Rt). Hon. Earl Stanhope; The Hon. Sir Arthur Lawley, G.C.S.I., G.C.I.E., K.C.M.G.; the Rt. Hon. Sir Herbert Maxwell, P.C., the Hon. Neil Primrose, M.P.; the Hon. C. T. Mills, M.P.; Mr. Shirley Benn. M.P.; Mr. J.	Allen Baker, M.P.; Mr. Moreton Frewen; Mr. Henry Vivian, and Mr. H. S. Perris.
The American delegation, which was much larger, included:	Mr. Joseph H. Chocate,
former American Ambassador to Great Britain, New Work; Judge Alton B. Parker, New York; the Hon. Robert Bacon, Boston; Mr. Henry Clews, New York; Mr. Cbauncey Depew, New Work; Mr. Howard D. The proceedings of the conference began on May 5 and terminated on May 9. During their continuance the American committee constituted themselves the hosts of the visiting delegates, and discharged that function with the utmost generosity. Great interest was evinced in the conference while it sat in New York, an interest which in part took the form of a hospitality which culminated in a banquet held on the evening of May 9. The visiting delegates were afterwards conveyed to Boston, Washington, Philadelphia, Chicago and other cities, where flattering attentions were paid to them; the Canadian delegates were unable to visit all of these places. It may not be out of place to add that the newspapers of the United States devoted to the proceedings of the conference a degree of attention which we were assured was quite unusual; while there was much editorial comment, couched in terms of a gratifying friendliness.
We feel constrained to state that apart altogether from the abundant hospitality accorded us, we have every reason to feel gratified at the distinguished personnel and cordial disposition of the American committee. In New York Mr. Joseph H. Choate showed the most active interest in the conference, and on several occasions acted as its chairman; Judge Alton B. Parker, who was Democratic candidate for the presidency in 1908. attended the conference regularly, and Mr. Theodore Roosevelt, former president of the United States, at his home at Oyster Bay addressed and entertained the delegates in a most cordial manner. President Nicholas Murray of Columbia University was active in the work of the conference; Mayor Gaynor of New York formally welcomed the delegates in a cordial speech; Dr. Thomas Nelson Page, the well-known author, bore an active part in the deliberations; Mr. Carnegie, Mr. Cornelius Vanderbilt, Mr. Henry Clews, Mr. William Church Osborn, Mr. George W. Perkins, and Dr. Louis Livingston Seaman exerted themselves to make the conference a success. Other prominent men in New York who bore a part in the deliberations or otherwise showed interest were Mr. Walter H. Page, the new Ambassador to Great Britain,

public opinion everywhere that the time has come when international rivalries and differences, though numerous and severe, may be.settled without the carnage and the horrors! of war. Although it be unreasonable to disregard the possibility of conflict arising in the future, out of mutual or partial misun-: derstanding, yet we gratefully recognize that the chances of misunderstanding have been largely eliminated by the degree in which modern science has facilitated intercourse and accelerated communication. We are therefore encouraged to hope that the development of letters, science and the arts, of commerce, industry and finance, of mutual knowledge, trust and good feeling on the part of those who owe different allegiances and who speak different tongues, may profitably absorb the energy of mankind, as well as offer opportunity for the display of the noblest and' finest traits of mind an4 of character.
Great Britain .has been a colonizing nation, and the United States has drawn to its population various and powerful elements from different countries and different flags. Therefore, a century of peace between Great Britain and her dominions beyond the seas on the on el hand, and the United States on the other hand, touches directly both the interest and the imagination of every land to which Great Britain's sons have gone, as well as those of every nation from which the present day population of the United States has been drawn. Such a celebration will not only mark the close of a century of exceptional significance and importance, but it will call attention to an example and an ideal that we earnestly hope may be followed and pursued in the years to come. What nations have done, nations can do.
We respectfully request that His Majesty's Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs and the Secretary of State of the United States do transmit this invitation, through the proper world official channels, to the governments of the world, in order that both by participation of governments and by the co-operation of men of good-will in every land, this celebration may be so carried out as to mark not merely the close of one hundred years of peace between English speaking peoples, but the opening of what we sincerely trust will be a fresh era of peace and good-will between all nations of the world.
The International Boundary.
In addition to the foregoing, at a sub-committee meeting held between the delegates representing the United States and Canada, for the purpose of taking up the matter of appropriate marking of the international boundary in commemoration of the first hundred years of peace between the two nations, it was decided that suggestions he made to the organizations of the United States and Canada, as follows:-
That they urge upon their respective Governments -
(a)	The erection of arches at the points where the proposed highways-Quebec and Miami in the east, and Los Angeles to Vancouver in the west- cross the international boundary.
(b)	The erection of shafts at a few historical and prominent points upon or on each side of the boundary (which, in the latter
Mr. BOR') IN.
case, should be erected in the immediate vicinity of tlie boundary) at omn'-s to be selected hereafter. This might properly include water-gates on opposite sides of the Detroit river, near the city of Detroit.
(c)	That such arches and shafts be briefly and suitably inscribed.
It was further felt that these outward and visible signs of the spirit of the occasion should not be restricted to the international boundary, but should also find a place in the great centres of population, often far distant therefrom, thus carrying the message of mutual good-will to the mass of both peoples.
It was urged before the sub-committee that an enduring monument in the shape of a memorial bridge he built across the Niagara river. This and other like projects appealed quite strongly to the sub-committee, but it felt that, involving as it does very large expenditures on the part of the governments of both countries, they might very properly be allowed to stand for further consideration until the respective committees shall have had greater opportunity to look more closely into these larger projects in accordance with the following resolution :-
' This sub-committee recommends that after the American and Canadian committees shall have decided upon a plan of celebration regarding boundary monuments, memorials and arches, a commits.'e of six, composed of three members from each of the respective committees, shall be appointed with instructions to consult experts in art, architecture and engineering with a view to the preparation of plans and the execution of the particular works to be undertaken.'

I do not rise to criticise this increase; I think the cost of living is felt by the employees of the Government to a greater extent than by any other class of society; but, as this translation is more or less under the supervision of the Debates Committee, I wish to express my regret that the Debates Committee has not been consulted with regard to the reorganization and re-classification of the translating staff. The Debates Committee is the proper body to supervise the translation of ' Hansard ' in the House of Commons. We had during this session a special meeting called by the chairman, the hon. member for New Westminster Mr. GUTHRIE.
(Mr. Taylor), and the complaints were many and loud with regard to the translation of ' Hansard.' I do not blame any translator in particular; I know that the majority of the translators are men of the highest ability; but, unfortunately, there are two or three on the staff who are totally inefficient and unable to translate decently. I can assure the members of the committee that it is rather annoying when one speaks in English in the House, to find his remarks the next morning or a few days afterwards translated into French which is far from being good French. I have given illustrations to the members	of the	Debates	Committeeduring the winter, and they all agreed with me that some of the translations of speeches	made during this and	thelast session have been simply horrible. I resent having my remarks translated in that way into French. We all love our mother tongue, and when the members of the French speaking minority in this House	speak	in English	theleast they can	expect	is	that
their speeches, shall be well translated. We have, as I stated, an excellent staff. I could name, for instance, men like Mr. Fortier Mr. Gascon, Mr. Gerin, Mr. Girard, Mr. Hughes, Mr. Labine. Mr. Lasalle, and Mr. Desaulniers, who are expert translators. I am told, and it was established to our satisfaction at the Debates Committee, that no revision of the translation is made before it reaches the Printing Bureau. We were told that the copy is rushed through the translation office to the Printing Bureau because we are anxious to get the French 'Hansard' at the next meeting of this House, and that we cannot afford to wait.
I can assure the majority in the House of Commons that we would much prefer that the publication of the unrevised French 'Hansard' should be delayed two or three days, if need be, so that we might have a proper translation of our speeches. We have impressed upon the committee the necessity of having a thorough revision made before the manuscript leaves the translation office for the Printing Bureau. We have stated to the committee that this is absolutely necessary, and the committee agreed with us. My good friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) agreed with me, and so did my friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) who is an old journalist. But our orders have been ignored, I am sorry to say, by the chief of the translators, Mr. Larbse. Be had it in his head that he knew it all better than we did, and so the system continued. Here is the trouble: The manuscript of the translation leaves the translators' office without any revision, goes directly to the Printing Bureau, and we receive, the next day, the unrevised French 'Hansard'. This unrevised edition

of the French 'Hansard' is the one that is distributed to the French press in Quebec and other parts of Canada. There are mistakes, there are absurdities, in that unrevised edition; but when the mistakes and the absurdities have left Parliament and are spread throughout Canada in the French press, they are there and remain there, and we have to wait some days before we get the revised edition of the French 'Hansard.' I say it is simply intolerable, and the will of the French members of the House of Commons on both sides should be respected. The hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Boulay) was present at one sitting of the committee, and he remembers how we impressed the committee with the necessity of obtaining this revision. I have never risen in the House to lay a complaint against the French translators, and I Tepeat it again: You have on that staff some very able men. There are experts in translation but their work is very often destroyed by others. I could give you instances if time were not so precious at this stage of the session. The hon. member for
New Westminster (Mr. Taylor), the chairman of the Debates Committee, can state
that when we brought the chief translator before the committee this winter, this official said that he was in the hands of the Speaker, and has ignored completely our orders.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not consider myself competent to deal. with a matter of this nature. It seems to me it ought to be as much as possible under the control of the Debates Committee. They make their recommendations, and I endeavour to see that they are carried out. With regard to defective translation, as an old member of this House, I may say that I have heard these complaints for the last thirty years, so that they are not new. Whether the translation is worse or better now than it has been in the past, of course I am not prepared to say. But it did seem to me that it would require very careful examination by experts in French and English translation to determine where the fault lies. There are at the Printing Bureau two men who, when complaints were made in this regard, were brought before me, so that I might ascertain whether or not they were faithfully revising the translation. So far as I could find they were faithfully endeavouring to do their work all right. Beyond that, of course, I could not go. There are many members of this staff, several of whom, I think it is admitted, do their work very well, and it is very difficult to tell who is doing the bad work. Therefore it did seem to me that if the intention was to find where the weakness was, it would be necessary to have an inquiry by competent men who understand that work in order to reach a conclusion. I did not feel that I was competent to deal with it. With regard to the arrangement of the staff, it is much the same as it has been heretofore. It was submitted to the Civil Service Commission with the request that they go over it, consult with the men, and arrange it according to their judgment. That was done, and of course I accepted the arrangement as correct.

It is well
understood, of course, that all employees of this House are under the supervision of Mr. Speaker; but when the reporting of the debates was introduced in this House in 1875, a special committee was appointed to supervise the debates, and ever since it has been understood that all the employees on that staff were under the orders of that committee. I do not know whether or not these officers are legally under the supervision of Mr. Speaker. Nominally they are, but in reality they have always been under the Debates Committee. All the Speakers that I can remember have done as Mr. Speaker has done at the present time-left the matter altogether in the hands of the committee. I understand, however, that

some of the translators refuse to recognize the powers of the committee, and that is the difficulty that has arisen in this matter.

I certainly think that
the state of things which has been described by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), cannot be tolerated. I was not aware that there were such gross errors in the French ' Hansard.' I have heard of them for the first time this morning.

You cannot
read it very carefully.

I must confess that I do not read it, but if I ever do read it, I shall probably find that they have made some big blunders in translating what 1 have .said. But on principle I think that the hon. member for Rouville is right in complaining that such things have happened, and in calling for a remedy. I agree entirely with hon. members opposite that the employees are under the guidance and direction of the Debates Committee, and any attempt to ignore the wishes or orders of that committee should not be tolerated at all. But I understand that this branch of the work is undermanned. A recommendation was made years ago when Mr. Gervais,' who is now a judge of the Court of Appeal, was chairman of the Debates Committee, that another good French translator should be added to the staff. Up to this date, that addition has not been made, for what reason I do not know. I desire to throw no blame on anybody, but, as the Speaker put it a moment ago, these complaints have been made for a long time. Some of these men may be incompetent; I do not know about that; but certainly some of them are overworked, and when a man is overworked it is not to be wondered at if he makes mistakes. I think we should take care of that .situation; and I would suggest that before prorogation there should be a meeting of the Debates Committee in order that an effort may be made to cope mith it. If that appeals to the Speaker and to hon. members who are members of the committee, an emergency meeting of the committee might be held. I do not know about Mr. Larose. If he has taken that position-I do not know that he has-he has no right to take it. However,
I suggest that something should be done at once to relieve the situation.

My hon. friend the Postmaster General states what is absolutely true: some members of that staff are overworked, but they are also handicapped. The mistakes and absurdities, however, do not arise from those who are overworked: they arise from the inability of some members of the staff-and we know them. Sir,
Sir WILFRID LAURIER
during this session I was asked by a former Consul General of France, whom my hon. friend knows well, one of the most distinguished men that we have had in Canada, to send him a copy of ' Hansard ' containing the naval debate. He was very much interested in that subject. I sent him the French edition and the English edition, and I wrote to him asking his choice. To my sorrow and shame, he replied that he would rather read the English version than the French. Here is a Frenchman, a devoted friend of Canada, who writes from Paris that he would rather read the English edition of our ' Hansard ' than the French edition. The majority of the staff are exceedingly able men, but they ara handicapped. Take now the case of Mr. Hughes, who is .suffering in his eyesight, or the case of Mr. Lasalle, who has practically lost the use of his right arm in writing. They appealed to the Speaker at the beginning of the session, and I must thank the Speaker for what he did for them, two very able and trusted translators. Yes, we should cheerfully give those civil servants the help for which they are in need, because, as my hon. friend knows, their work is most difficult. It is expert work, and if there are two or three inferior translators, with the best staff in the world you will have the medley that one can imagine. I would certainly favour the appointment, not of one, but of two other translators of the debates, so as to relieve men like Mr. Lasalle, Mr. Hughes, Mr. Labine, Mr. Gerin, Mr. Girard, and others. Thev are able men, but are overworked and handicapped. At present the translation is spoilt by the interspersion of very inferior translation done by a few others. As regards the supervision of the office, Mr. Larose is also an excellent translator; but he should obey the instructions and commands of the Debates Committee. When he is told that he should revise the copy before it reaches the Printing Bureau, he should obey our orders and he should not take it upon himself to say: ' Well, I will consult the Speaker, and I will not recognize your authority.' Mr. Larose is under our direction, and he must obey our orders. It is because there is no revision of the manuscripts made at the translation office before it reaches the Printing Bureau that we have these absurdities in ' Hansard ' which spoil the good work of efficient translators, and which belittle the value of our French ' Hansard.'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is desirable, of course, that the translation should be made as speedily as possible, and correctly made. Is it the opinion of the Debates Committee that the staff of the translation branch, which we are now considering, should be increased?

The Debates Committee did not pronounce on that during this session, because the question was the revision of the manuscript before it reached the Printing Bureau. We did not consider the other question; but members of the committee are here. Personally speaking, I have followed this work, I have it at heart, and I take it as a matter of pride that our French ' Hansard ' should be the equal of the English ' Hansard.' Therefore, I have no hesitation in saying that this staff should be strengthened. 1 ask my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Belaud), my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau), my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon), all the French members of the House who take an interest in ' Hansard,' if they are not of opinion that, the staff should be increased? I would give them a chance to be relieved of some of the work.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
With regard to Mr. Hughes and Mr. LaSalle, I might explain that Mr. Hughes has done very little work during the present session on account of his illness; but there have been others to do the work. The question which seemed to be of interest was in regard to the revision of the translation and whether the Tevisers should be here or at the Printing Bureau. It was represented to me that it would be an economy to keep them at the Printing Bureau, and for that Tea-son they were put there, because, as the revision commenced and went on at the Printing Bureau the copy was handed over to the typesetters so that the work of typesetting and revision could be carried on simultaneously. If they remained here there would be delays, and the holding back of copy for a time; because, if it were in the hands of the chief here, portions would have to be kept back until other portions were ready to accompany it. But if they were there they could deal with the copy as it came in from moment to moment, and the:ce would be no time lost. These officials revise the translation which goes into the hands of the printer. It seemed to me that there was some merit in that method, and therefore I did not recommend any change in it, although at first I did contemplate giving an order that the revisers of the translation be located here instead of at the Printing Bureau. In regard to the suggestion that there should be one or two more translators, the matter came before me in the midst of the session, during the time that this reorganization was going on, and, intending to have this reorganization made, I thought it well, instead of recommending new appointments, to add to the present staff at the commencement of next session. It is the intention to do that, although it is
not mentioned in this report, and therefore it may not be understood.
I would like to Know if the Debates Committee have been consulted as to the- reorganization which is here recommended.

I have to endorse fully the complaint made by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) as to the condition of the first edition of the French ' Hansard,' of the House of Commons, and also to express my regret that, after the matter had been very carefully considered, and a remedy suggested by the Debates Committee which we felt sure would prove to be absolutely effective, our recommendation was turned down, for some reason never disclosed to the committee, and the present ineffective means of dealing with the ' Hansard ' was continued just as it had been before the committee dealt with the subject. I may say that the Debates Committee have been ruled to have no authority at all except to discuss matters affecting ' Hansard '-that it has been ruled that we have no power even to make a recommendation to this House; so that all the Debates Committee could do was to write a polite letter to Mr. Speaker stating that in the opinion of the committee a certain course should be adopted to improve ' Hansard.' We found that the trouble could be very easily rectified, and we made a recommendation which involved not one dollar of expense or any increase of staff-simply that the translation should be revised before the printer got the copy, instead of after it had been printed and distributed, which is the course followed now. From the best inquiries I could make, the two gentlemen who are at the Printing Bureau making this revision are as capable men as can be found anywhere for the work. I discussed the matter with them, and they told me that if they were put, as we recommended they should be put, in the room with the translators, to get the translators' copy just as it came from their hands, and as the news editor of a paper gets his reporters' copy as it comes from their hands, they might revise it and do it just as well as, and even better, than they revise it now. They told me that the work would be no more to them, and that there would be no delay in handing the copy to the printer, and there would be no trouble of any kind whatever. If these two translators, were taken from the Printing Bureau, and put into the translators' office to take the copy and read and revise it before it went to the printer, I am satisfied that the cause of complaint, would be removed; and I have to express my disappointment again that after the Debates Committee had gone so thoroughly into this question and had called atten-

tion to the matter their recommendation was turned down.

I thank my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor), who is an old journalist, and who knows where the trouble lies. My hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) is also an old journalist, and he also knows where the trouble is. It is all very well to say that, in order to rush the printing of ' Hansard, you must send your manuscript to the Printing Bureau to he set up, and that there are two men there for proof reading. But that is not the way to cure the evil. Sir, French is a most difficult language, even much as you may be surprised, let me say that after some practice the French-Canadian member who speaks English in the House finds it easier after a time to speak English than pure and classical French. Let me explain how the translation is done. The copy is sent from the 'Hansard' office to the translators, and is divided into so many pages for each translator, and they begin work early in the morning. There are many different words in English which express the same ideas in French, and if the translator does not see the manuscript his confrere has, and does not understand the context, absurdities creep in. If the chief translator would take the manuscript and with the help of the two translators stationed at the Printing Bureau, examine it before it leaves the translating office, it would not be printed with the absurdities we complain of. Although the Debates Committee expressed the opinion that this should be done, I regret to say that the order of the Debates Committee has been ignored. If it is the opinion of the committee that two more translators should be added, this classification should be delayed until next session, and meanwhile the two translators would be appointed and the Debates Com-mitte would in the meantime examine more carefully the situation, and be in a better position to judge whether or not some persons are entitled to an increase in their salary.

I fail to understand how the recommendation of the Debates Com-mitte has been turned down. The usual course is for the committee to report to the Speaker its recommendations, and the Speaker has authority to carry out the recommendation of the Debates Committee. I fail to realize how the chief translator could turn down such a recommendation of the committee. We all realize that the work of translation is very difficult, and the work of revision is also a matter of difficulty. I believe the work of revision would require more than one man.

There are two men at
the Printing Bureau.
Mr. TAYLOR.

Are we to understand
that the two men at the Printing Bureau are translators, or only proofreaders?

They are appointed as translators and they are described in the reorganization as belonging to the translation branch, but they were sent by Mr. Larose to act as proofreaders. Any journalist knows that a man may be an excellent proofreader and a poor translator; or, on the other hand, he may be an excellent translator and a poor proofreader.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
My own opinion was
that the men should be up here. I went to see the place where they work and I found there was no room for them. It was contended that the urgent demand for having the French unrevised edition come out as early as the English made it necessary that these officials should be kept at the Bureau. I still thought there ought to be one or two translators up here, and I went to ascertain if there was room, and I found that the office was fully occupied. I left instructions to the effect that we would endeavour to remedy that next session and provide accommodation, so that we could have one or two men up here, and if it was still thought desirable to keep the others down there, they might continue to revise the proof after it came from the printer.

I realize that it is necessary to keep in the Printing Bureau a certain number of proof readers, and I endorse entirely the position taken by my hon. friend from Rouville, by the Postmaster General, and by the hon. member for New Westminster, that provision for revision should be made at once. But revision involves a vast amount of work, because, to have a proper revision of the translation, the English text has to be read with the French translation. I do not see how one man could do that; in fact, I do not think two men could do it. It would require almost as many revisors as there are translators. I have myself come across some painful errors in the translation; but, of course, errors will slip in anywhere. However, in some oases these errors are unexplainable. I am happy to say, however, that the large majority of these translators are competent. I do not know them personally, but I think as a general rule the translation is fair; and some of my poor English is sometimes put into very excellent French. I think there should be more than two officials added to the translation branch for the work of revision. I also submit that any recommendation that is sent to Mr. Speaker by the Debates Committee, should not be turned down or overruled by the chief translator. That is a thing I cannot understand.

If we abolished 'Hansard,' we would save ourselves a lot of trouble and much expense to the country. But if we are to have ' Hansard,' we should have good translation. My hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) says there are some incompetent translators on the staff. If that is so, it should not be. If they are incompetent, they should be appointed to some other position in the Civil Service, and be replaced by competent .men. It is not necessary to add two other translators and keep the incompetent men. So far as I am personally concerned, I have no complaint to make. I can say like my hon. friend (Mr. Beland), that my poor English is sometimes put into very good French.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps it would be better to leave this classification as it is at present, upon the understanding that if the Debates Committee recommend the appointment of two additional men, at the commencement of next session, their recommendation will be acted upon.
Hear, hear.

I had a few remarks to make a moment ago, but the hon. members for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) and for Westminster (Mr. Taylor) having since dealt with the subjects I wished to allude to, it is useless for me to revert to those same points now. I am not so competent, from a literary point of view, as is the hon. member for Rouville, to speak of the defects in the translation of the speeches, but I know that many complaints have been made at the meeting of the Debates Committee at which I was present. What is the cause of this, I could not say; but I have visited the office of the debates translators on more than one occasion ana I have witnessed that there prevailed some uneasiness. What should this disagreement be attributed to, I do not know. But I know that the complaints voiced by the hon. member for Rouville really exist and that they have been brought to the knowledge of the committee.
I have witnessed, also, that the chief translator, Mr. Larose, seemed to keep an independent office. He never registers his presence, and so we do not know when he Is absent or present. He seems to be in absolute command. He is a public official like the others and I think he should register his presence so that we might be informed as to his being present or absent. I often went to see him at his office and I never could succeed in meeting him. It is possible that his presence was required somewhere else. I do not know about that; but at all events he was not there. I have witnessed, moreover, and anybody can do so, that there seems to exist a complete dissent between the debates translators and their chief. I do not know whether the translators can be called his subordinates, but they do not
seem to depend upon their chief. I think this uneasiness could be done away with if the chief would remedy it by being more conciliating and by taking a share of the work for himself. I have witnessed that Mr. Larose contented himself with distributing the work to the translators. If such are his functions, they are very light. He should register his presence and take a part of the work like all the other translators, and he would earn his money better if he did so. I see that his salary is being increased; I have no objection to that, but he should have a certain amount of work to do for that money. Measures should also be taken to the effect of indicating if he is constantly at the office like the other employees and when he is really absent. In fact, he should take his share of work like the other translators.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does this stand?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As far as I can see, there is no reason for it standing over. Anything that requires to be done can be done by regulation. If the matter is left in my hands, when the committee make a recommendation it can be carried out without trouble.

Some of the work of translation is being sent from Ottawa to various parts of the Dominion, and it is thought that it would conduce to efficiency if all the work were done in Ottawa. The intention is to provide for ten men, and provision has already been made for naming them, and the next resolution standing in the Prime Minister's name covers this.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I found that this work
was being done by over a hundred translators all over the country. Much of the work was very defective and had to be done over again. It occurred to me that it would be much better to provide for a permanent force of competent men to do the work here, with a man over them. When I

suggested this, the Civil Service Commission provided an examination, and competent men have been chosen, whose names will be found at page 1416 of the Votes and Proceedings.

Who is responsible for
fixing the age limit after the examinations were held? Was it the Internal Economy Commission or the Civil Service Commission? People were notified to come to Ottawa to take the examination, no age limit being fixed. One gentleman came from my own town. When he asked me, as he was over forty, I told him I thought he would not be entitled to try the examination, the age limit for the Civil Service being thirty-five. He said that no age limit had been stated. He wrote to the secretary of the Civil Service Commission, who replied that there was no age limit. He passed the examination successfully, although not among the first ten. After the examinations were held, either the Internal Economy Commission or the Civil Service Commission fixed the age at forty. I know one man who held the fifth place, but who could not be appointed because he was a little over forty- forty-two, I think.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The limit was fixed by the Civil Service Commission, the Internal Economy Commission did not fix it at all.

Were they asked to fix
an age limit?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not know.

It seems very singular
that these men were allowed to go through the examination, and were then turned down because of the age limit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The statute fixes the age limit, I think. Apparently, the difficulty has arisen through some inaccurate information having been given to the gentlemen whom the hon. member has mentioned. I know nothing at all about it.

It is true, there is an
age limit, but some years ago the Minister of Justice gave an interpretation of section 31 of the Civil Service Act as regards technical work. Translation 'being considered technical work there is no age limit. But the point in which I am interested is that mentioned by Mr. Speaker, that this work was formerly done by any number of translators outside this House of Parliament, and it was sometimes very inferior work. Now, with a staff of expert translators, we should have good work, and I hope we shall have the public documents published in French more promptly. I said the other day that the French-Can-adian members of the House had just received the Auditor General's report for 1911 -two years late. Amongst those who successfully passed the examination were two supernumerary officials of the House, Mr. SPEAKER.
Messrs. Daoust and Allarie. After having passed the examination, they were under the impression that they could be appointed as translators, but it was found that they had passed the age limit fixed by the commission. They are good men, who have worked very assiduously for several years, and it would be a hardship if they were put out of their positions now.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
They are both good men, and it was my suggestion that they should be appointed as a result of the examination, but as they are over forty-five years of age they have passed the age limit and the commission instructed me that they could not be appointed. I am, however, endeavouring to get them employment elsewhere in the department.
Hansard section-'Reporting branch:

A rumour has apparently reached the reporting branch and the reporters of committees that some new restrictions are to be placed upon them as to how they shall spend the time between sessions, and there is a little alarm amongst these officials. When the Civil Service Act was passed, I think there was in it a clause exempting the 'Hansard' staff, and the reporters from being subject to the House of Commons between the sessions, and it was distinctly provided, I think, that they should be allowed to add to their salaries by doing any work they desired to do when the House was not in session.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is no change in that respect.
In the Stationery the office of chief of stenographers seems to be vacant. Has any selection been made?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Joseph Smith has
been doing the work, and has been found to be a very competent man for the position.
He is a good man.

I would like to emphasize that; Mr. Smith is a good man.
Post Office and blue-book division.

In view of the statements which have been made from time to time as to the number of persons of my pedigree who have been placed in the Civil Service by myself, I am pleased to be able to state publicly before my hon. friend the Postmaster General and the other French-Canadian members of the House that Mr. F. X. Lemieux, who has for some time been assistant postmaster in the House of Commons, is no relative of mine, although I would feel honoured to bear relationship to l'im, as he is an excellent official. My friends went around the province of Que-

bee during the election campaign with a list of all the Lemieuxs they could find in the blue books, and said: Look at what this Postmaster General has done; he has given all the important offices in the public service to his family. Let me say, once and for all, that only one member of my family was appointed to a position in the Civil Service. He was appointed by the Macdonald-Sicotte Government; he was my revered father, and had been over fifty years in the Civil Service. My friends the Nationalists and Conservatives made a list of every Lemieux they could find in the Civil Service list, and labelled them as being members of my family. I desire to say that this gentleman is not in my family, although I am glad to see that he is getting an increase.
Law Branch.-parliamentary counsel.
In this branch provision is made for a new official to be known as parliamentary counsel. Will this official be employed only during the session?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He will be a permanent officer, and will perform his duties during the entire year.
Will he'take the place of the Law Clerk of the House?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He will. It is understood that the Law Clerk, Mr. O'Brien, desires to retire, and it is only just to him to say that during my experience, both before this Government attained office and since, I have found him to be a most capable, industrious and devoted officer, from whom I have obtained a great deal of assistance.

Has anyone been
named for the position?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No one has been named, or even considered. The change was recommended by the Civil Service Commission and others who made inquiry into the matter, and it was thought advisable to reestablish the position of parliamentary counsel, which was established years ago, but which for some reason was discontinued.

I suppose his services
will be at the disposal of private members? If a private member, for instance, wishes ro introduce a public Bill, he may have it drafted by the parliamentary counsel, and have the benefit of his services?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly.
Has the report of the body who made inquiries into that branch been submitted to the House; and, if not, why the delay?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The reorganization really carries out the suggestions of the report that was made.
Is that report likely to be brought down?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
When? I asked some questions about that some time ago, and did not get very much satisfaction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We will bring it down to-day or to-morrow.

I think considerable inconvenience has been experienced because ox the fact that in the parliamentary restaurant the waiters are nearly all Englishspeaking. For my part, I have great complaint in this regard, because I do not understand much English, and I think there should be more French-speaking waiters in the restaurant. There is another, place to which the same thing applies, and which I do not frequent very much, but when I have some friends here we go there, and we do not find any person speaking French. I refer to what we call the buffet- the bar. This lack of French-speakirg waiters is sometimes very inconvenient.

I would suggest that the Minister of Inland Revenue should take the food inspector whom he appointed for the province of Nova Scotia recently at the magnificent salary of $100, Moses Delorey, and put him in the restaurant. We have no use for him in Antigonish, or in Nova Scotia. While he is a good judge of food laid before him on the table, he knows nothing whatever about the inspection of food, or the qualities of food in a commercial sense. He could not tell butter from margerine, or honey from tomato catsup. We have no use for him down there.
I suppose Mr. Chisholm, the preventive officer, has some use for him.
The preventive officers have no use for him.

I see a vacancy in
1-B, under the law branch. Is it a new appointment, or is it to replace somebody who is retiring?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This is to replace Mr. Loucks.

No one has been
named?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No.
Resolution reported, read the first and the second time, and agreed to.
On the Orders of the Day being called:
I would renew my request of the other day, whether or not any new legislation is to be introduced.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, there will be no further legislation. Possibly there may be two or three supplementary estimates, which I shall submit to the right hon. gentleman before introducing them.
Is it the inr tention to call up all the items which are now on the Order Paper?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

I would suggest "to the Prime Minister that some arrangement should be made in regard to returns ordered by the (House, but not yet brought down. I find about twenty returns for which I moved at various times from January up to the present that have not yet been brought down. Could the Prime Minister arrange with the officers of the departments to forward copies of these returns when they are completed to the members who moved for them?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

Mr. Speaker,
it is certainly regrettable that in a matter ol this kind there should be any difference of opinion between the Upper Chamber and the House of Commons. In my estimation the attitude which is taken by the Government is not at all warranted, and the action of the Upper Chamber is fully justified. To make the matter perfectly clear, it is necessary that I should put before the House the text of the Bill, the amendments made to it by the Upper Chamber, and then the reasons alleged by the Government why we should not agree to the action taken by the Senate. The Bill is a short one, and I may read it to the House. It is composed only of six actions. The first section is of no consequence; it is simply the title of the Act. The second section merely defines the meaning of the word 'Minister'; it means Minister of Railways and Canals. Then, the Bill provides as follows:
3. The Governor in Council may, in any year, and upon such terms and subject to such conditions as are prescribed by Order in Council, grant to the several provinces of the Dominion in aid of the improvement of existing highways or bridges, or the construction of new highways or bridges, or fori all or any such purposes, subsidies not ex-1 ceeding in the whole such sum as may in such year be voted by Parliament for that purpose.
4.	Any highway or bridge for which aid is granted to a province shall be improved or, constructed, as the case may be. according to descriptions, conditions and specifications approved by the Governor in Council on the report of the minister, and specified in each case in an agreement between the minister and the government of the province, which agreement the minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council, is hereby empowered to make.
5.	Each highway or bridge to be constructed'
or improved shall be defined and described in' such agreement, and provision may be made therein for the future maintenance of suchhighway or bridge in good condition accord-/ ing to a specified standard and to the satisJ faction of the Governor in Council.	'
6.	The minister, with the approval of the
Governor in Council and upon such terms and! conditions as are prescribed by Order in' Council, may undertake the construction of any new highway or bridges or the improve-: ment of any existing highway or bridges_ ini any province, and may expend in such imJ provement or construction the whole or any part of the sums voted by Parliament for such subsidy to that province:	Provided,
however, that the minister shall first^ obtain the necessary authority from the legislature of such province and the consent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
The Senate have not amended the fourth section. The sixth section they have suppressed altogether, and to the third they have added a sub-section. Before I give the amendment made by the Senate, let me again read section 3 of the Bill:
The Governor in Council may, in any year, and upon such terms and subject to such conditions as are prescribed by Order in, Council, grant to the several provinces of the Dominion in aid of the improvement of existing highways or bridges, or the construction of new highways or bridges, or for all or any sucli purposes, subsidies not exceeding in the whole such sum as may in such year be voted by Parliament for that purpose.
To which the Upper Chamber has added the following sub-section:
The sum of money voted in any year to be expended under this Act shall be apportioned among and paid to the several provinces of the Dominion in proportion to the population of such provinces respectively as shown by the then next preceding census.
Can any one take exception to a* provision being introduced into the Bill that the sum to be appropriated by Parliament each year shall be expended among the provinces according to population? Nobody on that side of the House can find fault with it; in fact, it is not found fault with, as I shall show presently, in the reasons that have been given in the motion now before the House why these amendments should

not be concurred in. It is admitted by the bon. Minister of Railways and Canals- and I think it will be admitted by the right hon. the Prime Minister and by everybody- that the money which is to be appropriated by Parliament for the improvement of highways should be apportioned among the provinces according to population, as stated by the census. If it is agreed that this should be done, why is it not incorporated in the Bill creating the law under which the money is to be expended? Can any good reason be given? I cannot understand what is in the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite to cause them to refuse to put in a law what they say shall be their course in carrying out the law, If it is to be their course in practice, why should it not be put in the law? The Government take exception to the provisions which have been introduced into the Bill by the Upper Chamber, and here are the reasons, as stated in the motion, why they do not propose to ask the House to agree to them:
1. Because substantially the same amendment has already been considered and rejected by this House.
Which is very true.
3. Because the amendment is unnecessary and undesirable, since (a) the Supply Bill will make provision for the apportionment of the proposed subsidies to the respective provinces foT the ensuing fiscal year; and since (b) such apportionment can be more conveniently provided for in the annual Supply Bill.
3. Because the said Bill defines the ends, purposes, conditions, limitation and qualifications to be established in respect of aids and supplies to be granted by this House,I and the same are not alterable by the Senate.
Im the first place, it is said we should not agree to the amendment because .substantially the same amendment has already been considered and rejected by the House. That is very true. Last year the same question arose, and the same difference of opinion existed between the House of Commons and the Senate. The House would not agree to the same amendment which was made by the Senate. This year the Senate does not agree to pass the Bill otherwise; and it comes down to this, that either one or the other must give way. Which should give way? Should the Senate give way to the House of Commons, or should the House of Commons give way to the Senate? Of couise, at some time or other, there will be an election upon this point, and it will be decided by the people; but in the meantime, what is to be done? If we are to be moved in this matter by the principles of reason which generally regulate the opinions of men, it seems to me that the House of Commons should give way to the Senate, because the weight of reason is altogether with the Upper Chamber and not with this Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
House. If there were any exception to be taken to the Senate's proposal, if the Government said that it was unfair, unjust or impracticable, then I could well understand the House of Commons saying:	We will
not give way, because wha.t we are isked '.o accept is not reasonable, just or fair. But, on the contrary, it is admitted that what is-asked by the Senate is so just, so fair and so reasonable that the (Government say:	We will act upon the very principle
which is embodied in this amendment. This amendment provides that the money to be devoted to the improvement of roads shall be applied in the different provinces according to population, and yet the Government say that they will not accept it. The refusal seems to be without any justification at all.
In their second reason, the Government merely say that the amendment is:
-unnecessary and undesirable, since the Supply Bill will make provision for the apportionment of the proposed subsidies to the respective provinces for the ensuing fiscal year.

No exception can be taken to this; it is very fair. But the Supply Bill is an annual Bill, and this, when it is passed, will be a permanent statute; and while this year the minister provides that the money shall be distributed according to population among the provinces there is nothing to prevent him next year providing that it shall be appropriated in a different manner. Since it is the intention of the minister that the money shall be apportioned among the provinces according to population, what reason can be given why that should not be provided for in the statute? The Minister of Railways will not contradict me when I say that pressure has been put on him from some quarters to

prevent a distribution according to population.
That is not true.

My hon.
friend should not say that.

There has been no

My hon.
friend should not say that, for if he has not, the Prime Minister has received applications-I	have received duplicates of
them-from the province of British Columbia, to the effect that the money should not be apportioned according to population, 'but that a larger proportion of it should be apportioned to British Columbia on the contention that the roads are more difficult of construction in that province than they are in any other. The minister has not been impressed by that argument, and I do not think there is anything in it; but still the pressure is there on the Government, if not on the Minister of Railways personally. The hon. minister heard last year a prominent member of the House, now Mr. Justice Lennox, suggest that the Government should not bind itself to have this money apportioned proportionately among the provinces, but that occasions might arise which might determine the Government to give a larger proportion to one province than to another. That being so, I can understand that the Minister of Railways, consciously or unconsciously-I will say unconsciously, because he says no pressure has been put upon him -has left the door open to the apportionment of the money next year differently from its apportionment this year. If it be not the intention to reserve the power to spend the money differently, then I ask the minister why he does not do as has been done under the provisions of the British North America Act, so that the provinces may know exactly, once and for all, what they are to expect, and be able to act accordingly? If we were to be guided simply by the good intentions of one party or the otner, as Detween man and man, there would be no necessity for courts of law or parliaments, for we could rely on a sense of fair play in every man as being sufficient. But it is because we cannot do so that we have courts of law and parliaments, and that is the reason why the Senate has thought it advisable that once and for ail, as soon as this law is passed, the conditions should be there to guide the Government in the application of it.
I pass on to another reason which is given by the Government why we should not agree to the Senate amendment:
Because such apportionment could be more conveniently provided for in the annual Supply Bill.	, .
l am at a loss to understand what this means. Why the apportionment should be made more conveniently in the annual Supply Bill than in this Bill, one cannot understand.
Another reason given why we should reject the Senate amendment is:
Because the said Bill defines the ends, purposes, conditions, limitations and qualifications to be established in .respect of aid and supplies to be granted by this House, and the same are not alterable by the Se,nate.
Well, the provisions of this Bill are alterable by the Senate, and for the very good reason that it has not been treated by the Government as a money Bill. Last year, as this year, this Bill was introduced without any message from His Royal Highness the Governor General, and when I raised the point of order that it was a money Bill, I was told it was not, and Mr. Speaker so ruled. Therefore, the Senate has properly treated it as not being a money Bill. But there is in this an argument which tells absolutely against the attitude taken by the Government. I will read it again:
Because the said Bill defines the ends, purposes, limitations and qualifications to be established in respect of aid and supplies to be granted by this House, and the same are not alterable by the 'Senate.
This Bill is alterable by the Senate. What is not alterable by the Senate is the Supply Bill. If next year or the year after the Supply Bill should contain a provision different from the provisions contained in the Supply Bill of this year, and should apportion the money to the provinces, not according to population, but according to what the minister believes to be the needs of one province as against another, the Senate would have to accept it without amendment, or to reject it entirely, which, of course, nobody would desire. Therefore! the very reason which the Government gives for rejecting the Senate amendment is a strong argument against the attitude taken by the Government.
Another amendment made by the Senate which has not been touched upon by the motion before the House, is the elimination of clauses from the Bill. Clause 6 reads:
6. The minister, with the approval of the Governor in Council and upon such terms and conditions as are prescribed by Order in Council, may undertake the construction of any new highway or bridges or the improvement of any existing highway or bridges in any province, and may expend in such improvement or construction the whole or any part of the sums voted by Parliament for such subsidy to that province: Provided, however, that the minister shall first obtain the necessary authority from the legislature of such province and the consent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council.



This means that the Minister of Railways contemplates going into highway building in the provinces, contemplates that he, having obtained authority from the legislature, and the consent of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, may build a highway in any one of the provinces. Without attributing any motive, but simply speaking from the rationale of the thing, what reason can be urged on behalf of the Department of Railways undertaking highway construction in any part of Canada? It is not in accordance with the fitness of things.
According to our constitution, the control of highways belongs to the provinces. In the older portions of the provinces, -where there is municipal organization, highway construction is carried on by the municipal authorities; but in those parts of the provinces where municipal organization has not yet been established, the provinces build the highways. The province of Ontario is a large builder of highways every year, so is the province of Quebec, and so with other provinces. Every province has a staff of engineers and others devoted to this work. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways has no such staff at h:s disposal, and if he goes into highway construction he must create a special branch of his department. In any case this work would not be permanent, but only occasional; and, not having permanent work to do the minister cannot- have a permanent staff. Therefore it goes without saying that the work had better be left to the provinces.
I cannot understand why my hon. friend should want to go into this work. It must be clear to him, on reflection, that he had better leave jt where it is, with the provinces. This matter has engaged the attention of the public at large, and especially of the municipal authorities. I moved, some time ago, for the correspondence between the Dominion Government and the provincial governments on this subject, but it has not yet been brought down. We may have it later on; I am satisfied there must have been correspondence between the Dominion Government -and at least some of the provincial governments on this subject. The legislature of Saskatchewan has passed a strong resolution on the subject, declaring that there should be a provincial conference to discuss with the Dominion authorities this whole matter. The Premier of the province of Quebec, Sir Lomer Gouin, gave an interview on this subject, in which he set forth his views in -a very temperate manner-views which, I think, should commend themselves to the House, and especially to the advisers of His Excellency. This interview appears in La Presse of Saturday, May 3, last. It is as follows:	.	., L
Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
It is to be regretted that the federal Gov-t eminent did not heed the suggestion to modify their proposed legislation.
_ The object of this Bil-l, as is well known, is to govern the manner in which the subsidies voted each year by Parliament for the improvement of highways generally are to be expended. It says that the federal Government may either grant a sum of money to any one of the provinces for the purpose of making, or improving certain highways; or spend, themseleves, the whole or part of the money for the above purposes, in the province.
In the first case, the province would have to have the work done under conditions and after plans approved of by the federal Government; in the second instance it would be necessary for the Government at Ottawa to obtain the consent of the provincial administration before any work was started.
I am an advocate of good roads and my greatest desire is to see our roadways improved as much as possible. The present legislation, however, is not satisfactory in my opinion, and to a certain extent dangerous. _
I say it is not satisfactory because there is no guarantee as to a fair repartition between the provinces of the money voted by* Parliament. It is true we have been told by the Government that according to the statute-book subsidies must be distributed among the provinces according to population, but, in my estimation, a clause to that effect would be more satisfactory. Governments are subject to change, and Mr. Borden's word would not bind another administration. Why should not the present Government do as the fathers of Confederation did? Why not do in connection with highways what has been done with respect to agriculture? This latter Bill provides that each province shall receive a stated sum; I do not understand why the same principle should not apply to the present measure.
I think it is dangerous in that it encroaches upon provincial rights and tends to reduce local administrations into bondage. Clause 92 of the constitution is very clear in this regard: ' In each province,' it says, ' the legislature may exclusively np-ake laws in relation to matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say,-	_
' 8. Municipal institutions in the provinces.
' JO. Local works a,nd undertakings of a local nature.
' 16. Generally all matters of local or private nature in the province.'
What then would be the position of the several provinces should this Bill pass the House in its present form? They would have to barter their rights and prerogatives fori the subsidy, or do without.
And, should we to-day allow the federal Government to interfere with the highways, they could, by means of similar grants, meddle with our school affairs and dictate to us a programme of studies and methods of teaching.
I do not want the impression to go abroad that I am antagonizing the Borden Administration. What I say to-day I would repeat to-morrow to any Liberal government that would introduce legislation so dangerous in>
character, and contrary to the spirit of thd

constitution. The vigorous stand which X made in 1905 upon the question of federal subsidies is well known. I am to-day as I was then, an advocate of provinical autonomy; the federal Government should respect our rights and give us full justice.
There is great force in these views, and I commend them to the House. There is one' thing noted there which is very remarkable. Two measures have been introduced this session to give aid to the provinces, one in agriculture and the other in highways.. The Bill to give aid to agriculture contained the provision that the grant should be apportioned among the provinces, and its distribution is made a part of the Bill. This provision _ is accepted by the Senate without criticism, and stands as law to-day. Why should not the same principle be introduced in this Bill? Why should the Government, introducing two measures absolutely similar in character and almost identical in purpose, discriminate as between one and the other? There is no possible reason for it so far as we have been informed, unless you suppose that behind it there are sinister motives and danger of far-reaching effects upon the elections. I do not wish to bring that consideration forward to-day; but, unless you give us 'better reasons than those given hitherto, we shall be forced to that conclusion.
