speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Bill simply provides two things:	in the first place, that the
Governor in Council may make a grant to the provinces, and, in the second place, that that grant shall be applied under certain agreements to be arrived at between the federal Government and the provincial governments. The money which is to be devoted to any one province cannot be diverted to any other province, and this House and the Senate will have perfect control over the situation when the appropriation comes to be made. I repeat again that the Senate would thus have as good control over that situation as they would have if this legislation were proposed by means of a Bill annually placed before Parliament. What was the object of the Bill? The object was to give to the various provinces of Canada, upon an equitable and just-basis, aid for the improvement of public highways. The Senate has not been content to accept the Bill as it was, but has attached to it a condition which we rejected last year, and which we are not disposed to accept this year, namely, that this House shall not be at liberty, even under the most exceptional circumstances, to make any deviation whatever from a strictly population basis. Suppose, for example, some great disaster occurred in one of the provinces, and that there was an urgent need in respect of that province that the population basis should be diverted from in some particular year. Is there any reason why that proposition should not be made and considered in the House of Commons and the Senate? I have expressed my strong opinion on two occasions in this House that this grant should be made upon a population basis, but my right hon. friend himself will admit that circumstances
Mr. BORDEN.
might arise under which he and every other hon. gentleman on that side of the House might agree that some deviation would have to be made from that basis in some particular instance. But if that did not commend itself to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, if it did not commend itself to Their Honours in the Senate, exactly the same remedy would be open to them as that which they have seen fit to exercise, in what I consider an unjustifiable manner, with regard to this Bill. In the one case they would be acting strictly within their rights; they would be rejecting the appropriation altogether because it did not commend itself to their judgment as being a just appropriation. In the other case they have gone beyond their constitutional rights and have seen fit to use their powers in violation of constitutional principles for the purpose of altering and changing the limitations and conditions which it is the undoubted prerogative of this House to establish.
As to the other amendment to which my right hon. friend alluded, and in respect of which the Minister of Railways and Canals will propose another motion in a moment,
I am equally unable to understand how the provision in the Bill interferes in the slightest degree with the autonomy of any province of Canada. I think it safeguards the autonomy of every province, even beyond the constitutional limits fixed by the British North America Act. I see no reason under the British North America Act why the Parliament of Canada might not undertake the construction of a road from one province to another. I see no reason under the British North America Act why the Parliament of Canada might not declare a particular road, running, for example, through the province of Quebec to its boundary line, to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. We could not do this under this Bill; we could not exercise even the powers that are conserved to us by the British North America Act, because it is distinctly provided in this Bill that under no circumstances shall the Governor in Council or the Minister of Railways and Canals spend one single dollar unless they have the authority of the provincial legislature and the consent of the provincial executive. We had this amendment under consideration last year; we have had it under consideration again this year on a motion of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. We did not see our way clear to accept it; and under the circumstances the motion which the Minister of Railways and Canals has proposed is the only motion which the Government, having regard to its self-respect, could present to this House, particularly in view of the fact that very offensive reasons were given by some speakers in the Senate in support of the modifications and amendments which they

proposed to this Bill. There was a direct suggestion from gentlemen there that it was the intention or desire of the Government to use this legislation for some corrupt ot unworthy purpose. That I think was the argument put up hy the leader of the Liberal party in the Senate as a reason why the Senate ought to amend the Bill in this way. I do not attach too much consideration to such an argument so emanating; but it is not to be expected that, when the action of the Senate is supposed to he based on arguments of that character, we should be very willing to accept them. We do not propose to accept them, and we propose to insist on this measure as it stands.

It
seems as if the history of this Parliament were going to resolve . itself to a large extent into a quarrel between the Government and the Upper Chamber of the Legislature, and, if so, I think it well for my part to intrude upon the House even at this very late hour >and to see that one member at least gets himself right on the quarrel to begin with. Up to now, Sir, history is rather on the side of the Senate. My right hon. friend, in the opening of the remarks which he has just made to the House, said that there was a clear issue as between the Senate and this Chamber on this particular measure, and proceeded to give as his reason for the clearness of that issue that the Senate ought to have been sure from the first that the Government would not accept an amendment which they refused to accept last year. Is my right hon. friend not presuming on the history of the dispute in assuming that that would be the correct finding of the Senate?
What was the main ground of the dispute between the Senate and the Government last year? It was not the Roads Bill, it was the Tariff Commission Bill. It was the Tariff Commission Bill which the Senate rejected, by which rejection they drew upon themselves an extraordinary diatribe from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) at the end of the session which produced an extraordinary scene in this Chamber, that is the call of three cheers for the Speaker, which were given in resounding fashion by a full assembly of hon. members opposite. What has happened to the Tariff Commission Bill? The Senate, according to the argument of my right hon. friend, had a right to expect that this Government were sincere or meant business in their quarrel with them on the Tariff Commission Bill, and they had a right to expect that the war which was declared in such vigorous terms by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on
that occasion would have been carried into the cojmtry. But what actually happened was that the Minister of Trade and Commerce disappeared from Canada and has been largely out of Canada ever since, and the Government of which he is so distinguished a member, _ has proved to the hilt the wisdom of the Senate on the Tariff Commission Bill, by not introducing the measure this year. I ask my right hon. friend what right he or anybody else has to expect the Senate to be so absolutely and confidently wise as to the motives and proceedings of this Administration. If we are to argue from last year, the Senate might reasonably have said to themselves: This Government, after all, is a somewhat imperfect Government but even they will improve with time, we have taught them something, combined with the efforts of Mr. Woodrow Wilson in the United States, about the effectiveness of a tariff commission, and they will probably learn wisdom on the question of roads also. That is my answer to my right hon. friend on the proposed clearness of this issue.
There was, as I pointed out, a great deal of unreality in the attack which was made upon the Senate last year and I am bound to say that there is a great deal of unreality too in the affection of the hon. gentlemen opposite and the Government they support for the people of this country, and the desire they have to improve their roads. If, at the bottom of their minds, their motives were to help the provinces in the matter of better roads, they would not hesitate to accept the amendments of the Senate. I do not hesitate to use that very strong language on this point.
Just think of what my right hon. friend has given as reasons for not accepting the amendments. One of his reasons is that certain members of the Senate have attributed unworthy motives to the Government. That is not an unusual procedure in politics. My experience of politics is that unworthy motives are being continually attributed by one side of politics or the other. Is that the way to approach the consideration of a matter of this importance? The question is are the Senate amendments right? If they are right, what would be the duty of the Government in regard to these suspicions? To say: We cannot accept a right amendment because unworthy motives have been attributed to us in connection with the Bill in the original form? So far from that being his duty, his duty is to disarm the suspicion held by the Senate and shared by some members on this side and held by a large number of people in this country. It is his duty to disarm the suspicion and to consider the amendments absolutely upon their merits.

The Senate would have been justified in amending this Bill, if for nothing else,	because	neither	we	nor	theynor anybody else can possibly know what	is the	object	of	the	Bill.
My right- hon. friend asked the question, what is the object of this Bill, and then, I quite admit, he gave his answer. He said it is to help the provinces in the construction of roads within the provinces. Now, that is all very well so far as it goes, but in the debates of last year an important supporter of my right hon. friend, who now occupies a seat upon a commission, the then member for Kootenay, dilated at considerable length upon the power that would be given under this Bill to construct a national highway from the Atlantic to the Pacific. That possibility in the measure has been referred to in the Senate itself by the leader of the Government in the UTV'er Chamber, so that we have this extraordinary position, that the Prime Minister suggested this afternoon that the object of the Bill is to help the construction of roads within the provinces, while the leader of the Government in the other HouBe referred to the possibility, under this Bill, of the construction of a national high vay across the whole country. The Govsrnment themselves do not know the object of the Bill, or if they do, they do not tell us, and they do not tell the Senate. In regard to the project of constructing a national highway, if that is the object of the Government, why do they not put it in the Bill? Why do they not state that that is their object? Let that project be debated on its merits, and I tell my right hon. friend that if he will take that course he will find that he has less support even from the Conservative provinces than he has at the present moment. It may be all very nice for people to travel from the Atlantic to the Pacific in automobiles, and to call at the city of Calgary, and have a good time there, but-the farmers who keep tire city of Calgary and a lot of people who are driving automobiles, and who want to get their grain and stock along decent roads to market, will not be very much interested in that kind of proceeding. What they want is help to make the roads in the provinces. I have had an experience in this connection. When I first came to this country my team used to stick three times regularly every day between my home and the railway station. That is where, as a farmer, I wanted a good road, and that is where the farmers want good roads. That is where the farmer had provision for good roads under the British North America Act, when, by the wisdom of the Imperial Parliament, the construction of roads was placed in the hands of the provincial legislatures, and not in the hands of the federal Government who now want to usurp Mr. CLARK (Red Deer).
[ that position. That is my comment upon what is said to be the object of my right hon. friend. If any other member of the Government can step in between the leader of the Government in this House, and the leader of the Government in the Upper House, and tell us what the Government mean to do, we shall be better able to give a reasonable decision on this question.
My right hon. friend resents very much the imputation of motives. Mr. -Gladstone once said that we should never impute motives, and as a counsel of -perfection it is very good. But can we expect my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) to reach that point of perfection? Be hints here that some minister in the present Government has used the proposed expenditures upon roads to influence public opinion. I understood him in that sense.
He promised expenditures under this Bill.

Then we are not interpreting motives, we -are witnessing actions. What is the good of my right hon. friend, who can put up a good argument when he has a good case, assuming this _ air of wounded virtue and objecting to his motives being impugned, when what he ought to do is to explain the actions of his * colleagues, and not concern himself with suspicions or motives. The Government ought to get themselves cleared up on this question. If they are a set of angels, let them produce fruits meet for repentance.
I do not want to say very much more on the subject. If there is no sinister motive, dispel that suspicion and accept the amendments of the Senate, and we shall have a chance of improved highways in Canada. It is a pity that we cannot arrive at an agreement on the subject at the present moment. The country is in a condition of very great peace after having fought imaginary Armageddons for five years. I propose that we should cut the battle of Armageddon out of the Book of Revelation, and proceed to produce the millennium in our own way. And one of the ways of getting a little bit of the millennium will be to improve the highways.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The Government can do
so, and at the same time establish some of that peace of the millennium and also peace between themselves and the other branch of the legislature on this particular subject. They can get to work at once instead of dangling this thing as something to be voted for by the people, and as something to use on platforms in condemnation of those who have criticised - it. I am not imagining this sort of thing. I have referred to the leader of the Government in

the Senate. His colleague in law practice is the representative of Calgary in this House, and the latter went to Calgary last fall and said that if the farmers were struggling with the difficulty of taking their grain to market, they should remember that this Bill for the improvement of highways went to the Senate and was never seen again.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend from Peterborough says, ' hear, hear.' He is just as accurate in his history as the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) was on the occasion to which I refer. It was necessary to say that the Bill was never seen again to prove that the Senate killed it. What did happen was that it was seen again ; it is being seen to-day in an amended form. It was not a case of homicide, it was a case of infanticide. If the Government have a good policy either upon highways, or upon anything else, let them produce it, and let them get the political credit that will always go to a Government that produces a good policy, and that helps the people. But do not let them have the suspicion hanging around that they want to get credit for the policy, when they intend to use the money spent under the policy for the benefit of heelers of their own party.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister spoke in very moderate terms. I would just like to say that while I accept his declaration that he means well under this arrangement, I do not think he is serious in asking us to accept his own intentions as being a guarantee for all time as to what would be done under this Bill, if it were passed in its present shape. He was surely hard up for an argument when he referred to the possibility of disaster as a justification of this Bill. If I understand him correctly, he said that a disaster might at any time destroy roads and might create an urgent need. The words were quite familiar to me. On the road question, the policy of the Prime Minister seems to be to introduce his permanent policy for the relief of an emergency. Surely my right hon. friend was not serious in giving that as his only justification for differing from the Senate on this question. I might use an argument that was used on the other side of the House in the debates which occupied so much of our time this winter. I might point out that in the case of an emergency we would always have the power to grant immediate relief. I borrow that argument from my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro). In the course of the debate, I asked my hon. friend a simple question about the possibilities in emergencies, and as to some explanation which I wanted to get in regard to the
policy of the Government on the naval question. I think I asked him whether one contribution constituted his sole idea as to Imperial federation, and the hon. gentleman gave me a speech on earthquakes. He spoke in terms of earthquakes. He said that if we had earthquakes we could contribute at once. I take the argument from the naval debate, and present it to my right hon. friend to soothe him in contemplation of the possibility of internal tempest in Canada. I am glad to withdraw his mind from the possibility of Imperial tempests, and to console him with the certainty that Canada will always be ready to deal with disaster. This is not a question of disaster. I do not think that argument carries you very f &r
I do not want to introduce anything of a very strong party flavour at this time, but my rigiht hon. -friend, if he is inclined to carry this dispute with the Senate to its legitimate outcome, must be prepared to submit it to the judgment of the people.
I felt sure that would be the case a little time ago and I felt sure of it when I heard the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) speak at the end of last session. I am sure that if he had been here now and if he had made another speech like that, following on the declarations which my right hon. friend made on various occasions in regard to anotner matter, we could not, in order to put an end to the embroglio that has arisen between the Senate and the House oi Commons, have avoided a general election. I give my right hon. friend credit for sincerity on that question of a general election. I am not inclined to taunt him with the non-fulfilment of all that he has given us by way of pledges on that question because I have said in this House before that holding an election, especially with a great Imperial issue in the balance, would be a questionable line of policy. Still, unless the Government will learn from the Senate, as they have already done on other matters, in the long run this question will go to the electors. I am sure that my right hon. friend, on personal grounds, would not altogether dislike the occasion. I know that he would be happier in many other positions than in his present one. I think I have read his mind and I have no doubt that he sometimes communes with himself and in the lines of Hamlet wonders. . . .
Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer
The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune,
Or to take up arms against a sea of troubles,
And by opposing end them.
I am sure he holds that kind of communion with himself; but if he does, there is another minister who is in a, different camp

Surely the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has not well considered some of his arguments. This Dominion Government cannot go into a province and make an agreement with that province by which they can override the municipalities, because the province cannot make an agreement of that kind. 'Then, where is his argument?
Look at the Bill.

That is not the point; the point is this: the provinces have no power to make an agreement which would override the rights of the municipalities, and, therefore the objection of the hon. member falls to the ground. The hon. gentleman knows very well that the Dominion Government could build roads from the Pacific to the Atlantic without this Bill, if they saw fit.
There is no doubt about that.

Very well. Then the hon. member tells us that this House can make the Bill good by accepting the amendment of the Senate, and my answer is that the Senate can make the Bill good by withdrawing its amendment. That argument, therefore, applies with equal force to both situations. The hon. gentleman tells us about his experience in South Renfrew, but he can well understand that the people of many sections of South Renfrew were made apt scholars on that question by the policy of the provincial Government, of which he was a member. That Government made plenty of promises as to roads.
That is not a very good answer.

It is a very good
answer, because it is the hon. gentleman himself and the Government to which he belonged in the province that made these apt pupils on the road question. The people were told time and again, by that provincial government, that they would get roads in South Renfrew if they sent such and such a man to Parliament. That was what was taught the people of Ontario by the Liberal Government for twenty-three years, and it is time the hon. gentleman should get some^ of his own medicine; he should not complain. The hon. gentleman complained that this Bill would lead to the exercise of political influence by the Dominion Government, but the proposal of the Senate increases the political influence by handing it out to the various provinces to use it. Legislation generally is intended not to keep people from doing right, but to keep people from doing wrong, and the argument of the hon. gentleman in this instance is to the effect that people should be kept from doing right. The relations between the Dominion and the provinces, and their rights constitutionally, are to some extent a matter of growth, rather than a matter of law, because necessity must have its way in dealing with all these great questions, and we know that the provinces have dealt with the road questions ever since 1843, and yet the complaint of the whole country is that we have not good roads. Is it not time some other authority had

something to say in helping the people to get good roads?	_
A great deal is said about provincial autonomy and all that kind of thing; but I say that the people want good roads, and the proposal of this Government is to help the provinces to give the people good roads, and that is the question that is before the people and not the constitutional issue. It is a question of doing what the people require to be done in the public interest, and yet hon. gentlemen opposite see fit, through the action of the upper House-the same political blood runs through the veins of the gentlemen opposite in this House, although it may be a little more lively; it is the same breeding and the same everything-and they are afraid something will be done for the people. That is what is troubling them, but I am not afraid of that. I would be glad to see something done for the people, and I do not care particularly who does it, so long as it is done. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen opposite to suspect the intentions of the Government, but they would have a much stronger case if they let the Government go on-but they have not the courage to do that-and then attack them if they do wrong. It is time we did something to improve the roads in this country. Take France, with its 18,000 miies of municipal roads. My hon. friend from Red Deer is very much afraid of an automobile going through his country.

I am afraid
of my wagon sticking.

Very well; if you run
behind the wagon you will be perfectly safe.
I keep my dogs there.

New York State has had some experience with automobiles, and the taxes on the automobiles maintain the roads. That would not be a bad idea for this country to adopt. I do not care how many wealthy men from the States or anywhere else come through Canada over good roads, because I look upon them as a splendid advertisement of what this country is and what its prospects are. It would be a good thing for the poorest man in the country to have automobiles coming here and, wealthy men in them. I am not going to quarrel *vs'ith my neighbour because he is rich; if all my neighbours were rich there would be a better chance for me. I don't want a man to be so shaken up on our roads that he will be profane before he ends the journey. I would rather have him travel over a good road. I am not afraid of automobiles nor of good roads. I do not think it would be wrong to have some leading roads of distinctive character in this country; on the contrary, it would be Mr. BRODER.
a good thing. I believe the Senate has made a mistake. The people of this country realize that it is time this question had a chance to be tried, and let the results either commend or condemn those who are responsible for carrying the idea into effect.

Just a word or two in reply to the Iron, member for Welland (Mr. German). It seems to me extremely unfortunate for the country at large that a great scheme that means so much to the farming community should be kept in abeyance because the members of this Parliament who sit on the other side oi the House and form the majority in the Senate have not sufficient confidence in the honesty and integrity of this Administration to believe that money appropriated in the' manner proposed will be fairly and properly spent for the improvement of highways in the several provinces?
I listened with considerable interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark). Before I came to this House I had followed that hon. gentleman's record with considerable interest. I looked upon him as a radical of the radicals. I
had heard him humourously termed ' Red Michael,' and, as I was somewhat the same complexion myself and had often had my attention drawn to the attributes that the word ' red ' seemed to impute, I expected to find in the hon. gentleman a vehement, fiery man, with the courage of his convictions. But since I have had the honour of a seat in the House, my views of the hon. gentleman have entirely changed. I have almost reached the conviction that he and I should change positions, that I should go over to the Liberal party and that he should sit among the Conservatives. The ex-Radical has become a most extreme Conservative. He supports an Upper House in everything. Whether it be a navy question, on which I give him credit for having strong constitutional views; or a banking act. of which he frankly admits he knows nothing; or a question of roads, of which, he says, he knows something-in every case he supports the Upper House against the House elected directlv by the neople. To summarize the whole question,-and these are the conclusions expressed by the people I represent,-we want good roads in Ontario, more particularly in eastern Ontario, and eastern Ontario welcomed the news that the Dominion would contribute a sum for the construction of these roads. It may not be known to hon. gentlemen opposite-it is to the member} who come from Ontario-that the eastern part of Ontario has not the electric service that the western part of the province has, because electric power is so expensive that it is impossible profitably to operate electric roads. It is equally true that during the regime of the late Administration, in the Government of which the late Minister of Railways and Canals had a portfolio, it was charged that in a good many instances the road money of the province of Ontario was improperly spent. I am not going to say whether or not those charges were correct; it is an unfortunate thing in public life to-day that in the administration of public money those who are dissatisfied with its expenditure are always ready and willing to say unpleasant things about those who have the spending of the money. But so long as governments are governments, and men are men, I suppose governments will spend the money where they think the best advantage will come to their party without shocking public conscience. In other words, they will deal fairly with the people, but more or less with the idea of serving their own interests.
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for Rouville says, ' hear, hear.' I am speaking frankly, as I understand this matter, and I want the House to understand me.

I admit that governments are frail. I believe that this is a big issue and that the people of the country want better roads. I think this House and the Senate should rise above the partisan considerations which are allowed to crush out such a beneficial measure simply because they have a dread that something may be improperly done. The right hon. leader of the Opposition frankly tells us, as does the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, that the principle that should _ underlie these appropriations should be distributed upon a population basis. This is the difference between the two parties; the Conservative party says: we are going to spend the money ourselves; the Liberal party and their friends in the Senate say: you are not going to do anything of the sort; we are afraid you will spend the money in a corrupt manner. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) admits that the Minister of Railways and Canals is honest and straight-forward, and that this measure will be carried out without favour and without graft. If he believes what he says, why does he not rise above those partisan considerations that seem to influence him and his party and vote for this Bill ? If in the working out of the measure it is true that the Minister of Railways and Canals is not such a man as the hon. member for Welland represents him to be, then I say it is time, when the estimates come down in another year, for the members of the Opposition to refuse the money and to hold the Government to account.

That was
proved in Renfrew.

What was proved?
Si,- WILFRID LAURIER: That the Bill might be used for corrupt purposes.
It may have been proved in Renfrew; I should not be surprised if it was, because than the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals there is no better exponent of such a policy.
We should not expose the Minister of Railways to temptation.

I have always believed
that it is easier to avoid temptation than to resist it, but I believe that men are sometimes big enough to resist temptation and not avoid it. For that reason I think the members of the Opposition should give the Government an opportunity of carrying out a policy that means so much to the farming communities of this country.

I.understand that some reference was made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) to certain assertions I made in reference to the Highways Bill last year. I did observe that this Bill was of importance to the prov-Mr. NICKLE.
ince in which I reside, and I desire to repeat that I consider this Bill to be of paramount importance to the people of Alberta. I ventured the other evening to point out that the question of good roads was more important to the people of Alberta in one respect than freight rates, and I have since learned that on account of the bad condition of the highways the residents of one of the most fertile portions of the province, namely the Milk River district, had to pay last year the exorbitant sum of thirty-five cents a bushel to have their crops carried, by tender, if you will, from the farms to the railway stations. This Government entered upon a comprehensive scheme in relation to the improvement of highways. The Prime Minister of this country promised that if he were elected to power he would endeavour to improve the highways of western Canada. Sitting upon the same platform with him in the city of Calgary, I heard him make that promise to the electors of that city, and last fall when I held my annual meeting with my constituents I directed their attention to the fact that this Government implemented more of its pre-election promises in one session than any government that had ever held power since Confederation. I pointed out that the will of the people and of this Government had been thwarted by the Senate, and that the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition had said from his place in this House that he desired to associate himself with the Senate in its action in thus thwarting the will of the people last session. I understand that the hon. member for Red Deer has taken exception to the remarks I made on that occasion. I desire here and now, as I did then and there, to repeat that this House has passed a certain Bill based upon a recognition of the necessity of having good highways, not from a narrow provincial standpoint, but upon the principle of encouraging good highways as a national asset in Canada, and that it ill becomes the Senate of Canada, representing no people, at variance with the very spirit of democracy, to tnwart the will of the people. I did point out to the people of the constituency I have the honour to represent, and my remarks have been criticised by the hon. gentleman whose professions are radical and principles Conservative, whose free trade ideas find expression only in a desire to build up a protective-battleship industry in this country, and who is always ready and willing, at *any excuse, although he as never able to manufacture a reasonable one, to follow the behests of his party, wherever it may lead him. That is his history since he has come to western Canada, and I suppose it will be his history until he goes down to immortal fame as the great prototype of that school of thought which has no followers in this Dominion. I say frankly that any gentleman who comes

into this Parliament with one eye on the press gallery and the other upon 'Hansard' cannot expect very great consideration at the hands of any member who desires to see the will of democracy expressed.
There is behind this Bill a great and abiding principle, and it is this: shall the will of democracy be thwarted and destroyed by an irresponsible body of men sitting in another chamber? This Government came into power with a mandate from the people to develop a system of national highways; this Parliament has passed a Bill on two occasions for the encouragement and development of national highways, not limited to one province, applicable equally to the provinces of the East and the provinces of the West, and the will of this Parliament is being thwarted to-day, as it wTas last year, by an irresponsible Senate. It is time that the Senate was reformed. For more than fifteen long years in western Canada we heard shrieks and cries about reforming the Senate. The Senate has been reformed by the right hon. gentleman opposite to such an extent that they now echo his opposition in this House of Commons to the will of democracy. That is his idea of reforming the Senate, and the people of western Canada are getting sick and tired and weary of it. In the province from which I come they desire to see the Highway Bill passed and an appreciation of national necessity given effect to. I say that the people of western Canada and of the province in which I live will hold the right hon. gentleman and his hollow echoers in another chamber, responsible for their conduct in rejecting this Bill which has been passed by the will of the people of this country. The right hon. gentleman may throw up his hands and say; Quite so-; I am proud of them. When I point out these facts to an audience in the province from which I come, I am told that it was the House of Commons and not the Senate that killed the Bill. It is a reflection upon the intelligence of the people of this country to say that it was the Commons that killed the Bill. Is the will of democracy to be set, aside for the will of the minority? Is this Government to bow to the will of the minority because they have a hollow echo in another Chamber where there is a Liberal majority? That is the position, and yet a man of the intelligence of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) stands up to the people of Calgary and tells them it was not the Senate that killed the Bill, that it was the Conservative party in the Commons that killed the Bill, and he expects the people to take any stock in such an argument. Is it any wonder that the people laughed and jeered at any such thought? They appreciate to the full just what it means.
In the province in which I live any
arrrangement that might be made for the use of this money would have to be made with a Liberal Government and not a Conservative Government. It is true that during the last few months the money of the people has been squandered for election purposes in Alberta. It is true that one hundred men brought in from outside carried a seat for a minister in the very district in which the hon. member for Re'd Deer lives. It is true that an Alberta telephone gang made it possible for Duncan Marshall to be elected Minister of Agriculture. It is true that an employee of the Department of Public Works of Alberta, working upon the highways, has been committed for trial and must stand his trial before the Supreme Court of Alberta for intimidation of electors in connection with the roads and highways of the province of Alberta. His name is Lawler. He was committed at Clyde. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) might tell the House something about that, because his journal made a fitting reference to it.
I presume that Lawler was from Manitoba.

No, he lives in Alberta, and in the recent election there was not a man from outside of Alberta who came into that province on the Conservative side, but the province was filled with heelers from Saskatchewan and Manitoba on the Liberal side. I could give the names if the hon. member for Edmonton would like to have them.

As my hon. friend is so far out of order in dealing with the subject -of the elections in Alberta, he might just as well go on and give us the names. For my part, I would be very glad to have them.
If this House has time to spend in that sort of entertainment let us have all the names my hon. friend has in regard to the elections in Alberta.

If my hon. friend wishes to raise the point of order, and at the same time insinuate that I wish to delay the business of the House, perhaps I should not deal with the election. I have the evidence and the papers-
Let the House have the benefit of them.
They are in my desk upstairs, and I can get them in a few moments.
The hon. gentleman has brought this matter to the attention of the House; let him give the information.

I will give the information briefly. There is a constituency in Alberta called Clearwater. It sends to the legislature, thanks to the gerrymander of a Liberal Government, one member. Its

total voting number is forty-seven. That is Liberalism rampant in Alberta, that is the Liberalism that has the sign manual of the approval of the hon. member for Edmonton placed upon it. It is true that there are little dissensions as to his giving it the imprimateur of his approval. The Attorney General has a little doubt as to the political morality of the hon. gentleman for Edmonton and I understand that the hon. member for Edmonton has some doubt as to the political morality of the Attorney General. But between them they devised a constituency at Clearwater with a voting population of forty-seven. At the recent election in that constituency there were three candidates, McKenny the Government candidate, Taylor the Conservative candidate, and Joseph Clark, who wrote a letter to the Liberal party, another candidate. These three gentlemen together polled forty-seven votes. When the votes were counted, unfortunately it was found that some of them were tied up in envelopes. But in this instance they were not able to steal them as in two other constituencies, about which perhaps hon. gentlemen would like to hear-
Thank you.
-by men who were brought before a judge at Medicine Hat.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member is going very far from the subject of the motion before the Chair.

Thank you. I should not have trespassed on the time of the House, but I wished to point out that in the constituency of Clearwater a hireling of the local Government named Lawlor, sent there as an election agent of McKenny to improve the highways, is now standing trial before the Supreme Court for intimidating electors in connection with highways. It is with this Liberal Government that we would have to negotiate in connection with the expenditure of public money on highways. But we are told that the Senate has decided that this cannot be done-that even that brand of Liberals cannot be trusted.
I summarize the matter in this way. This Government promised the people of western Canada that it would pass legislation that would enable it to devote federal money to improve the national highway system of western Canada. That was said by all parties to be absolutely essential and necessary. This Government came into power on a mandate from the people to carry out their pre-election promises. They did so last session. They placed this Bill on the statute book. The Bill was killed by the Senate. The Liberal party desired to associate itself with the Senate's action. This session the Bill was reintro-Mr. BENNETT (Calgary).
duced and repassed. The Senate has again destroyed it, and again the Liberal party in this House desires to associate itself with the Senate in destroying this Bill and preventing the people of western Canada from getting some measure of relief, because it would afford us some measure of relief; and the thirty-five cents a bushel that we have to pay to transport wheat from the farm to the railway must continue, because a discredited minority are able to get in another Chamber an echo of their voice, and thwart the will of these people. I protest on behalf of the few farmers in my constituency, because it is largely city, against the action of this minority, for we all know that one word from the right hon. gentleman opposite and his servile majority in the Senate would obey his behest and do what he asks them to do.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member ought to take back the words ' servile majority.'

I shall withdraw the
words ' servile ' and say ' willing.'

The hon.
member has no right to say that. The majority in the Senate is quite independent, and can act for itself.

They have not shown
any sign of it.

I
do not intend to traverse at any great length the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett, Calgary) in regard to the elections in Alberta, but as you have been good enough to allow him to take the latitude he has taken I hope I may be permitted to take, let us say, measurable longitude. My hon. friend has drawn attention to a case in which a man who happened to be employed by the Government of Alberta in road work has been brought into court for improper practices in the elections. 1 am at a loss to understand in what way that fact and that result, so far as it has gone, is any reflection upon the Liberal Government of Alberta. I call my hon. friend's attention and the attention of the House to the fact that in the province of Manitoba elections do not go that -way. Where a Conservative Government is in power the man who votes against that Government is lucky if he is able to keep out of jail without any question of law.

I cannot allow my hon. friend to to make such a statement. Time after time insinuations of this kind have been made in this House. I want to say here and now that there was no man arrested in Manitoba who was not known to the officers oi the law of that province as being a political crook of long standing.

The House will observe
that as soon as what by courtesy we may call the argument made by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) is turned back on his friends on that side of the House, it produces what would be vulgarly called a roar. We do not have to find fault with such talk as my hon. friend from Calgary puts up. It is absurd, and everybody knows it, but when we return the compliment, it produces a response from that side because it is true and everybody knows it. When my hon. friend says that the men who were arrested in Manitoba, put in jail without trial, and kept there unwarrantably were known to be crooks, may I be permitted to say, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend has made a statement that he knows is not true.
Order, order.
It is absolutely true.

speechtext:

A young man of the name of Prince, horn in St. Boniface, Manitoba, where his parents reside, employed in a law office, engaged in the study of law in Winnipeg, who, I do not think, is more than 21 years of age, and who cannot by any possibility have had any serious connection with any previous elections in Man- .

Because he was too young.

friend knows that lots of his own friends who are not more than 18 or 20 years of age, have a great deal to do with elections.

language, as Prince himself is, and he was shadowed immediately by the hirelings of the Government of Manitoba, by leeches-
Red line leeches.

-who are eating up the revenues of the province of Manitoba, who are part of the standing army of election thugs kept up out of the treasury of the province of Manitoba, under the able administration with which the Minister of Public Works was connected.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it would be well for the hon. gentleman to direct his attention to the motion before the House.

I shall be very glad to do so: but since my hon. friend from Calgary introduced matter that was so absolutely foreign to the question under consideration, and used such intemperate and unwarranted language, I thought it would not be out of place to see if the rule would work the other way.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understood the interference or allegation to be that this money might be used improperly in connection with the expenditure on roads, and that the hon. member for Calgary gave an illustration from another source of how that was being done. But the hon. gentleman is directing his attention to an election in Manitoba, which does not seem to me to have the same relevancy.

I thought the point my
non. friend from Calgary was trying to make was that because the Government of Alberta was Liberal, therefore it was crooked.

Mr. Lawler
was doing road work, and it was in connection with the intimidation of the voters of Clearwater that he was sent up for trial. The Liberal Government of Alberta now declines to prosecute him. equal that.	.

My hon. friend brings out very clearly the point I thought he was trying to make, that because the Government of Alberta was & Liberal Government, therefore it was not to be trusted with the management of public affairs, and particularly with the control of road money. And more than they want.

Perhaps a little more
than they want. In regard to the matter under consideration, I desire to say that the Government of Alberta builds the roads of that province directly as a Government work, and the people of Alberta believe that that Government is able to do, and as a matter of fact does, good work, and renders a satisfactory return for the money spent on the roads in that province. If my hon. friend from Calgary wants any evidence on that point, I refer him to the elections in which he took such a distinguished part, and as the result of which the Alberta Government have a majority of something like two to one.
Over fifty per cent of the electors voted against them.
Like the election of 1911.

That may or may not be correct, but, to use an argument made use of repeatedly by our friends on the other side of the House, the Government of Alberta represents a majority in the legislature., and is therefore entitled to the con-trolJof the affairs of that province. Perhaps my hon. friend considers he has had sufficient on this subject of the Alberta elections, because if he does not, we can give him plenty more.

I would be delighted to have an hour or two with my hon. friend on the evidence I have.
Mr. OLIVER. My hon. friend chooses this time and place when he knows it is not convenient to take time, and when he knows he has the protection of the Chair in maintaining decorum in this House. But when he was in Calgary, he hired a bunch of thugs to put up the arguments which he himself was afraid to put up.

I must rise to a point of order. My hon. friend has surely had enough of that. I desire to say with reference to the men to whom he refers, that I did not know they were there. They were a few ex-soldiers and ex-sailors who resented the action of the hon. gentleman in sitting when the National Anthem was sung.

Mr. OLIVER.
