speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. member (Mr. Oliver) should direct his attention to the question before the House.

I am desirous of doing so, but I am sure you will recognize, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Calgary has interrupted me repeatedly and unjustifiably, and I am merely replying to his interruptions. I have no wish to diverge from the subject under discussion, but I ask not to be interrupted if I am not to be permitted to diverge. What I was trying to establish was that the province of Alberta, discharging its responsibility to the people in the matter of the construction of roads, is doing so in conformity with the constitution of Canada and in conformity with the will of the people, and that when this Parliament undertakes, by legislation that has been passed through Parliament by the will of the majority, to say that this Government knows better how to build roads in Alberta than the Government of Alberta, I disagree absolutely. I will suggest that if the Government of Canada as at present constituted, will attend properly and well to the business of the Dominion under its jurisdiction under the terms of the British North America Act it will find all it can manage satisfactorily, all that is within the compass of its ability to manage, and it will do well to leave to the provinces of Canada that which is specially their business, just as, might I suggest, it will do equally well to leave to the Government of the United Kingdom that which is particularly the business of that Government. This Government is spreading itself a little farther than its merits warrant when it undertakes to deal with matters which are properly the business of the Government and Parliament of the United Kingdom, and equally to interfere with that which is especially the business of the various provinces or Canada.

Did you not do it
when you were in office?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

The hon. gentleman remembers that when he was in power, he

constructed in my own county twenty-one miles of road with money out of the Dominion treasury.
Sure.
Did you interfere with the duties of the province?

No. At that time and up to the present time this Government would not be interfering with the activities of that province by building roads in Manitoba. I must admit that I -was speaking of the province of Alberta. The interference contemplated by this Bill, if exercised in the province of Alberta, would be unwarranted, injurious and unacceptable to the people of Alberta. I know that the Manitoba people want roads, that they want them very much, that they could not get them from the provincial government, and that they would be glad to get them from anybody.
It was because they did not have the money.

They did not have the money. When this Government has, under existing conditions, a revenue greater than the absolute needs of the country require, I consider that the provinces have a right to share in that money. Just as the revenues of the Dominion grow, so the needs of the provincial governments grow, and it is right and proper that the Dominion Government should make provision out of its increased revenues to meet the increased needs of the several provinces. In so far as this measure deals with that condition, I am prepared to support it, and the amendment of the Senate is exactly the provision that will compel it to meet the case. What we want, and all we want, is that when this Government has money that it can afford to devote to the building of roads, it shall give that money to the legislatures of the different provinces in proportion to their population, to be spent by their governments as the people of these provinces see fit. It seems to me that is a fair and reasonable pronosition, and that it is the only fair and reasonable proposition. It is not fair or right that when this Government has a large surplus it should be allowed to devote that surplus, or a share of it, to purely provincial purposes, except according to the principles of the British North America Act applicable to the division of Dominion moneys among the provinces. That is the only way that it should be allowed to deal with the question. It is able to deal with it under the Senate amendment to this Bill, and I want to say that, in so far as the province of Alberta is concerned-and there is already before the Government a memorial from the province of Saskatchewan on the same
point-they object absolutely to the Government of Canada interfering with that which is their special business and which they can discharge with greater advantage to their province than can this Government.

I would like to add one word; and the hon. member for 'Calgary (Mr. Bennett) will pardon me if I do not enter into the merits or demerits of the provincial elections in the part of the country from which he comes. We in our province carry on our elections in an honest way, and we are always somewhat shocked and sorry to hear of such things as happened out in Macdonald in the province of the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), or has happened in the province of Alberta. I hope that the people in certain portions of Manitoba and Alberta will be the better for the argument that has taken place on both sides of the House to-day in reference to provincial elections in those provinces.
But what I wanted to point out, Mr. Speaker, was that when the hon. member for Calgary u*ir. Bennett) made the statement that the Senate killed the Bill, which stands upon the Order Paper as an ' Act to Improve the Highways of Canada,' he said something which was altogether wrong. The Senate has simply amended it in line with the spirit of the British North America Act. Section 118 of the British North America Act, with respect to grants to the provinces, states that the sums therein stipulated shall be paid annually in aid of the provinces at a rate equal to eighty cents per head of the population as ascertained by the census of 1861, and in the case of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, by each subsequent decennial census until the population of each of those two provinces amounts to 400,000 souls, at which rate such grant shall thereafter remain. Grants to the provinces are made, according to the British North America Act, in proportion to population. It seems to me that the amendment is altogether in keeping with the spirit of the British North America Act, and that when the Senate enacted that the constitution should be lived up to, it did not kill the Bill, but it amended it in such a way that the House of Commons ought to accept the amendment. If the Government assume the responsibility of refusing to concur in the amendments made by the Senate, they absolutely and emphatically kill the Highways Bill, because the amendment is a constitutional amendment; the money will be spent for the roads in the provinces and by the provinces. When the Senate amended the Bank Act, the Government accepted the amendments and passed the Bill in this House as



amended. It would be just as reasonable to saw that the Senate killed the Bank Act by its amendment, as to say the Senate killed the Highways Bill by the amendment they made to it. I assume the full responsibility for the words I may have uttered in regard to the Highways Bill, and when we go before the people, as we must go sooner or later, and I hope it will be soon, the Ministry must assume full responsibility for having killed their own creature, if they refuse to aeeept the Senate amendments to the Highways Bill.

The position of affairs with regard to this Bill has been distorted by hon. gentlemen opposite in the House and outside the House. It is evident the Government does not want to pass a Bill through this Parliament, to provide for highway construction in this country. The course adopted by the Government in the last two sessions shows to any unprejudiced mind, that their desire is to masquerade before the people of this country as anxious to assist highway construction, when really they do not want to do anything of the kind.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman is going too far.
In what way?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not permissible to impute improper motives to any member of the House.

I have said that the Government of this country do not want to have this measure passed, and the language I used was but an amplification of that idea. If hon. members are not permitted to make a statement with regard to the course of the Government upon a public question, which has been already so curtailed in this House, the freedom of debate will be once more further curtailed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I do not think
the hon. member has the right to criticise the ruling of the Chair. I referred to the well-known rule laid down -by almost every Speaker of the British House of Commons, that it is not permissible to impute improper motives to- any member of the House. If the statement of the hon. member, that there is no desire to- pass the Bill except for masquerading purposes, -is not imputing an improper motive, then I cannot understand what would be.

The language you
have just used, Mr. Speaker, is not the language which I used. What I stated to the House, and what I am prepared to reiterate, is, that the Government did not desire to have this Bill passed; that they are holding ont to the country that they Mr. DEVLIN.
do desire t-o- pass it when, -as a matter of fact, they do not. I think that is parliamentary. It is not imputing improper motives; it is a description of the position of one political party, which I have aright to -criticise as I have done. The fact is that the Government came to the House last year and said: We want to assist the provinces to construct highways; and they repudiated any idea of being anxious to proceed with the construction of highways themselves. The minister declared that the money to be devoted to this purpose would be divided among the provinces according to population. When the Bill came down, there were clauses that would indicate that that was th-e desire of the Government; but there was clause 6, which enabled the Government to arrogate to themselves the expenditure of this money, if they desired to do so. There is where the difficulty is.

It could not be done
without the consent o-f the province.

Quite so. The minister recognizes the constitutionality of the right of the province to be the sole authority to control the highways, but clause 6 enables the Government, if they found a province that was willing to give in to them, to take the right to themselves to expend the money in that province.
The Prime Minister told us they were dividing this money according to population in -the Supply Bill, and when he did so he admitted the constitutionality of the contention of the Opposition; he admitted the sole right of the provinces to deal with this matter. He wants to have clause 6 in the Bill for some particular reason. Last year when the Senate held that the Dominion should not retain that right to -expend the money, and that the Bill was not in accordance with the avowed purpose of the Government, and undertook to reform the Bill in accordance with the avowe-d intention of the Government, the Government threw out the measure. Then the gentlemen opposite went up and down the country talking about the terrible Senate and the terrible Grits who would not allow them to do anything for the highways of this -country.
Hear, hear.

The gentleman who says: 'hear, hear,' thinks they were able to pull the legs of the unsuspecting voters by such guff as that. This year the Government -comes along with the same Bill, asserting before high Heaven their desire to observe the constitution, and their leader asks Parliament to recognize his -sincerity, because he has put in the estimates an amount to be voted to each province. But. again, there is in the Bill this unconstitutional clause 6 for the purpose of enabling

them to control the expenditure of the money in certain cases. Then, when the Senate does what it did last year, and reforms the Bill in accordance with the expressed views of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Eailways, the farce is again gone through of declaiming against the Senate because they have inserted the very stipulation which the Government themselves say they want in the Bill. The Conservative party are pretending they want to assist the provincial governments of this country to have improved highways; but in the Senate and elsewhere the leaders of the Conservative party speak about a great highway for automobiles that is to run from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Their idea is that the expenditure under the direction of the Minister of Eailways will he on some highway intended to provide for automobile people going from province to province. They did not desire to help the farmers of the West, those constituents of my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) for whose interest his heart bleeds every hour of the day-in imagination. The Government does not intend to do anything for these people, nor do they intend to do anything for the farmers of eastern Canada. No such notion actuates any hon. gentleman in regard to this question. In the back districts of South Eenfrew, my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) has shown, and all over this country, there are a lot of political heelers watching this section 6. They want it to go into effect. They had visions of inducing the Minister of Eailways, through the patronage dispensers in the several constituencies, to divert to their use quantities of road money which would he very useful in their business if the Government goes to the country. That is the view of the Government in regard to highway improvement. On the other hand, our position is this: For the last forty-six years' the improvement of the highways of the country has been carried on by the provincial governments. Every provincial government has a department dealing with this question-organization perfected, information collected, laws adjusted, so that the highways can be best improved in the different provinces according to their varying traditions.
We say, therefore, give this money to the provinces and let them spend it in accordance with their several policies; let the thing be done in accordance with the principle that had been manitained for the last forty-six years of governmental life in this country. Let us have this work of highway improvement really carried on. The Senate said last year that they wanted to have highway improvement, and wanted to have this money go to the provinces. The Senate say this year the same thing-they want this done in work carried on in a constitutional way. But the Government, by this
379i
motion, negative that proposition; they say they do not want tne highways improved or the money to go to the provinces. There is the difference between the two parties. Some hon. members on the other side have suggested that hon. gentlemen on this side are worrying about the question of responsibility. I desire to say that I assume full responsibility for my attitude on this question. I am prepared to go to my province and say to the people that if this Government want to make laws, they should make them in accordance with their declared intentions in Parliament. The laws of this country ought not to be left to be interpreted according to the vagaries of a Minister of Eailways and Canals, or the theories of a Prime Minister; our laws should be written documents and should mean what they say. I am prepared to say to the people of my province that the Senate have done that which is in the interests of the people of the country. I am prepared to show that the only method by which the federal Government can assist the improvement of highways is that which we propose, and to point out the fact, indisputable before any audience in Parliament or out of it, that the Government does not want to assist highway construction and is only pretending to do so in order to mislead the people.

I desire to call the attention of the hon. member to statements which he has made, which I believe are out of order. The decisions of Denison-and they are practically the same as the decisions of Peel-declare that it is out of order to impute unworthy motives to members of the House or to the Government collectively. If it is not imputing unworthy motives to say that the Government are not sincere and do not mean what they say, I do not understand the force of English words.

It would naturally occur to one that, if these statements of my hon. friend from Pictou are out of order, it would be quite proper for the Prime Minister to take objection to them. But it is most remarkable- that every member of the Government can sit there and listen to these statements. There must be something in them, or we should hear some objection from these hon. gentlemen. I am not going to take up more than a moment or two, but I do not feel like giving a silent vote on a matter of such great importance. I am like the hon. member for Pictou-I take full responsibility for my conduct in regard to this matter. I hope there may be an opportunity to vote against the Government .and the course they are pursuing. My'hon. friend the Minister of Eailways made the positive statement introducing this legislation last year, and again this year, that it was his

intention that this money should be distributed to the provinces in proportion to their population. But the Prime Minister this afternoon gave an entirely different version of it. True, he attempted to argue by saying that there might be a calamity in one portion of the country, and if so you must come to their assistance. But how are you going to come to the assistance of one portion of the country except at the expense of another? How are you going to give the province of Ontario $100,000 more than they are entitled to without taking that sum from the other provinces, or else increasing the grant? Why, you have there a confession from the Prime Minister himself. I do not know whether you will charge me with imputing motives, Mr. Speaker-I am simply stating facts And I think the merest neophyte in public affairs can draw the inference very readily.
Then, if that were not enough, you have the statement by another member of the Government in another Chamber that the intention of the Government was to build a highway, an automobile road, from ocean to ocean. If that is the intention, Why do not these hon. gentlemen come down and say so?
Who said that?

Hon. Mr. Lougheed in
the Senate. And that statement is absolutely inconsistent with the statements made on behalf of the Government in this House, for it would take more to build the portion of such a road that would run through Ontario in proportion to the population of the province than to build the part running through Nova Scotia. If that member of the Government is right, then the members of the Government in this House are wrong. I would suggest that it would be better for them to get together and compare notes. I make this statement regardless of whether it is imputing motives or not-I do not believe the Government intend in future years to divide this money among the provinces according to population. Any citizen of Canada who will read this amendment and the report of this discussion must come to the conclusion, especially from the lame defence of the Prime Minister this afternoon, that they do not intend in the future to divide this money according to population, but merely to do so this year and next year to divide it as they please. If they intend to divide the money according to population and to hand it over to the provinces to handle, they would agree to the elimination of this section 6.

A week ago this .House voted $1,410,000 for dredging in the maritime provinces. That is a vote for the maritime provinces generally, and all that money is expended under the direction of the Minister of Public Mr. CARVELL
Works. For the whole of Canada over three and a half millions is voted this session by this House for dredging, all to be expended under the direction of the Minister of Public Works. There was no man in this House who imputed improper motives to the Government in that. The whole of it may be given to New Brunswick, to Nova Scotia, or to Prince Edward Island; it is altogether in the hands of the minister. It would be exactly the same in the expenditure of the money for roads if the matter were left in the hands of the Minister of Railways and Canals. What difference is there? The Governor in Council can direct how this money shall be spent. Are we to assume, we two hundred and twenty-one gentlemen who occupy seats in this House, that these moneys, as some hon. gentleman has suggested, will be used corruptly? The thing is ridiculous. It is no argument to say that this money will not be used for the benefit of the people. As to the talk about automobile roads, we in Prince Edward Island cannot use the money for automobile roads, because we have no automobiles. But we can use the money to improve our roads, and we require money for that purpose. We are a small province; our revenues are very small; and it is absolutely essential that these revenues should be increased in order to provide for the necessities of the public service. The -people of Nova Scotia as well require that money. What in the world is the objection urged against this measure? There is no real objection; it is simply and purely opposition to the Government; the vote passed by the Senate is a re-echo of the vote registered by the Opposition in this House. There is no argument to support the objection made, and to justify opposition to every Act introduced in this House in the interests of the people of Canada. The Agricultural Aid Bill was opposed very strenuously in this House, but when it went to the Senate they did not vote against it because they felt that it would not be in their interests to oppose all Government measures brought before them for consideration. Last year they made the mistake of opposing this Act and passing an amendment which could not and would not be accepted by the Government, and this year, at the suggestion I suppose of the hon. gentleman who opposed the Bill in this House, the same amendment has been submitted, and cannot possibly be accepted by the Government. I think it is a crying shame that there should be withheld from the people of this country the appropriation provided for in this measure, of which they stand so greatly in need.

Now that we have got away from the matter of the conduct of the elections in

western Canada, a subject that was neither interesting nor edifying, I would like to make some observations with respect to the principle involved in this Bill when it was first introduced into this House in contradistinction to the principles involved in the amendment passed by the Senate and now under discussion. I think that the animadversions upon the action of the Senate in respect of this legislation indulged in by hon. gentlemen opposite is neither according to the rules of the House nor a dignified procedure on their part. The Senate under the British North America Act has its functions to perform with respect to legislation. It has the right to exercise its judgment, and I am sure that it was never conceived that that body should be a donkey-engine so far as its consideration of the measures passed by the House of Commons is concerned. It was never in the minds of the fathers of Confederation that that body should be created merely for the purpose of registering its approval to legislation sent before it" for consideration by this House. I think it manifestly unfair and unjust in every respect that hon. gentlemen of this House should take any position of antagonism or hostility to the Senate. We may not agree with their conclusions; yet their decisions are entitled to the respect of hon. members of this House. I have been amazed in listening to some of the arguments of hon,. gentlemen opposite with respect to the action of the Senate. I think they came with very ill grace from hon. gentlemen opposite, because I think that the tendency of present-day legislation is towards abrogating the functions of Parliament.
The underlying principle in this Bill is similar to the underlying principle of every Bill that has been introduced _ by this Government since it came into power, and that underlying principle is this:	Not parliamentary action
and conclusion as to detail, but the delegation of the powers of Parliament to a body of men known as the Governor in Council. Every Bill-the Railway Act, the Agricultural Act, the Naval Bill-has had incorporated in it the principle of relinquishment on the part of this House of the powers that properly belong to the representatives of the people, and the delegation of those powers to the Governor in Council. Within the last week we have witnessed the extraordinary spectacle of fifteen or sixteen members of this House arrogating to themselves the rights and powers of arranging legislation and formulating an Act, bringing it before this House and having it go through without, in so far as their supporters are concerned, one word of discussion. If it were not that there were on that side those
who are free to give utterance to their convictions, this legislation, which was created by fifteen men, would not have been subjected to any expression of opinion or any opposition.
I have watched the trend of parliamentary government in Canada for some time, and it seems to me that there is a tendency on the part of all cabinets to arrogate to themselves supreme power, not merely with respect to the administration of affairs, but with respect to legislation in Canada. When hon. gentlemen opposite realize that matters are cut-and-dried; that they are placed before this House not for consideration on the part of the supporters of the Government, but with a view to haying them become law by reason of the machine-politics that is growing up in Canada to an extent that it is becoming a menace, they would have the Senate placed in the same position as that in which the Government have placed their own supporters. That was not the purpose, as I interpret the British North America Act, of the establishment of the Senate. They were to be a brake upon the representatives of the people as elected, but a brake instituted to protect the rights of the people and to protect the minority. There is no question of the fact that if you give too great powers to a body of men, they become inebriated and intoxicated as it were, with that power, and the tendency is to have the sense of power carry them away beyond the bounds of reason and of judgment. The Senate of Canada was created for the purpose of restraining that tendency and to be a protection to the people of Canada. I hold that the Senate of Canada in that regard represents the people of Canada just as fully and completely as do the representatives of the people in this House.
My hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) and my hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder) have stated that we alone are the representatives of democracy, and that the Senate of Canada could in no sense be deemed to be democratic. Mr. Speaker, if this is a democratic body controlled as it is by fifteen men, then I do not understand the meaning of the term democracy. If legislation is to be brought here that is marked out and mapped out and by reason of the machinery that is incident to a Cabinet is to go through, willy nilly, without discussion and without consideration on the part of the people, through their representatives, then it seems that is not democracy, and the men who sit on the other side of the House, I will not use any harsh terms and say are gagged by reason of the position in which they are as supporters of the Government, but I will say men who sit as supporters of the Government are restrained by reason of circumstances and

environments and conditions from voicing criticisms or making suggestions; they cannot be truly said to voice the democracy of Canada, and therefore we need not arrogate to ourselves as members of this House, any monopoly of the right to represent the people of Canada in this regard.
I protest against this form of legislation. I protest against the trend of legislation in that direction. I protest against approving, day after day and week after week, the idea that a Cabinet are not^only the administrators of the affairs oi the country but are practically the sole legislators in Canada. I call as witness many hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. We had an instance here to a certain extent when a certain railway subsidy went through this House, I think no later than yesterday, and I venture to assert that that legislation was adopted by the Parliament of Canada against the well formed judgment of manyjhon. members of the House who sit to your right, and I venture more than that to say that the legislation is not in harmony with the views of the people of Canada. Whatever there may have been in the past, whatever our views of legislation may have been with regard to railway subsidies in the past, I submit that that view has changed among the people, and very materially changed. But it is not simply to that that I was taking exception. We hear a great deal about machine politics in the United States. We have heaTd a great deal in Canada of recent years of the same thing, and perhaps it is a tendency of governments to encourage the power of the political machine. Every enactment that has been offered in connection with the great public services of Canada during this session and during the last session has breathed the idea that a political machine shall soon he worked and that the representatives of the people shall be suppressed and repressed, the aspirations of the people, their views are not to be considered and alone are we to consider what the Cabinet thinks, regardless of whether it may meet with the approval of their supporters or of gentlemen who are opposed to them politically.
My hon. friend from Dundas made a remarkable statement. He said that the highways of the province of Ontario which had been cared for by the provincial governments of the past, which had had the supervision of the municipalities throughout that great province, were in a deplorable condition and that it was because of that, because of the improper management of those highways, that it was time for the Parliament of Canada to step in and take a hand in applying a remedy. Is that consistent with the proper idea of democratic government? Is it consistent with the spirit of the British Mr. EMMERSON.
North America Act? Is it in any way in accord with the ideas which the people of all Canada have? I think not. If the provincial legislatures and governments and municipalities have failed under their circumstances, w'ith a full knowledge of all the local requirements surely we, the central government, removed from the particular locality, cannot claim that we will he able to improve the conditions throughout Canada. But this is a matter with which the people of Canada have to deal; it is a matter which the people of Canada in the exercise of their provincial rights and of their franchises in political matters have a right to determine and I say it is for them to apply the remedy.
I know that some will argue that an autocratic and despotic government is the best for the people. It was too long ago for me to have any memory-indeed, it was before I had an existence-that there was a great fight in Canada over the question of responsible government. My reading has taught me that the Tory party of that day, the Family Compact party of that day, urged the very same arguments against responsible government that are being urged today in respect of the methods of legislation with respect to highways, agriculture, navies and other things in Canada, that it is simply a repetition of history. And I venture this statement, which may perhaps be considered extravagant, that if we go much further in the direction which we are at present travelling under the leadership of this Government, there will have to be another fight for the rights of the people and a revolution with respect to the privileges which were accorded to us by the granting of responsible government. The centralization of power and of patronage, the usurping by the Parliament of Canada of the rights of the people-these were the conditions that existed prior to the time when responsible government was granted. In those days they had a Governor in Council, they had an assembly of legislators appointed by the people, but what power had that assembly? They had the power to vote supplies, it is true, but in so far as the expenditure of the money was concerned, they were in no sense considered. The money was spent by. the Governor in Council; the Governor in Council was all powerful and supreme, and we are drifting back to those antediluvian days, to those days of barbarism, from the standpoint of government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member is
anticipating a question upon the Order Paper; he is certainly travelling wide of the question before the House.

I was using this as
an illustration of the giving of power to a minister to legislate with regard to detail, and with all due deference to your Honour, if it is to be deplored that legislation by the Parliament of Canada is subject to the influence of lobbyists, it is all the more deplorable that lobbying may be applied to one man who is a minister, or to fifteen men who compose the Cabinet. Under the Parcel Post Act all the details are to be decided by the Postmaster General; and does anyone doubt where will^ be the express companies and their emissaries, between now and the 1st of January, when the Parcel Post Act comes into effect? In like manner where will be the representatives of those interested in the branch

lines, between now and the next session of Parliament? I have no doubt they will he found in the ante-chambers of the Privy Council and in the departmental offices. In the days anterior to responsible government, legislation as to details of expenditure was conducted by the Governor in Council, and history is repeating itself in the passage of these measures which enable the Governor in Council and heads of departments to legislate as to even essential details.
The Prime Minister spoke of the action of the Senate as a personal reflection on the Cabinet and a want of confidence in the Government of the day. I do not look upon it in that light. These gentlemen will not always be in office; this enactment is for the future as well as for the present, and it will form a precedent for future action on the part of Parliaments and of Governments, and in that sense it is iniquitous. 1 do not look upon this question from the standpoint of the personnel of the Government; I look upon it from the basic principle of the character of the legislation itself. I would have no reason to question the integrity of the Prime Minister and his colleagues; my condemnation is of the principle which arrogates to the Government the rights and the duties of Parliament. I recognize this Bill as being in itself hypocritical, because the Prime Minister cannot deny that the amendment of the Senate is simply in accord with his own verbal assurances to Parliament. If these assurances are sincere, and I hope they are, I feel that my right hon. friend would be only doing himself justice if he incorporated the Senate amendment as a rule of conduct with respect to the expenditure of public money for this and future Governments. Under this measure, and measures of a similar character, we have the Government of the country, through its,
I will not say servile supporters, but through men who are supporting them, and whom they can in many ways, which I need not describe, influence-the assailants c-f the rights of the people, and we have on the other hand the Senate of Canada standing as a bulwark to defend democracy and the people's rights.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have the honour to inform the House that I have received notification of a vacancy having occurred in the representation of the electoral district of the south riding of the county of Lanark by the death of the Hon. The House proceeded to consider amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 185, to amend the Government Railways Act.- Mr. Cochrane.

I move:
That the Senate amendments to Bill No. 185, an Act to amend the Government Railways* Act, be not concurred in, for the following reasons:-
1.	That the said amendments are contrary to one of the principal purposes of the said Bill.
2.	That the said Bill appropriated public moneys for purposes, and it is the undoubted right of this House to direct and appoint in such a Bill the conditions, limitations and qualifications required for its object and purposes; and the said amendments are contrary to the privileges of this House.
That a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint Their Honours with the above reasons for not concurring in the said amendments.

If I may for one moment refer to a past debate, I would call attention to the very debate which we have just concluded, in which my hon, friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) spoke at

some length of the difference between the elective chamber and the upper chamber. The hon. gentleman posed as the champion of democracy. But I think it is evident that at the present time the democratic body is not the elected chamber, but the nominated chamber. To-day the Senate is the champion of popular rights. If ever there was an instance of this, it is the one to which it is my duty at once to call the attention of the House., I will read the Bill which is under discussion; but let me premise the reading by a word descriptive of the general purposes of the Bill. This measure provides for the leasing by the Government of existing roads in connection with the Intercolonial, for the building of new roads, and for the purchasing of new roads. All these things- leasing, building and purchasing of railroads-can be done by the minister with the authority of the Governor in Council, and without the authority of Parliament. In so far as building is concerned, the minister is not authorized to build a railway which exceeds twenty-five miles in length, but he can use his discretion subject to the Governor in Council, about building a road of less length; and he need not have the authority of Parliament. He can purchase a road of 200 miles in length without the authority of Parliament. Is that popular rights? Is that parliamentary government as we have understood it? Is that what we are to expect from the Government now in office? Now, let me read the Bill:
The Minister of Railways and Canals is authorized and empowered, subject to the authority of-
Whom? The Parliament of Canada? No.
-the authority of the Governor in Council, to construct, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire in whole or in part, any line or lines of railway, branch line, railway bridge, railway station, railway terminal, railway ferry or other railway work in the provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, or in any of the said provinces, which in his opinion can more conveniently and usefully be operated as part of the Government railways system, or which may be deemed necessary or desirable for the more efficient operation of the said system: provided however, that a copy of every such lease or contract of purchase shall be laid before Parliament within one month after the execution thereof, if Parliament is then sitting, or. if Parliament is not then sitting, within ten days after the opening of the next session thereafter.
In other words, the Minister of Railways can build, lease, or purchase, and the only power this Parliament has over those operations is that within one month after the opening of the session a copy of the contract shall be laid on the table of the House. Parliament cannot act; the transaction is complete. This is more serious than it appears on the surface to be.
I said a moment ago that the hon. minister can build a road twenty-five miles in length without the authority of Parliament, but if he undertakes to build more than twenty-five miles he must have the consent of Parliament. So far as the purchase of railways is concerned, Parliament has no authority whatever. I may be to-ld by the promoter of the Bill that Parliament can refuse to vote the money. What then?
I know that Parliament can refuse to vote the money, but the moment the contract is signed the 200 miles of railway becomes the property of the Government. I do not know what would be the consequence if Parliament were to refuse to vote the appropriation. The transaction may be right or it may be wrong; Parliament may be disposed to approve of it, or it may not, but at the same time, even though Parliament may refuse the vote, we are bound by the contract signed by the minister and approved by the Governor in Council. If this is parliamentary government, I do not know what parliamentary government means. I would have expected that the Government would have provided that the contract could not be completed until it was ratified and confirmed by the House.
I am well aware that there is a disposition in this House to help those parts of the province of New Brunswick which have local railroads, and that it has been the policy of this Government and of the late Government to make these roads a part of the Intercolonial system. Of that I am well aware, and of that I entirely ap-orove; hut if the Government undertakes to purchase property and afterwards refers he contract to Parliament, that is irregular. I hope the Government will hesitate before it caries this matter further, That is the amendment which has been offered by the Senate? I appeal to gentlemen on the other side of the House to apply their intelligence to it and say whether or not it is a reasonable one:
That every such lease or contract of purchase shall he laid before Parliament for ratification.
Is there any hon. gentlemen on the otheT side of the House who will criticise that amendment? Are we to be told that this amendment should not be accepted? Are we to be asked to denounce this action on the part of the Senate? Again I ask, who are the defenders of parliamentary government and democratic principles? Not the majority in the House of Commons, surely; but the members of the Senate of Canada. If there ever was an occasion upon which the truth should be affirmed, it is the present occasion, and I submit that we should approve of the action of the Senate, and not reject the amendment which they have offered.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My very distinct recollection with regard to this Bill is that when it was originally introduced by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals by way of resolution, criticism was directed against it by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. When the debate was resumed, I sent an amendment over to my hon. friend the member for the city of St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). I discussed it with them; it was unanimously accepted by them, and the Bill with that amendment went through without a single word of objection and with the' absolute assent of hon. gen-* tlemen on the other side, after I had privately discussed it with the hon. gentlemen who I have mentioned; and others, and when some question was raised about reducing the twenty-five miles to twenty, the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), insisted that it should remain exactly as it was, because he hoped to have a branch constructed in his own county. Therefore, when my right hon. friend denounces this Bill as perfectly outrageous, he is castigating most severely the gentlemen who are sitting beside him, because this amendment was agreed upon distinctly after a formal and informal discussion across the floor of the House.

I did not take any part in that discussion. Whatever may have been the attitude of my friends around me or of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, when I came to look at the Bill there was one feature of it which greatly surprised me, and that was that the Minister of Railways, with the authority of the Governor in Council, has the power to purchase a line of 200 miles and complete the contract without any reference to Parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is quite obvious that
the right hon, gentleman did not know what had been agreed to; otherwise he would not have made the speech he delivered this evening, because in so far as he found fault with the Bill his speech was a direct criticism of the hon. gentlemen who sit around him, and to whom I submitted this amendment before it was unanimously adopted by the House. Apparently the Bill passed the House with the assent of every hon. gentleman, with the exception of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Except with the consent
of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition. So far as this House is concerned, my right hon. friend is a minority of one against 220 hon. gentlemen, who Sir WILFRID LAURIER. I
were perfectly willing to pass this Bill in the form in which it was passed. I repeat again that, after a discussion both formal and informal, and after the amendment which I sent over for criticism to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House had been accepted with the addition, I think, of one or two minor amendments, the Bill went through this House without one single word of dissent from any hon. gentleman. After all that has taken place my hon. friend indulges in most absurd statements about the Senate being a democratic institution in this country and sees very .great evils as likely to arise from that which his own friends, without one w ord of dissent, unanimously accepted when we discussed the Bill in committee. I do not think that much more need to be said except to point out that the Bill - as the Senate has amended it is of absolutely no use. The amendment takes away the whole substance of the Bill. The idea was that the Minister of Railways and Canals, having already made a certain study, as his predecessors did, of the railway lines in the provinces of Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia which might advantageously be acquired as feeders to the Intercolonial, could be trusted, with the aid of his practical officers, his experts, to purchase a line not exceeding two hundred miles in length. I would have been willing to cut it down to a smaller length. But no hon. member opposite suggested any modification. What does the Bill amount to at the present time? The Minister of Railways can to-morrow, without this Parliament, do anything he can do with this Bill, he can go and make a contract, and submit that contract to Parliament and have it ratified and the Bill permits him to do that. He could do that without the Bill which he could do with it. Therefore the Bill means nothing in its present form.	It did mean something in its previous form. I desired no powers that might he regarded as excessive, nor did the Minister of Railways desire excessive powers. When the question was raised in committee I thought that the Bill as first submitted went too far. I discussed it with the Minister of Railways and he concurred in that opinion and we submitted an amendment to cut down the powers that were being conferred upon the minister, as at first suggested, but still to give him the power of doing something effective, in the way of acquiring these lines, knowing that whatever steps he took must be taken not only on his responsibility as Minister of Railways and Canals but also upon the responsibility of the whole Government, who would possibly not be considered as likely to run into any bargains that would shock the conscience of Parliament or involve an unwise and

unjustifiable expenditure of public money. The acquisition of these lines has been agitated for a long time. My hon. friends opposite passed a measure which I think in the end was not found very workable. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) introduced a further measure in the summer of 1911 which was not reached on the Order Paper. Since that time the Minister of Railways and Canals has been endeavouring to make some progress, but he has found himself with no power even to negotiate. Therefore he disclosed his general intention to Parliament and sought from Parliament a mandate to take up the matter with the various lines. I fail to see that under the circumstances there was any need of such action by the Senate, and I can only say that if the Senate persists in its stand the result will be _ to postpone for another year any action with regard to the acquisition of these lines. I Should be sorry if that result was brought about, but it seems to me that no other is possible if the Senate does persist.

As my right hon. friend has referred to me in connection with this Bill, I think perhaps it is right that I should make some remarks, and I may say that my recollection of what took place is exactly in accordance with that of the Prime Minister. I think, in justice to the right hon. the leader of the Opposition, that I should say that he was engaged in other matters at the time this Bill was under discussion, and I do not think that he saw the amendment which my right friend the Prime Minister proposed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think that is so.

The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), and the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson), who has always taken a very warm interest in the acquisition of branch lines, all read over the amendment, and so far as we are concerned, I think we are committed to it. I certainly was very glad to see that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister went as far as he did. We in the lower provinces, especially in the province of New Brunswick, have been looking for years towards the acquisition of branch lines on the part of the Intercolonial. When this House passed the Bill in 1910, the Senate thought proper to amend it in such a way as seemed to make it quite unworkable. At all events, the then Minister of Railways felt himself unable to make any progress. The people of New Brunswick are getting weary of waiting, and as I Have said, those of us who represent the lower provinces were, I think, all very glad that good progress was made. After the Bill passed I had a consultation with the right hon. the leader
of the Opposition, and he made to me the same objection to the Bill that he has made to-night, therefore he has been entirely consistent in his position with regard to it. Now, the question is what should be done. The Senate is an independent branch of the legislature. It has a right to take whatever view it pleases upon public questions, and ought we not, in view of the great importance of the matter, to do as was done in 1910, have a conference between the committee of this House and a committee of the Senate, with a view to agreeing upon an amendment which would be acceptable to both parties. It seems to me that there is not very much in issue. The amendment, as I understand, is simply that such lease or contract of purchase shall be laid before Parliament for ratification. The Senate has omitted one of the most important features of the Bill, that is the entering into a contract to build twenty-five miles of new road. The Senate does not object to that. Surely it is just as objectionable to allow the Minister of Railways and Canals to enter into a contract to build twenty-five miles of new road, and to commit the country to paying the contractors for that road, as to authorize the minister to acquire a branch which is already built, which is .connected with the Intercolonial, which is a feeder to the Intercolonial, and which it might be advisable to purchase in the public interest. It seems to me that if the contract for the lease or purchase should be laid before Parliament for ratification, so also should the contract to build twenty-five miles of new road. So I think that there is ground for a conference. It seems to me that the matter might be gotten over in this way. The right hon. leader of the Opposition says that there might not be the same objection to leasing branch lines of the Intercolonial. Possibly there might be a compromise. The minister might be authorized to lease a feeder of the Intercolonial without the authority of Parliament. That is, if in any particular case, the minister might think it would be in the public interest to acquire the absolute right to the railway, he might put in the lease a provision that the minister, with the approval of Parlia-[DOT]ment, might purchase the road at a price which should be named in the lease, within a certain period of time which would be specified. It does seem to me that in view of the great importance of this matter, in view of the fact that this has been going on year after year, that resolutions have passed this House unanimously in favour of the acquisition of branch lines, and that if the Bill is lost by reason of the refusal of this House to concur in the amendments of the Senate, we will be just where we were four years ago, not one

step further advanced, nothing accomplished, and as I have said, the whole work will have to be done over again. Do not my right hon. friend the leader of the Government and my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition think it worth while that an effort should be made to arrive at an understanding with the Senate, to approach the matter in a conciliatory spirit from the standpoint of the vast importance to the maritime provinces of the early acquisition of branch lines upon equitable terms, so that an amendment could be put through which would be satisfactory to the Senate, to the Government, and to the members of this House? I throw out this suggestion because I am one of those who believe that it is of vital interest to many sections of the maritime provinces that these branch lines should be taken over and made a part of the Intercolonial system. I believe that that result would be of enormous benefit not only to the sections of the country which aTe served by the branch lines but to the Intercolonial system itself.

My right hon. friend the Prime Minister also referred to me in his remarks, and perhaps I may be permitted to say a word or two. My recollection of what took place coincides with his, and I can reiterate practically what the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has said. In response to the expressed wish of the people of the maritime provinces and of the province of Quebec I did undertake to introduce legislation affirming the principle of taking over branch lines on terms, and I made an endeavour to outline those terms in a statute. No person except one who has undertaken that task can quite fully appreciate the difficulties encountered the moment he proceeds to put any such act into practical effect. Each road has a distinct condition of its own, and any general principle laid down as to how a road should b i approached or dealt with might be applicable to one, but not to an adjoining road. One road may pay a revenue over running expenses; another may not. A third may have prospects of future revenue, another may not. But still I think it is the wish of Parliament that these roads, which the people need, should be taken over, even if they will not pay, in order that they may have a continuance of the transportation facilities which they have enjoyed or have transportation facilities where they have not previously existed. On an adjoining road a strictly business basis might be adopted, and business principles applied. These are the difficulties which arise. One line can be leased, another must be purchased. The better way is to buy it outright. So that the different Mr. PUGSLEY.
conditions make it impossible to frame a statute that can be applied to all. I am very much interested in this question of taking over branch lines, and I would urge upon the Government that as there is not much between the Senate and this House-

for continuing the construction up to twenty-five miles, or to any mileage I asked him to make an amendment limiting the power of construction to ten or fifteen miles, but he was not disposed to do so, and so anxious was I that the measure should go through, and that this long talked of absorption and construction of branch lines should be actively undertaken that I waived the objections on principle that I had to the character of the legislation.
