Civil Government-Department of Justice- to increase the salary of the deputy minister to $10,000, $3,000.

['There is some force in what my non. friend has said. The matter will be brought to the attention of the Government and they will give it consideration. I quite agree that the passage of estimates in the form we have been doing is not really the best we might hope for in this House, and we will endeavour at the next session to so arrange the business that the estimates will be brought down at a little earlier date.\nResolutions reported, read the first and the second time and concurred in.']
That requires an explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is unable to be here this evening, and I have undertaken to look after his estimates. This item is to increase the salary of the Deputy Minister of Justice from $7,000 to $10,000 a year. It is felt that the present Deputy Minister of Justice is a lawyer of very great eminence, and that a lawyer of eminence is required to fill the position of Deputy Minister of Justice and that, having regard to the professional incomes that are commanded to-day at the Bar by men of standing in the legal profession, $10,000 is only a fair and reasonable amount to pay the deputy minister. There is another element in connection with

it. Mr. Newcombe, the Deputy Minister of Justice, frequently appears on behalf of the Government before the Supreme Court and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. Up to a few years ago he was paid counsel fees in addition to his salary for services rendered in these courts, but I am told that a few years ago the regulation was changed so that to-day he can only be paid the amount of his salary and he receives nothing additional by way of counsel fees for conducting business of that sort. The result of that has been that where previously his salary was $7,000, a considerable amount was earned by him in addition.

Who made
that rule?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand that it is under the Civil Service Act.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think it was a decision given by one of the judges of the Supreme Court. In cases where the Crown was successful costs were taxed against the unsuccessful party and in that way the Deputy Minister of Justice received counsel fees. But it was held that inasmuch as he was an official of the Crown receiving a salary, counsel fees could not be collected. That is my recollection of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The official of the Department of Justice who is present tells me that under the Civil Service Act of 1908 it is impossible for the deputy minister to receive fees for the services rendered in addition to his regular salary.
Does he not receive something for acting for clients?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think there have been a few cases where that has occurred. I know that in the case of Lovett v.s. the King, which was really a contest between Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as to which province was entitled to the succession duties on a portion of the estate of the late Mr. Lovett, Mr. Newcombe was retained by the Government of Nova Scotia, but in all the cases in which he has taken retainers I understand that he has done so with the permission and approval of the Minister of Justice.
I noticed in the newspapers that he held a brief for the province of Nova Scotia in the criminal appeal on behalf of two persons who had been condemned to 'be hanged.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend may be
quite right in regard to that. I think there have been certain occasions upon which the province of Nova Scotia has availed itself of Mr. Newcombe's services. He is a member of the Bar of Nova Scotia and it has always been with the full permission and approval of the Department of Justice that Mr. HAZEN.
he has done this. He has never neglected his duty as deputy minister in acting for the province of Nova Scotia. .

Mr. Newcombe is undoubtedly a very able lawyer and a very efficient member of the service, "but I doubt very seriously the wisdom of paying the deputy minister more than the minister himself is paid. The minister is an able lawyer, and he only gets a salary of $7,000 a year. I do not believe it is conducive to better appreciation of our Government that the deputy minister should be paid a higher salary than the minister. This session we have undertaken to pay Mr. Gutelius, manager of the Intercolonial railway, $20,000 per annum, which is a very high salary. But, as railway managers are paid, to-day it may be necessary to pay it, and at all events it is in the nature" of an experiment. But, when it comes to a department, either the salary of Mr. Newcombe is too high, or the salary of the minister is not high enough, and it seems to me that the minister should be paid a higher salary than the deputy. I believe, however, that there has been a great deal of loose practice in the Department of Justice. I cannot be very severe with my hon. friends on the other side, because the same thing prevailed under the late Administration; when Mr. NewcomDe was allowed to take retainers and appear as counsel in courts of law. Without breaking any secret, I always found fault with the practice, and I think it should not have been allowed. I am very glad to hear this has been put an end to and that it will not. be permitted in future; did not I understand the Minister of Marine to say that the Deputy Minister of Justice would not be allowed to take retainers in future?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have no authority from the Minister of Justice to say so, and I did not intend to convey that idea, because I do not know.

I understood that Mr. Newcombe was given this additional increase of salary on the understanding that he would not be permitted to take retainers, and that he would not be allowed to appear as counsel for the Dominion either.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is not what I intended to convey. I said that at one time Mr. Newcombe was paid by the Government for services he rendered as counsel in the courts, and that under the existing law he could not receive anything of that kind now, in addition to his $10,000 salary. The effect of-that was to reduce the salary which he formerly received by several thousand dollars per annum. I have no instructions

from the Minister of Justice, who asked me to take charge of his estimates, to convey the idea that Mr. Newcombe will not be allowed under any circumstances in the future, to accept any retainer of any kind.

I am sorry to say that I do not think we are justified in voting this increase to Mr. Newcombe if he is to be allowed to take retainers. There is no excuse for that at all; he should not be allowed under any circumstances to do so, and unless the minister is prepared to say he will not be so permitted in future, I shall not for my part consent to this increase of his salary.
'' How much was paid last year to the Deputy Minister of Justice by the Government? I remember we voted something extra for his services.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not recollect the
amount.

My recollection is that the committee was informed last session that it was in settlement of the account of Mr. Newcombe against the Government up to that date. If that is correct, then the rule, to which the minister referred, must have been made, if made at all. But judging from his answer to the leader of the Opposition, I am afraid no such rule has yet been made, and the impression left on me is, that *his gentleman will go on drawing fees in addition to this increase of salary. It is in my opinion a most anomalous state of affairs that this deputy minister should be in receipt of a salary very-much larger tha;i his minister. That is one aspect of it and the other is that it produces a very bad effect in the other departments. A few days ago I told the committee, and I repeat it now, that the argument advanced in support of this increase; that if it is not given Mr. Newcombe will leave the department, is an argument that has not prevailed in the past. A few years ago, the then Deputy Minister of Railways was offered a much larger salary than he was receiving as deputy minister. He would have remained in the service had his salary been increased, and this not being done he left the service. I do not think there is any sound logic in the position the minister has taken in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: When Mr. Butler was Deputy Minister of Railways, I think his salary was $8,000 a year, while the salary of the minister was only $7,000. My recollection of the amount voted to Mr. Newcombe last year is that it was in settlement of all services rendered by Mr. Newcombe up to 1908 when that new rule came into effect.

Mr. Butler was deputy minister and chief engineer and he re
ceived a salary of $5,000 as deputy minister and $3,000 as chief engineer. When Mr Butler left the department, two men succeeded him in these offices and the same salary sufficed to pay the two. The amount paid Mr. Newcombe last year was an account that had been accumulating for several years, as fees for appearing for the Dominion in several cases, and it had been previously recognized in a way but never paid until last year.

In considering the increase in salary to the Deputy Minister of Justice, we should consider the other recommendations which the Minister of Justice is making. I think it will tend to demoralize the Civil Service if these votes pass. It is proposed to give the deputy minister $10,000, to increase the salary of the assistant deputy to $5,000 a year, which is the same as that paid to the deputies of other departments; to increase the salary of the secretary up to $5,000 a year, and to provide for two additional legal officers at $5,000 each. We therefore have in this department the deputy minister getting $10,000 a year, and four other officials receiving a salary of $5,000 a year each which is the salary of deputy ministers in other departments. It is contrary to the Civil Service Act, and it seems to me it is going to create very grave dissatisfaction in the different departments of the Government; it is a. gross injustice to the other departments. Take the Deputy Minister of Public Works, and I speak of him because I am familiar with his enormous responsibilities and arduous labour, and he receives $5,000 as do the deputy ministers in the other departments. In the Department of Justice it is proposed to make an exception of an extraordinary character, and I do not think it is right. For instance, the chief accountant in the Department of Finance does not receive $5,000 a year, and yet he has charge of the entire finances of the country. I am not disposed to dispute that it is desirable to raise the salaries of the deputy heads of the departments; I think that question is worthy of careful consideration, but it ought to be done as part of a well-considered plan, and made applicable to the departmental heads. It is not a'dvisable to pick out one department and give to its officials far higher salaries than are paid to the officials of other departments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My observation of
the Department of Justice during the past eighteen months convinces me that, in the first, place, it is urgently desirable that a man of Mr. New-combe's experience and ability should be retained. The present Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, when Minister of Justice, spoke to me more than once about- the very great loss that would be sustained by the department and the coun-

try if a man of Mr. Newcombe's ability and nearly twenty years experience at that time should be led to remove from the department by the inducements which can be found for such a man in any large city in Canada. There is absolutely no doubt about it that a man of Mr. Newcombe's very great ability as a lawyer could command an income of $20,000 or $30,000 in Toronto, Montreal or Winnipeg. I think I am underestimating the amount of his probable income when I name these figures. Altogether apart from his very great ability, the mere fact that he has been in the Department of Justice for about twenty-two years means that he has an experience that is of simply infinite advantage to the country. Now, we are face to face with this situation-we cannot expect to have a deputy Minister of Justice of this country, a man of the requisite ability and experience and pay him only $7,000 a year. The incongruity which my right hon. friend has pointed out, that there is a larger salary for the deputy than that which is received by the responsible minister, is perfectly apparent; I do not deny it for a moment. But, we have no proposal at the present time to increase the salary of the Minister of Justice or any other minister. Those salaries remain the same as they were over forty years ago. Perhaps that will have to be taken up and considered by the House at some later date. But in the meantime we are confronted with the possibility of losing a man of that ability and experience; and I venture to say that if we undertook to replace Mr. Newcombe with a man of equal ability, though even without the experience that he has, we should find it very difficult indeed to do it for Sin.onn n- even $15,000.
As to the other positions which are alluded to by my hon. friend from the city of St. John, I think it is necessary in the Department of Justice to have a larger staff of thoroughly trained lawyers than we have at the present time. The matters which require consideration by the Department of Justice are continually increasing in volume, in complexity and in importance. I know that in connection with matters of very grave importance to this country, matters touching international relations, matters touching the interests of this country under conditions made by hon. friends opposite, we have found a great deal of difficulty in getting the persistent, continuous attention from the Department of Justice we should have if there were a stronger and larger staff than there is there at the present time. It is necessary in these instances to go outside for counsel from time to time. I am thoroughly convinced that a great deal of work which must necessarily be performed by counsel retained for particular occasions could be done more thoroughly and effectively, and perhaps more satisfactorily, if Mr. BOB-DEN.
we had a stronger staff of lawyers in the Department of Justice. Under conditions as they are in Canada, we cannot get men of the necessary ability and training, men with legal experience, unless we pay them a reasonable salary. For that reason, I do not think the proposals which have been made by the Minister of Justice in the estimate submitted to the House are undesirable; on the contrary, I think it is absolutely in the interests of the country that there should be a stronger and larger staff in the Department of Justice than wep have had jn recent years.

So far as I
am personally concerned, it is certainly invidious to have to criticise an item of this kind, when the gentleman concerned is Mr. Newcombe. I am glad to bear the highest possible testimony to the ability of Mt. Newcombe. But at the same time, I must say to my right hon. friend, what he knows very well himself, that there is no such thing as a man indispensable; there is always somebody to take the place of another. In my own experience, we have had a succession of able men as Deputy Ministers of Justice. When Mr. Bernard retired many years ago, he was succeeded by Mr. Lash, a man of immense ability, as we all know, and he by Mr. Burbidge, also a very able man; and he by Mr. Sedgewick-four eminent men. No doubt, it would be very much to be regretted if Mr. Newcombe were to withdraw from the service; but I do not doubt that somebody could be found to fill the office with credit. As to increase of the staff, I have nothing to urge against what the right lion, gentleman has said. I am satisfied that we did not leave the staff, when we left office two years ago, as strong as it should have been. Mr. Fraser had died two or three years before, and also Mr. Power-two men of eminent ability, experts in their respective ways. Mr. Power, for a certain class of work, could not be surpassed, and Mr. Fraser as a draftsman, was equally able. So, I have nothing but commendation for what my right hon. friend says in favour of the strengthening of the staff. But, looking at these estimates, there is in them a source of demoralization of the whole service. If you are to do this for the Department of Justice, you ought to do it under a rule which will apply to every department. The Department of Justice is very important, but no more important than others; Railways, Public Works, Interior, Inland Revenue, Customs, and all the rest are very important departments, and each must be manned as well as possible If "you do what is here proposed in relation to the Department of Justice, you lay up for yourselves any amount of trouble -although I do not know that that would break my heart-but what is far worse,

the public must suffer, for by this action you are placing the Department of Justice beyond the rules of the Civil Service. There will be constant dissatisfaction in the other departments if the officials are not all treated in the same way. Mjr hon. friend said that the Department of Justice should be strengthened, but I must say that he has not been very ardent in the task of strengthening the service of the Department of Justice. What about the Solicitor General? My hon. [DOT]friend has now been in office nearly two years, and he has not yet attempted to consider the matter, or, if he has considered it, he has not yet appointed anyone to that position. Does he mean to say that he cannot find a substitute? Is there no man to fill the position of Solicitor General? I can point to one without going very far from my seat at the present moment. My hon. friend has not done this, but he has made provision for the appointment of two additional legal officers. He has a disposition also to increase the salaries: we have the Deputy Minister at $10,000, Assistant Deputy Minister and Secretary at $5,000, and two additional legal officers at $5,000 each; that is a very large increase. The objection I have to all this is that it is contrary to the regulations of the Civil Service Act, and in my humble estimation is liable to be attended with very serious consequences.

What duties are to be
assigned to the two officers who are to be appointed at $5,000 each in violation of the terms of the Civil Service Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They will be lawyers of
good standing who will do counsel work in connection with the department, and such other work as may be necessary for them to do from time to time.

Have they
been selected?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No. The Minister of
Justice says that his experience in the [DOT]department is that money could be saved and work done very much more efficiently if one or two men of standing and education were paid $5,000 a year. He believes it to be a step not only in the interests of efficiency, but in the interests of economy.

All this is
for economy?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is all for economy.
Will these officers have authority to do work outside of Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. They will be men
capable of doing such work, and no doubt they will be employed to some extent for that purpose.	.

The minister will remember that when discussing the removal of Mr. Caron, I made some remarks in which I pointed out the necessity of having a lawyer located at Moncton to handle the claims against and on behalf of the Intercolonial railway? Last night we passed a Bill introduced by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) increasing the amount of all claims which can be tried in the local courts from $200 to $500.	That will
necessitate even more work along that line that the legal representative had before. Up to a few weeks ago the board of management of the Intercolonial railway could be sued by any person having a' claim against the Intercolonial up to a certain amount. That board having passed out of existenee, unless the Act is remedied the old state of ;affairs will exist and the Government of Canada will be sued direct, as there is no substitute named in the Act. This will complicate matters, and nullify to a great extent the Act passed last night as an amendment to the existing law. I would suggest to my hon. friends the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Justice that they take immediate steps to remedy the defect of the Bill we put through last night-this could be remedied by the Senate-and name some person "who could be sued on behalf of the Government for these small claims. I would suggest also that the Minister of Justice take one of these officials he is appointing at $5,000 and send him to Moncton to be the legal representative of the Intercolonial at that point. This .arrangement would keep the work under the supervision of the Justice Department, and comply with the principles of those who hold that the King should not be put in a subservient position in matters of this kind. I would make so bold as to suggest that Mr. Caron is the man for that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I presume my hon. friend the member for Pictou considered that matter in introducing his Bill, because the fact of the abolition of the board of management of the Intercolonial railway must have been well known to him at the time the Bill was put through the committee. I have not carefully read the Bill, but if the hon. member for Pictou is about the House I will see him this evening and suggest that if necessary, steps be taken to have such amendment made in the Senate as will make his Bill effective.

The hon. member for Pictou called the attention of the Minister of Railways to that alleged defect last night.

Who is that deputy minister ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There was a congested
state of affairs in connection with the business of the circuit court in the city of Montreal, and in order to relieve that congestion, three judges from the rural districts were called into Montreal. It was agreed that they should be paid fifteen dollars a day for their services, and this is to provide for the payment of the amount as agreed upon.

Is it the intention of
the Government to appoint an additional judge for the circuit court of Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Minister of Justice is not here to-night, and I am sorry to say I cannot give the information; I shall have to wait until his return.

I wish to express the opinion of the Bar and of the judiciary that an addition is necessary. The Secretary of State is a member of the Bar and lie will, I am sure, say with me that such an addition is much needed because there will always be congestion under present conditions. The present congested state of affairs may be relieved by calling in the country judges but they do this work in Montreal at the expense of their own work in their respective districts. I believe the Minister of Justice is aware of the state of affairs in Montreal. At the same time, I want to put in a good word for the present three judges, Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonisk).
Chief Justice LeBoeuf, Mr. Justice Purcell, and Mr. Justice Dorion. They receive only paltry salaries and, for the amount of work they have to perforin, I think thei.r salaries are entirely inadequate.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

Hear, hear. It was only regarded as a temporary expedient. I think that something will have to be done of a more permanent character in order to have the business at Montreal expedited.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows that in 1910 a treaty was entered into between Great Britain, Japan, the United States and Russia under which all pelagic sealing on the part of these countries was abolished,

and under which it was agreed that Canada should be paid fifteen per cent of the catch of the United States at the Pribilofi islands, fifteen per cent of the catch at the Japanese islands, and ten per cent of the catch at the Russian islands, and that an advance payment of $200,000 should be made to Canada on account. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
