The different claimants such as the Victoria Sealing Company and other corporations, will no doubt be represented by counsel, and I think it will be in the public interest-and this is the view of the commissioner-that there should be counsel to represent the Government when the evidence is taken and the facts are inquired into.
Department of Marine and Fisheries-contingencies, $1,000.

Does this
item Tefer to the fisheries protection service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It refers generally to the contingencies of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

Then I suppose it may be used for the fisheries protection service as well as for any other service. I wish to offer a few remarks on the item of fishery protection, since it affects the rights of the common people of Kings county along the Gaspereaux river. It has been generally understood for some time that hydro electric power would be developed on this river. I wish to say that I am in accord with the development of this power, as I am of all other developments which might be for the benefit of Kings county. I hope it will induce industrial activity, and give employ-

ment to the people, as well as furnish cheap electric power throughout the district. Furthermore, it is anticipated that a large expenditure will be entailed in making the development, thus furnishing employment [DOT]to many men. I may say with becoming modesty that I have been of very considerable service in removing some of the barriers to its development. But there is one thing that I wish to draw to your attention. I have noticed with some dismay that a Tuthless effort is being made by corporations and capitalists to trench on the inalienable rights of the common people. In the Gaspereaux district the fisheries have always contributed' a very important and necessary part of the living of the people of that valley. For centuries a large number of people have derived not a little profit, and in many cases a considerable part of their living, from the fish that frequent these waters. In fact, I do not believe that the people themselves realize to what a very great extent this right has been profitable to them, and I doubt if any just or adequate compensation could be arrived at in exchange for that right. Large quantities of fish go up the river to the Gaspereaux lakes to spawn and during the season the whole inhabitants lay in a winter supply or prepare quantities of these fish for market.
It is understood that the plans of this hydro electric company include the diversion of the whole water flow of this river. It is stated that the lake will be dammed and the entire flow of water will be carried in a trench some nine miles to White Hock, and then dropped in the valley below-a vertical fall of over three hundred feet. If the river is thus robbed of all its water, it will be impossible for the fish to ascend the river to the lake to spawn; in other words, the fish will not propagate, and the fishermen will thus be deprived of a very important asset of much greater value to them than even the ministry can realize. It may be claimed by the promoters of this undertaking that inasmuch as all properties required must be purchased either by private agreement or under expropriation proceedings, all owners will be paid any consequential damages suffered. But I wish to point out that at present there exists on this river an abundance of free fishing stands where gaspereaux can be and are dipped, and salmon taken. Therefore, it is on the people of moderate circumstances who have been in the habit of availing themselves of these stands that a severe and unjustifiable loss will fall if the present plans of the promoters are carried out. It is the rights of these people that I wish particularly to see safeguarded. I therefore draw the matter to the attention of the minister, asking him Mr. POSTER (Kings, N.S.).
to enforce existing regulations, and, if necessary, to promulgate additional regulations so that the existing rights and privileges of the citizens to which I refer may not be ruthlessly interfered with.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The matter to which my
hon. friend from Kings county refers is a matter of importance. I presume that the work, to which he alludes, is being carried on on the Gaspereaux river, for the development of electric power, and under the' authority of an Act of the Legislature of the province of Nova Scotia. I do not wish to express any opinion as to the validity of that Act, but I presume that, until the contrary is shown, we must take it for granted that the Legislature was acting within its rights in granting such a charter.
I understand the complaint of my hon friend to be that the development of this power will so divert the waters of the Gaspereaux river that there will not be sufficient water left for the fish which go up the river in large numbers, and which constitute a not inconsiderable item in the l!ving of a number of the residents along that stream. At the hon. gentleman's request I shall take it up with the department, carefully look into the matter, and have them take such steps as they can for the purpose of preserving the fisheries.

I think it would be
very praiseworthy on the part of the minister to do that I remember that years ag^ it was the custom of the students of Acadia college to visit each spring the waters of the Gaspereaux and regale themselves with the splendid fish to be caught there. I know as the result of conversations with residents of Wolfvdlle that they have very high hopes as a result of the development of this power on the Gaspereaux. The citizens in that locality are very much interested in the results of that development and they are optimistic as to the benefits that will result to them. I would be sorry to see the fisheries endangered, but I am sure that the people in that section of Kings county would not like to see the development of this power retarded. The minister has a very difficult task before him in seeking to adjust the conflicting interests that are apparent.

I have been waiting
most of the session to mention a matter to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries in relation to my own constituency. I refer to the regulations regarding fishing for salmon in St. Mary's river. The St. Mary's river is one of the largest rivers in Nova Scotia, about fifty miles in length, and a great salmon fishing river. About. ten miles is tidal water, the salmon go up through the tidal water and the people residing along that part of the river where

the tide flows are allowed to set nets for salmon while those residing above the tide are not allowed under the existing regulations to catch the salmon with nets. This is looked upon as a hardship by the farmers residing along the river and it really has a bad effect because the tendency is to make them all poachers. They cannot understand why they should not be allowed to catch a few salmon for their tables. There is no good reason. If they were allowed two days in the week, say, to fish, in those waters above the tide, and if the law were strictly enforced, I feel certain that it would be much better for the fishery and better for everybody than at present. The same situation existed on one or two rivers in New Brunswick and I understand that the regulations were relaxed in those cases. I want to ask the minister to look into the matter and endeavour to frame some regulation which will enable these people residing above tidal water to catch some salmon in the St. Mary's river. This matter was brought to the attention of the Department of Marine and Fisheries prior to the time that my hon. friend took charge of it, but the influence of the officers of the department seems to be against the proposal. I feel certain that the proposal would work well, that it would tend to the preservation of the fishery and I would ask the minister to give it some attention during the recess.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I shall certainly comply
with the request of the hon. member for Guysborough to give this matter consideration and get reports on the subject from the fishery officers of the department. But the regulation to which he refers is one which applies to all the rivers. Under certain regulations people are allowed to catch salmon in the tidal waters while in non-tidal waters they are not allowed to catch salmon. They are allowed to catch fish in tidal waters by angling and not with nets as my hon. friend states. The salmon go up the rivers for the purpose of spawning. In the fall they go down the rivers and go out to sea and in the spring they come to the rivers and go up for the purpose of spawning. The theory is that the very minute they get into non-tidal water they get into water in which the conditions are favourable for depositing spawn, and it is not desirable to allow the fish to be caught in such numbers as will be the case when nets and weapons of that sort are used. My hon. friend is quite correct in saying that some exception has been made to the regulation to which he refers. Some years ago, before I came into the department, an exception was made in regard to the river St. John in New Brunswick. Large numbers of salmon, and they are increasing from year
to year I am glad to say, are going up that river. The head of the tide is a point just above the city of Fredericton, and from that point on to Grand Falls, which is the barrier that prevents the salmon from going farther up the river, no fishing was allowed. Some years ago a change was made by which, in certain portions of the non-tidal part of the river, fishermen were allowed to use nets on alternate weeks.

Has that regulation
worked out well?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It has not, as far as I can make out, satisfied anybody. The officials of the department were absolutely opposed to it; still it was done. The people who live on the tidal waters think that they have not privilege enough and that they ought to keep their nets down for a longer time than the regulations permit. But that is not unusual with the regulations about fishing. The only satisfaction they give is to the officials of the department who find that after the regulations have been in force a number of years the fish have increased. I will have the matter very carefully looked into. There is not an occasion upon which a petition comes to the department asking for an extension of the season that some very good reasons are not given in favour of it. The policy I have adopted now is not to extend the season in any single case.
Except before an election.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, I will not do it then. It is a great pity that the close seasons are not made statutory, instead of being a matter of regulation. If they were statutory a minister could not make a repori to Council and get them changed on a day's notice. It would be far better in the interest of the fisheries and the enforcement of the law if they were regulated by statute.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will look into the matter referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair), and we will endeavour to consider it on its merits, notwithstanding his statement that the officials have been hostile in the past.

At present the people living on the tidal waters are allowed to fish the entire six days of the week. Would it not be fairer to restrict them to three or four days in the week, and allow the people living above the tidal waters to have a chance. That would be fairer all around and would be better for the fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend
write me a letter making his proposition, and I will submit it to the officials?

I assure the minister
that this regulation is satisfying the people who live along the river St. John. I have either the blame or the credit of being the father of this regulation, and I want to stand by it. Before the regulation was put in force people persistently poached and caught all the fish they could, and the officials did not have very much heart to prosecute them. After the regulation was put into force they got notice that they must respect the law and prosecutions were laid against some, and fines inflicted and collected. With one or two exceptions, the law is being respected to-day. However, I will give in confidence to the minister, the name of one fishery warden in the county of Carleton, who is a determined out-and-out poacher, and that one fish warden and his brothers are in the business every night during the season, not to speak of every day.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I suppose he was appointed on the principe that an old smuggler is the best to prevent smuggling.

With that exception, the officers are trying to do their duty, and to-day there are more fish in the St. John and Tobique rivers than ever before. The regulation is working out splendidly and the people are satisfied. If the conditions in other rivers are the same as on the river St. John, the regulation can be applied with great advantage. Why should not the people along the river have the right to fish? Why should they be prevented because there is an antiquated law which says that men can fish in tide water and not ia fresh water. I hope the minister will not repeat the experiment he tried during the progress of the local election in New Brunswick last year, and allow them to fish one month straight ahead instead of the alternate fortnights. If they are allowed to fish one month right ahead Sunday and Monday as they did then, and never take their nets out of the water, there is sure to be trouble. However, that was during an election, and I suppose the Government of the day had to get the votes whatever way they could.

Is it true that the
department intends to establish a wireless station on the top of Mount Eoyal in Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Application has been made to the city of Montreal for a site, and if it is granted a wireless station will he put there. It is in connection with the general aids to navigation we have all along the coast.

Will the minister give me some information with respect to the lobster hatchery at Georgetown in my province? The hatchery was Mr. HAZEN.
built some four or five years ago and from its beginning it gave good results. This year a change was made in the management and the results are altogether unsatisfactory now. John McDonald was manager and he has been removed, and I understand that the men who distributed the spawn have been changed. The Paquet Brothers, in Souris, boat-builders, supplied a suitable boat for several years, and gave satisfaction in collecting and distributing the spawn, but I understand other people are doing the work now.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The collection of spawn
is advertised for by public tender and the lowest tenderer gets the contract, and he must have a boat in accordance with the requirements named in the advertisement. I cannot say who has the contract this year. The manager at the hatchery is Mr. Murdock McLean. The report I got from the officers of my department is that the work is progressing satisfactorily. '
At what date was that report made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I asked about it a few
days ago and was told that the work was getting along satisfactorily.

My information is that
the boat supplied now is entirely too large and draws too much water to come close enough to the canneries to get the spawn. My information is that on the 15th of last month, although the season commenced on the 26th of the previous month, there was not an ounce of spawn in the hatchery.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will take the hon. gentleman s statement in ' Hansard ' and make investigation, because it is contrary' to t-ti6 iniormation. X have received.
iur. nuuriES (Kings, P.E.I.):	I desire to ask with reference to a matter I mentioned the other afternoon-whether Captain Norman McIntosh of the life-savin<* station at Souris has been dismissed, and it so, for what reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Norman McIntosh was
dismissed on the recommendation of Commander Thompson, officer in charge of these life-saving stations. I do not wish to put on 'Hansard' the reasons for the dismissal. I do not think it is desirable from Mr. McIntosh's own standpoint, but I would be happy to tell my hon. friend personally, the reason. It is on the report of Commander Thompson that the dismissal is made and it is to promote the efficiency of the service. There was no charge of political partisanship, the action was taken on the recommendation of the responsible officers of the department.

It is most unfortunate
that the minister introduced the spoils system into the life-saving service on the coast. The facts came out in answer to a question asked in the House that out of nineteen life-saving crews on the coast of the maritime provinces the coxswains of twelve had been dismissed, and that of these, seven were dismissed without investigation. I feel certain that prior ^ to the change of Government the life-saving service was looked upon as one that should be altogether outside the changes of politics.. I know that the only life-saving station in my constituency was in charge of the same man in 1896, and from that time on until the Change of Government in 1911. But he apparently showed some tendencies towards the Liberal party, and he had to walk out, another man being appointed in his place. Surely, there is some part of the marine service that might be left out of politics, and one would think that above everything else it should be the life-saving service. The men who man the lifeboats should be the best oarsmen in the harbour, and they should be men ready to take risks. The coxswains of these crews were brave fellows. Search the records and you will find that on more than one occasion some of the coxswains who were dismissed without investigation won medals and other decorations for bravery shown in efforts to save life. It appears that heroism does not count with the present Administration, and even the life-boat service is to be made a part of the spoils system like any other branch.
Where can I see the report to which the minister refers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman wif come to my office to-morrow.

The minister will be
busy. He knows that there have been many dismissals .from his department _ in my county and I have not said anything about them. I had reasons for mentioning this one.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will see the deputy minister, he will be afforded an opportunity to read the report.

I desire to ask with
regard to the dismissal of Captain Tohn Champion, in charge of the life-saving boat, at Alberton, Prince county, P.E.I.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have no record of the
matter before me, but I will get the information to-morrow morning.

I would call the attention of my hon. friend to the fact that Captain John Champion was a man of great experience and had saved many vessels. He was removed from office without investigation. He was not a man who took an active part in politics. He was appointed to the charge of the lifeboat by the late Administration because of his qualifications for the position. After he was dismissed he took charge of a boat to go out and save the crew of a schooner. He did this not in connection with the lifesaving station, but with a boat of his own. It seems hard that a man so well qualified for the position .should be removed.

In March last I put a
question on the Order Paper with reference to the issuing of new licenses for lobster packing in South Cape Breton. I did this

because some men were talking of establishing a co-operation lobster packing house, I got the information of the minister that it was not the intention of the department to issue more licenses until the Shell Fish Commission had reported. Now I find that at the very place where they intended to start their co-operative lobster packing plan a new license is issued.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is that Mr. Neville?

I think so. I am glad Mr. Neville has got his license, as be is a friend^ of mine and a very fine man. I think if we had got the information at that time there would have been others, especially a number of fishermen, who would have gone into this business, and they rather blame me for it; they think I was in a position to give them the proper information.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In granting a license to
Mr. Neville, the department was not influenced at all by political considerations, because he is an active member of the party to which my hon. friend belongs. We *wanted to treat Mr. Neville as fairly as we could, and when we made answer to my hon. friend we were perfectly sincere in doing so. It transpired that previous to that date Mr. Neville had been informed by the inspector of the district that a license would be granted to him, and some other officials had told hiim the same thing, with the result that Mr. Neville incurred certain expenses in connection with getting material and building a factory. Under ail the . circumstances, when the matter was submitted to me, I thought it would not be fair to refuse a license to Mr. Neville.

The bon. minister's explanation is quite satisfactory.
To provide for the pension of Inspector J. B. Allan, Royal North West Mounted Police, at the rate of $450 per annum, from January 1, 1900, to March 31, 1914, less superannuation allowance, for the above period at $280 per annum; and thereafter the pension of $450 per annum he continued and paid at the said rate, $2,702.50.
Mr. BORDEN- I can explain this item by reading the following memorandum:
Inspector Allan was rendered unfit for further service in the police owing to a gunshot wound in the right shoulder, received while endeavouring to effect the arrest of an escaped Indian prisoner, Almighty Voice. He was retired on the 1st January, 1900, under the Superannuation Act, with ' an allowance of $280, per annum, instead of being granted a pension for wounds, which -would have amounted to $450, per annum, and it is now proposed to rectify this and grant him the larger pension from the 1st April last, with arrears from 1st January 1900, less the amount Mr. CARROLL.
he has already received under the Superannuation Act.
The Comptroller of the Royal North West Mounted Police made a report in regard to this matter, which is in part as follows:
Captain John Beresford Allan, of the active Militia of Canada was appointed an inspector in the Royal Northest Mounted Police on the 1st Ausgust, 1885, and was superannuated on the 31st December, 1899, with an annual al-low'ance of $280 per annum, being unfit for further service in the force, owing to a gunshot wound in the right shoulder, received while endeavouring to effect the capture of an escaped Indian prisoner, Almighty Voice.
Had Inspector Allan received the wound on active service, which necessitated his retirement, he would have been dealt with under the pension clause for officers of the militia of Canada, and would have received a pension for life of $300 per annum.
An inspector in the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, while serving with the active militia has by statute the relative rank of a lieutenant, but in the present case, as In-speetor Allan was a captain in the militia when he was appointed to the police, nearly fifteen years before his retirement, it seems only fair that his pension should be based upon that rank, which in the second degree, namely:	An officer rendered materially incapable as a result of -wounds received in action, would amount to $450 per annum.

This case
was dealt with during the regime of the late Administration, and I understand that the action taken was based on the regulations then prevailing in the mounted police force. If it had been possible to give Mr. Allan a greater gratuity than he received, I am sure we would have been glad to do so. He was treated as' a member of the police force, and he is now treated as a member of the militia, which he was not. I have no doubt that Mr. Allan was a most efficient officer, and deserved as much from the country as he received, but the trouble is that we have rules, and if we make exceptions to those rules in dny particular instance we invite violation of them in the future. I must say that while I sympathize deeply with inspector Allan, I think the precedent is a bad one.
To defray the expenses of Mr. Thomas; Adams, of the Local Government Board of Great Britain, on liis proposed visit to Canada in the interests of national housing and town planning, $2,500.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Conservation Commission requested us to obtain the services of a gentleman, whose name I do not recall, and who was in the same service in Great Britain, to come here for the purpose set out in this item. The gentleman whose services were first requested was not able to come, but this gentleman, Mr. Thomas Adams, who has had a great experience, is to come for the purpose of giving addresses of that kind in Canada.

Allowance to William J. Stewart, chief hy-drographer, for services performed under Order in Council of 19th October, 1912, in relation to questions under consideration by International Joint Commission, $1,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When we came into
office I found that there was no special provision in the public service for safeguarding the public interest in respect of very important questions that were continually coming up for consideration by the International Joint Commission; some of the questions that arose related to one department, some to another. They were all more or less of an engineering character. Some related to more than one department and the difficulty was that between two stools one could come to the ground. It was thought desirable to have some person whose undivided attention could be given to such questions. I looked around the departments and came to this conclusion that Mr. Stewart, both by his experience and ability as an engineer, and by the experience which he had derived as a member of a commission which had to do with these international matters, would be the person best suited for the purpose. I detached him by Order in Council from the Hydrographic Survey, and since that time he has been giving his undivided attention to this work, with very good results to the country. Under the circumstances, I think it no more than right that Mr. Stewart should have the remuneration now proposed.
Is this the same gentleman who has been appointed on a commission to investigate the levels of the St. Lawrence?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He had experience on a commission of that character.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He received no extra remuneration for that.

He will come in next
year for that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think so.
Would the minister like to say he would not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would not like to make
any rash promises.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend is disposed to think that this is an undesirable allowance, he is not seized of the circumstances. I venture to say that Mr. Stewart has been of service to the country of a value, of one hundred times the amount put in the estimates as compensation for him.

While that may be all
very true, nevertheless I feel that I have a right at least to voice my views. To my mind it amounts almost to a scandal the manner in which the civil servants of this Government are being boosted by $1,000, $2,000 and $5,000. Here we vote $10,000 this
afternoon for the salary of an ordinary deputy minister. Where will it land us? This gentleman may be everything my right hon. friend says, I presume a good officer and one who has done good service to Canada, and he has no doubt got good pay. Why he gets another thousand dollars I do not know. Almost every day we are called upon to boost up some man's salary in a manner not provided for in the Civil Service Act.
Patrol of the northern waters of Canada* $40,000.

Before that item is passed I would ask the minister for some information about an item which appeared in the Ottawa Journal a few days ago stating that the vessel purchased for that expedition was not up to reqiiirements.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I read the paragraph referred to, and as I thought it might be brought up in the House, I immediately asked for information on this point. I have received the following memorandum from Mr. Desbarats:
I understand that Captain Bartlett intormed Mr. Stefansson that he did not consider the Karluk was the type of vessel to winter in, the northern seas. Mr. Stefansson told him that as the Karluk had already wintered! there several times, and as she was the usuali type of whaling vessel of which a number! wintered every year in the Arctic sea, there! was no reason why she should not be able toi do for the Stefansson expedition what she did for the whaler6.
The vessel is the usual whaling vessel built for Arctic work and numbers of these vessels winter every year near Herschel island and in other parts of the Arctic.
The vessel has been thoroughly overhauled in the Esquimalt dockyard and is considered by those who inspected her to be in a first-class condition and equal to any of the vessels of the whaling fleet.
The vessel wras built with the entire approval of Mr. Stefansson.
Steamboat inspection-further amount required, $10,000.
-Mr. HAZEN: Owing to the expansion of the steamboat inspection it has been found necessary to appoint an officer with technical knowledge and experience to assist in carrying out the increased work. While this looks like an increase, it is practically no increase. A gentleman in the outside service is simply being appointed to the inside service. The gentleman has been -acting as superintendent of naval construction for the department. He used to be paid at the rate of $4,000 a year. The arrangement under which he came out from England was that he should receive $2,500 as salary and that he should also have household expenses, but these came to between $2,500 and $2,700, so that in paying him $4,000 we are not paying as

much as before. The remaining $6,000 is for travelling expenses of the new chairman and this other gentleman, also for incidentals.
Fisheries-to provide for the expenses of investigating claims for compensation under the Pelagic Sealing Treaty, $10,000.
It seems to me that the explanation given by .the minister in regard to a former item would rather apply to this one.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My explanation was intended to apply to this item. There must have been a mistake.

The other item must
have had reference to the costs of proceedings before the International Joint Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is not in my department.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That item is to cover the expenses in connection with the commission which deals with boundary waters.
To provide for the cost of building fishery patrol boats for British Columbia, $75,000.
How many boats are to be purchased, and are they to be built in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is a revote. The item was voted last year, but the amount was not expended. It was voted for the purpose of providing one fishery patrol steamer, but after further consideration it was decided to build a number of small boats which would be stationed at different parts of the coast. Five new boats are being built under contract, tenders having been called for. They are for British Columbia waters.

Will they be built in
Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The contractors are British Columbia contractors.
To provide for payment to the Department of Public Works, of the ice-breaking tug Sir HectoT, which was lost when going to the assistance of the fisheries patrol steamer, Lady of the Lake, $16,238.
I suppose this is a payment by one department to the other?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
That would rather uphold the contention that when other departments owe the Department of Railways they should pay what they owe.

Hear, hear.
To provide for amount required to assist in the establishment, maintenance and inspection of cold storage for bait, the conservation and development of deep sea fisheries, and to provide for better transportation facilities for fresh fish, $30,000.
Mr. HAZEN.
Is it the intention to assist bait freezers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that there is legislation under which bait freezers get assistance, and there is some arrangement under which the Department of Agriculture grant assistance to cold storage plants which have provision for bait. There is a provision-I cannot give the exact details-under which bait freezers, as I recollect, on being constructed up to a certain standard, and having a certain capacity, are paid a proportion of the cost of construction.

My understanding is
that the subvention has been withdrawn from the smaller bait freezers along the coast, and that they are not now assisted.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend may be
right; I cannot answer offhand.

What proportion of this
vote, if any, is for the Pacific coast, and for what purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Practically none of this vote is for the Pacific coast. Under an arrangement that was made, before I came into the department, for the purpose of developing trade in fresh fish to the West, the Government undertook to pay a proportion of the express charges upon that fresh fish. The policy has been eminently successful, and has resulted in a very much increased transhipment of fresh fish, principally from the province of Nova Scotia, and from other parts of the Atlantic coast to Toronto, Montreal and other cities. The increase in the trade has been so great that we have more money to pay as our proportion of the express charges, and this item is largely for that purpose.
Miscellaneous-grant towards the building fund of the Royal Geographical Society, England, $4,866.66.
What is that for?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is a grant towards the erection of a building by the Royal Geographical Society in England. Australia gave a grant, and so did New Zealand, I think. This society is doing very important work all over the world, a work that is, and has been of service.
Are there to be exhibits in the building?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, the building is to house the society.
To provide for the expenses of the Conservation Commission, $8,000.
What is to be done with this amount?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot give the details as to the exact purpose for which it is required. It is reported to us

by the commission that they require this further amount. They are conducting a variety of work of investigation in different parts of the country, work of an educational character, and I have no doubt that the money is required.

When the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture were under consideration we were informed that while the Department of Agriculture was carrying on demonstration work, the Conservation Commission was doing the same. When the commission was first established, I understood that its duties were to be educative and advisory and not demonstrative. Apparently they are entering upon the work of demonstration in agriculture, paralleling the work of the Department of Agriculture. It seems to me to be rather undesirable that the Government of Canada should be carrying on work that might be regarded as overlapping that of another branch of the service.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will recollect that some questions were raised about this before, and I gave an explanation to the House in the form pf a memorandum from the commission which I think was very satisfactory. My hon. friend, from Beauce (Mr. Beland) who is a member of that commission, also gave very full and, I think, very satisfactory information with regard to it. I do not think there has been any interference with the work of the Department of Agriculture; at all events, if there has been interference or duplication, undoubtedly it should be checked. The observations that my hon.. friend has made in that regard will be taken into account.
Civil Government-Department of Railways and Canals-to provide for one valuator on first division, subdivision ' A,' $3,000.

The other day when we concurred in an item of $25,000,000 for the Transcontinental Tailway, my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) was not in the House, but I asked my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) to remind my hon. friend that we wanted to have more information as to the Quebec terminals of the Transcontinetal railway, and my hon. friend the Postmaster General told me he would remind the minister that we would expect some information about that.
I am sorry that I did not get the message.

Then I will tell the Minister of Railways what I want. I may say that the arrangements which were made with the Grand Trunk Pacific, some four, five or six years ago, have been cancelled. It was understood practically between the commissioners of the Transcontinental railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific that the station would be at the Champlain market. The commissioners bought the Champlain market from the city of Quebec as a site for that purpose. They paid $100,000, and it was cheap at the price. My hon. friend told me the other day that it was not the intention of the present commission to have the station of the Transcontinental railway at the Champlain market, that that would simply be the site of a small station, but that they would have a union station for the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Pacific railway, and I do not know if he mentioned another railway at the Palais, that is where the station of the Canadian Pacific railway now is. I do not know if the Canadian Pacific has agreed to that arrangement.
Yes. Provision is also being made for any other railways that wish to come in.
But has any concrete arrangement been made with anybody about it?
The agreement is not signed yet, but the plan is agreed upon.

My hon. friend will admit that at this stage it is not very satisfactory. This arrangement should have been signed. Last year, in the last days of the session, I drew the attention of my hon. friend to this very question. I reminded him that when we left office tenders had been received and accepted for a station at the Champlain market. This has been cancelled, and my hon. friend told me that he was going to Quebec to arrange everything.
We have.

My hon.
friend has not; he has simply made a tentative arrangement. These things have been decided, but it is not sufficient to decide a thing. You must put it in writing and have it carried out. My hon. friend told me the other day that the station was to be at the Palais, where the station of the Canadian Pacific railway is to-day. The Grand Trunk Pacific, in order to reach that station, must, after leaving Cap Rouge, go back to the St. Charles river and then run over the Canadian Northern for some distance. Then it will have to make a connection with the Canadian Pacific railway, and from the Champlain market, where there is to be a small station, the Grand Trunk Pacific would have to go round by the wharf of the harbor commissioners to the station of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It cannot do that unless there is a loop some 600 feet in length, which my hon. friend told me was

to be done by the harbour commissioners. All this is simply in contemplation, and nothing has been done. There is no arrangement, as far as I know, with the harbour commissioners to build that link, there is no arrangement to have running powers over the Canadian Pacific line, there is no arrangement to have running powers over the line of the Canadian Northern Railway. Am I right in this?
The agreement is not signed, but it is all agreed to, and the draft agreement is being prepared as fast as possible.

Why has it
not been signed ?
Because the agreement has only been arrived at within the last few weeks.

It is simply in contemplation, it is in the mind of my hon. friend and others, and it has not been reduced to writing. If the agreement was reached three weeks ago, surely there are clerks enough in the office of the commission and in the Department of Railways and Canals to have this agreement put in writing and signed. I do not doubt my hon. friend's intentions, but I do doubt his zeal. I do not think he is perfectly zealous in the desire to have this railway built at all in Quebec. I do not think I do him any injustice in saying that. The line has been blemished from Cochrane to Quebec.
No.
Yes; these momentum grades, in my humble estimation, are a blemish on the road. That section of the road is not of the same character as the rest of the road.
West of Cochrane it is the same.

I am all the
more sorry for it then. Has the agreement been signed with the Canadian Pacific railway for running powers ?

No, but this will all be put into the one agreement. It is not an easy matter to get so many different corporations to enter into an agreement. The city of Quebec only said a week ago what it would do.

I know it is not an easy matter to get an agreement of this kind. When anything which was settled, has been unsettled, it is not an easy matter to settle it again. If my hon. friend had carried out the bargain which we made, and had placed the station at the Champlain market, there would be no difficulty at all, but my hon. friend had
Sir WILFRID LAURIER
the commission prevail upon the City Council of Quebec to change the location. Has any agreement been made with the harbour commissioners to build that line of railway ?
No.

Until that agreement has been made, until you have that railway constructed, what is the use of your agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway ? Even if you have an agreement with the Canadian Pacific railway to use their rails, that agreement is not worth the paper it is written upon unless you have the link necessary to connect the two lines.
It will not be necessary to have that link at all to get down to the harbour, because the Canadian Pacific railway goes down to the harbour now.
But the Canadian Pacific railway does not go to the Champlain market station.
No.

Therefore,
there is a link to be built, and my hon. friend told me that it was to be built by the harbour commissioners.
Yes.
There is no agreement with the harbour commissioners. Has the plan been prepared for the station at Champlain market ?
No.
Is that pardonable ?
Yes.
No, it is not pardonable. This line is to be completed next year, and yet not a thing has been done to provide terminals at Quebec. For this gross negligence there is no possible excuse.

I am sorry that the right hon. the leader of the Opposition takes it so much to heart. I can state most emphatically that the commission has worked upon this matter zealously for a year. It is not an easy matter to get several corporations to make an agreement. In fact, the agreement is not completed yet at Winnipeg, although the negotiations were undertaken a long time before we came into office. The matter as regards the Quebec terminals is definitely settled now; it is a mere question of drawing up the agreement and getting it signed, and I have -no hesitation in saying that ~we will be ready to receive the Grand Trunk Pacific when it is ready to operate.

All we can do is to take my hon. friend's word for it. It is not easy, as he says, to get so many companies to enter into an agreement and it is because of the circumstances under which the difficulty has been created that I feel strongly upon the point. This agreement should have been signed long ago. I am told now that an agreement had been made with the Canadian Northern but not signed. No agreement has been made with the Harbour Commissioners. If that line is to be built by the Harbour Commissioners they have no money for it, and it will not be built when the road is completed.
Does the hon. gentleman think there is room enough at the Champlain market to handle the traffic that I hope will come on that Transcontinental road?

It would be
sufficient for the passenger traffic, but 1 admit it would not be sufficient for the freight, which would have to be accommodated higher up. The passenger traffic of the Canadian Pacific railway, landing from their steamers, is provided for under similar conditions on the wharf there.
Railway Department-to provide for a valuator, $3,000.

It is absolutely necessary to have a land valuator in the department. The Transcontinental Railway Commission have a splendid man who has given good service and we propose to take him right over at his present salary of $3,000.
Have the new freight tariffs on the Intercolonial railway been prepared, and what percentage generally of increase in freight rates has been made by them?

There has been an
increase in the tariff and the justification for it is the great increase in the wages of the,men and in the cost of coal. The average increase would not be over five per cent, but in some instances it is of course more. The new general manager has instructions that if any industry is hard hit by the increase, he should arrange to let them out. I do not think there is enough of an increase to affect any industry, but if there is, he has authority to arrange it.

There was a surplus of nearly $1,000,000 last year on the Intercolonial, which would be sufficient to provide for the increase in the salary of the employees and the additional cost of the coal. This being a public utility, owned and operated by the Government for the advantage of the people, the minister is imposing an unfair burden upon
the business enterprises of t he maritime jrovinces by these increased rates. The idea of a public utility is that it should be operated in the interests of the people, and not with a view of making money. By increasing freight charges, the minister continues a very onerous discrimination against the business interests of the maritime provinces. Nova Scotia is the great manufacturing province in the East, and the Minister of Railways controls the only line of transportation that can take the products of that province to other portions of the Dominion. The Intercolonial railway was built as a term of Confederation, in order to bring the extreme East of this Dominion in touch with the central portion. When the manufacturer in Nova Scotia ships over the Grand Trunk railway, he meets the additional difficulty at Montreal, if his goods are destined west of the city, of having his products handed over to another line of railway. There is, therefore, this double handicap against our manufacturers. We are great purchasers of the staple articles produced in central Canada, and if has always been the policy of all governments to recognize that in westbound traffic there should be special consideration foT the products of Nova Scotia, in order that they might be ible to find a market in central Canada. The minister, by imposing these extra rates, is handicapping the business of Nova Scotia. In view of the large subventions which have been given, without any condition, to enterprises in central Canada, the minister is not treating us fairly if he is going to put this additional drag upon the possibility of our .sharing ;n the progress of the country. I protest on behalf of the business interests in my province against this increase in the rates.

On behalf of the farmers and smaller shippers over the Intercolonial railway, I enter my orotest against the increased rates on the Intercolonial railway. It will mean an increase of about forty per cent on the smaller shippers and farmers and it is going to hurt us in this part of the country. I represent an agricultural community and we ship a great deal of agricultural products to Cape Breton, and the increased rates will seriously hamper the farmers and shippers of cattle and farm products generally. On local traffic, there is I am told an increase in the rates of about forty per cent. A farmer taking goods from the shire town of Antigonish to his home in the country, formerly paid at the rate of twenty-five cents where he will now have to pay thirty-five cents. I protest against this. It will not bring any great increase of revenue to the Intercolonial, and it seriously injures the farmers and smaller shippers.

The increase in freight rates will in my opinion reduce the revenue of the road in our province. As a matter of fact on a short haul of ten miles it is cheaper to carry light freight by teams than to ship it by the railway, as I know from personal knowledge. It will reduce the value of the road to the people, and I believe it will reduce the revenue also. The fact should be taken into consideration.

I also protest against
the increase in rates, on behalf of the lumber interests in the county of Gloucester. That system supplies a large part of the lumber originating in New Brunswick. There are more railway ties taken from that district than from all the rest of the province of New Brunswick. This affects just as much the small operators as the large interests. The farmer with his sons will go into camp along the road and take out quantities of timber and ties. They carry their provisions for the camps and the men, and this will mean that they will have to pay higher rates on these goods. It will certainly handicap these people very much, and I should be surprised if it did not raise the price of ties along the Intercolonial. I hope the hon. gentleman will take this into consideration when he deals with the matter.

I am trying to run
the Intercolonial on a business basis. I can understand that there may be some occasions when it will be a hardship to raise the rates. I think the hon. member for Antigonish must have been quoting on lots of one hundred pounds or less. That increase has taken place. There may be instances where the increase is a little too much. In reference to what the hon. member for Pictou says, I suppose he has reference to the steel industry. That is certainly a big industry. But I think my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) will bear me out that it is questionable if we ever made a dollar in hauling that material to Montreal at the rates which are in existence. I believe that we should give the lowest rates at which we can live. But with the increase in wages, rolling stock upkeep, I am satisfied that increases in rates are necessary. More than that, the larger of the two industries referred to would have the advantage of water rates, and we cannot carry what they can get it done for by boat. I have no desire to make money on the intercolonial, but I do desire, if possible, to have rates that will keep up the rolling stock and give a good service. I am satisfied that the business men will appreciate a good quick service, even if the rates have been raised somewhat in order to give it. It will be my endeavour to give them more in advantage than will offset the increase in the rates.
Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish).

I will point out one industry that will be handicapped. That will be the coal industry. As the hon. minister knows our province is the only place in -Canada east of Alberta in which there is a coal supply. The navigation of the St. Lawrence being closed in the winter time, and some of our more important coal mines being so situated that they are not able to ship by sea even in the summer-
Our coal tariff has not gone up yet.

Then, perhaps I
may be able to say a word to the minister that will induce him not to send it up. Under the conditions I have mentioned, the people in northern New Brunswick and in the province of Quebec who desire to obtain coal in the winter time are compelled to obtain it over the Intercolonial. If the minister puts in force a higher tariff it will prevent the coal miners of Nova Scotia from sending their coal over the same to points at as great distances from the mines as are now reached, and will also do an injury to the people who need that coal in the winter. No doubt, he will say he is serving the public by increasing the tariff as it will make the consumers of coal contribute more to the revenues of the road. I asked the minister not to increase the tariff on the carrying of coal from the East to the West, because it will mean that American coal will be placed in Montreal where, with cheap transportation on the Intercolonial, Nova Scotia coal is now sold.
There is not much brought by train from Nova Scotia to Montreal now, even in the winter season. I will take the recommendation of the hon. member for Pictou into consideration.

The other day I
called the attention of the minister to increases in local rates on the Intercolonial. I presume he is familiar with the details, and I should be glad if he would give a statement of the character of these increases, and what they mean.

I have given one
explanation, but I am quite willing to give another. These increases are due to the increased cost of coal, rolling stock, maintenance and other things. We do not think that the rates bear with hardship upon any interest, as I said before; but where there is hardship, where there is interference with the carrying on of a business in a legitimate way, we will meet it with a special tariff or otherwise.

The explanation is not very comprehensive. I do not offer criti-

eism for the sake of criticising, but I do believe this .increase of rates is a great disadvantage to the people of eastern Canada. -We have listened recently to discussions with respect to discrimination on the part of railways against western Canada in freight charges, and answers given in this House show that the matter has been under consider tion by the Eailway Commission, in answer to the complaints which have been made to the commission, the railways have said that there has been no discrimination as against the western patrons of railways; that the freight rates in the West were not too high, and that the freight rates over the railways in eastern Canada were too low. That has been the issue between the railways and the patrons of railways in tire West. My hon. friend in tie action he has taken has given a pretext for the answer made by the railways to these complaints. He has said to the people of western Canada: your rates are all right; the rates of the railways in eastern Canada are too low. He has demonstrated that fact by increasing freight rates on the-Government railway in eastern Canada. Private railway corporations will not be slow to take advantage of that provision; they will not be slow in advancing that argument before the Eailway Commission, and it would be a complete and ample justification to the Eailway Commission for any resistance the railways may make to the application which has been made by the western people who have occasion to use the railwsvs in the matter of freight. The people of eastern Canada who have occasion to utilize the Intercolonial have done so under conditions which have prevailed since Confederation. The freight rates which have been charged upon that railway have been reasonable, certainly none too low; and to make the increase that has been made is simply dealing with the people unfairly. We all recognize the fact that the building of the Intercolonial was an offset against the expenditure incurred in the construction of canals. There was expended upon the canals of Canada about $90,000,000, and the Intercolonial railway was constructed in the interests of the maritime provinces and in the interests of Ontario and Quebec. One expenditure offset the other; one was an investment in canals for the benefit of Canada; the other was an investment in the Intercolonial for the benefit of Canada. My hon. friend has made an unprecedented increase in the local freight rates, in many instances an increase of forty per cent. As an illustration of that, take the minimum freight charged, which bears very heavily on the people who live a short distance from the centres. The minimum charge on the Intercolonial for a package of freight
was twenty-five cents, and that, is increased to thirty-five cents, an increase of over forty per cent.

That is only on one
hundred pounds or less.
Mr. EMMEESON; It is the minimum charge and it has been recognized that twenty-five cents is a reasonable minimum charge to make. The increase of this amount to thirty-five cents bears heavily on the people generally. I grant you that it has a tendency to interfere with business in the .centres. If a man lives fifteen miles outside of the city of St. John and goes to that centre to do his shopping, sending out a package weighing less than one hundred pounds, he is obliged to pay thirty-five cents, whereas heretofore he wa3 called upon to pay only twenty-five. In the matter of many other charges an increase has been made in many instances of four cents a hundred pounds, and that interferes with the local traffic over the Intercolonial between St. John and Moncton and intermediate points, St. John and Halifax and intermediate points, and so with reference to the other sections of the road. I think that it is an unjust increase and will not only bear heavily upon the small purchaser and the people generally, but will be a direct interference with the business of the towns and villages along the line of the Intercolonial. What justification is there for it? We have considered estimates to-day with respect to the renewal of the Welland canal, which has been already once rebuilt, and upon which it is now proposed to expend $50,000,000. We have abolished the freight tolls over these canals, in the interests of whom? Certainly not in the interests of the people of the maritime provinces. I make the assertion, knowing that it cannot be successfully contradicted, that the freight that goes over the Welland and St. Lawrence canal systems never touches the maritime provinces.
Steel rails are shipped from Sydney to Port Arthur.

That is through traffic, and it comprises only a very small portion of the traffic that goes through those canals; the main bulk of it is for export trade. So far as the maritime provinces are concerned, they do not participate in the benefits that accrue to the business interests by reason of the abolition of tolls on the canals. I am not complaining of the abolition of those tolls, but I do protest vehemently against the increase of the burdens of the people of the maritime provinces. We have on many occasi^is had illustrations with respect to the feeling that there is against the Intercolonial. My hon. friends opposite have taken ex-

ception to an amendment made by the Senate to a certain Bill, using it as an excuse or a pretext tor not proceeding with the expansion of the Intercolonial and the absorption of branch lines as feeders of that road. It is true the Senate amended this Bill, and it is equally true that a few years ago when the Senate amended a Bill sent to them by a former Government, the Bill was treated in such a way as to make the exercise of its powers impossible. They made it an impossibility to absorb these lines or make them part of the Intercolonial. By their amendment they provide an excuse to my hon. friend, who is opposed to the policy of the absorption of branch lines, who has stated in this House, practically, that he is opposed to that policy.
I never did.

I would not wish to misrepresent my hon. friend but he has spoken very slightingly with respect to the character of the roads which would serve as feeders of the Intercolonial railway. He does not repre-ent them as feeders.

Under the Bill that
you have produced yourself you could not take over a road.

My hon. friend is not strictly accurate with respect to that statement, I remember that, when I had anything to do with the management of the Intercolonial, on; road, the Canadian Eastern railway, was taken over and I remember how I had' to fight that through this Parliament against the most violent opposition on the part of the railway critics then sitting on this side of the House and every minutiae in connection with the road had to be explained. My hon. friend .says that they could not put into execution legislation which I had brought in. My hon. friend knows that the very legislation to which he refers was brought into this House, it is true, by political friends of mine, but I took exception to the character of the legislation as I have taken exception to the character of the legislation proposed by my hon. friend. It was not a matter of party politics with me, it was a matter of the advantage that would accrue to the Intercolonial and to the people of the maritime provinces and, indeed, to the people of all eastern Canada if that policy had been put into effect. My hon. friend has made changes in the management. I am not criticising him in respect to that, I have told him that I believed it was in the interest of the Intercolonial that there should be one manager instead of a divided i*anagement, that the responsibility should be put Upon one man instead of having a divided responsibility. My criticism was imnersenal. I commend my hon. friend Mr. EMMERSON.
for his action in reversing that policy and adopting the policy of appointing one general manager upon whom is placed the responsibility of operating and managing the railway. I think now, as I thought a few years ago, that it would be very much better for the Government to be responsible for the management of the railways, to select one of the many bright young men *who are to-day in the employ of the railway and give him an opportunity, instead of importing someone from another railway.
I make this statement, that the education and training which a man receives on a private corporation railway does not fit him for the position of manager of a government railway, the conditions are different, the sentiments are different, and he never can adjust himself to those new conditions. My predecessor in office, the late Hon. Mr. Blair, tried it and it failed. He tried it more than once. Others have tried it and every experiment has signally failed. In the management of the Intercolonial under my regime responsibility was placed upon Mr. Pottinger, who was, it is true, a member of the managing board. I have nothing but good words to say of Mr. Pottinger but I felt that if, when Mr. Pottinger's term of office expired, I had had the responsibility, I would have taken one of the young men who had been trained on the Intercolonial and given him a chance and tested him. A few years ago I had an opportunity of travelling over practically all the great railway systems of the United States. I found on different western railways superintendents and managers who had received their training on the Intercolonial and this led me to the conclusion that if the Intercolonial could be the nursery of managers and general managers and superintendents for foreign railways it certainly could be the nursery for the training of young men who could manage our own railways. You bring a man from a foreign country and place him upon the Intercolonial. It is true he goes there with every prejudice against it in the first place; he goes there with the idea, and the press and people of the country outside of the maritime provinces have heralded it abroad, that there is incompetence and lack of ability and every man who is selected from another railway and sent there to manage the Intercolonial goes there under the impression that there is no man connected with the road qualified to fill the position. They make this known to the employees of the Intercolonial and so arouse the resentment and the antagonism of the employees of the railway and practically make certain that they themselves will prove failures. I think my hon. friend would have been better advised if he had given a chance to some of the many young men whom I could personally

name, and give them an opportunity of proving the stuff of which they are made. The Intercolonial last year had a surplus of $1,000,000. It is estimated that this year, *even under the conditions which prevailed last year, the surplus will be much larger. That certainly does not show that there was any emergency with respect to the increased freight rates, and there certainly should be no necessity for placing additional burdens upon the people in the maritime provinces and the Canadian public in order to operate that road free from loss. If with the so-called low freight rates on the Intercolonial the revenue and earning power of that road has grown steadily from year to year, I venture to say that with the natural increase of the traffic on the road, without adding any additional burden, the Intercolonial would lay aside year by year an increasingly large surplus. Therefore from that standpoint alone there is no justification in my hon. friend placing this additional burden upon the patrons of the road in the maritime provinces and in Quebec there is no increase with respect to through traffic. Who gets the advantage of that? The Intercolonial reaps an advantage, but the business interests of Ontario reap the fruits, and yet the business interests of the maritime provinces are to be discriminated against in the matter of their freight rates. During the past year there has been an increasing number of accidents and destruction of rolling stock on the Intercolonial. I do not know from what cause, and yet despite that destruction of property my hon. friend is in a position, by reason of the increased traffic on the road, to add very materially to the motive power of the railway. I think that new management was necessary for the Intercolonial railway. I make the statement that during the past winter, and indeed during the past twelve months, not a train on the Intercolonial reached its destination on time. The railway has become a byword and a reproach in that respect, and the travelling public are reduced in numbers because of the want of regularity in the operation of the trains. I venture to say that the Canadian Pacific railway, the competitor of the Intercolonial, reaped an abundant harvest as the result of the lack of care, to say the least, in seeing that the trains on the Intercolonial were operated on time. Every hon, member of this House who has any knowledge whatever of the management of the Intereol-onial railway will agree with the statement I am making. Perhaps my hon. friend feels called upon to increase the local freight rates in order to pay the comparatively large salary which is being given to the present general manager of the Intercolonial. I am not going to criticise the amount of that salary; I 'believe if Mr. Gutelius is the right man he will earn his 381
salary, I have always felt that we did not pay large enough salaries to the men holding responsible positions on the Intercolonial railway. I know it will be said, it is already being said, that in order to have a man brought from the United States, as Mr. Gutelius was brought, and to pay him a large salary it is necessary to increase the freight charges on the Intercolonial, and yet members of the managing board are retained at a very meagre salary, one entirely inadequate to the services which they perform and to the responsibilities which they are obliged to assume. I think this increase in the freight rates is an outrage, I think it is unfair, I think that it has been done without proper consideration. If I had an opportunity to go over the different schedules and classifications I could demonstrate to this House that the increases that have been made range from twenty-five per cent to fifty per cent. They are unjustifiable under the conditions which prevail today with regard to that railway, and when we contrast the treatment of the Intercolonial with the way in which we are treating the canal system, it seems to me that the increase in the rates merits the severest condemnation on the part of members of this House, as I believe it will receive the most severe condemnation on the part of the people of eastern Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I
entirely agree with the views expressed by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Emmerson) with regard to the importation of foreigners to manage the Intercolonial. But- I must give every one his share of credit. In justice I must say that when our opponents were in power .they inaugurated that system by the importation of Messrs. McGovern, Handheld, ' Joggins, Lozo, Burpee, and finally the notorious Brady.
It was introducing a bad practice, for we certainly 'had, .as the hon. member for Westmorland has just stated, men who were qualified in the eastern provinces, without having to get them from abroad. To-day, the same system is unfortunately continued and all the leading officials of the intercolonial are strangers. Messrs. Gutelius, Brady and Tiffin came ito us from the Canadian Pacific. We ought to have in the province of Quebec and in the maritime provinces men who are capable of holding those positions.
I shall not discuss the merit of Mr. Gutelius. He is said to be a prominent railway man, but time will fell. I must, however, differ with the hon. member for Westmorland on one point. I believe his salary is a little too high. Until now we have managed the Intercolonial with men who were paid from four to six thousand dollars a year, and with one leap wre jump to twenty thousand dollars per annum.
revised Edition

This is rather extraordinary and I think there should have been a halting place between those two amounts.
But there is another thing which exists and which I desire t'he House to take note of, because it is a crying injustice towards the province of Quebec. I think the House will agree with me that for the last forty years the appointment of leading officials has been made with utter disregard of the province of Quebec. It is an injustice that should have been noticed and remedied before this day. This remark holds good not only with regard to leading officials, but also to all the officials holding positions which are fairly lucrative. With the exception of Superintendent Macdonald, we have not one man in the province of Quebec who is drawing a high salary. The chief- inspectors of masonry, the .superintendents of buildings, cars and locomotives are all men from New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. So much the better for those men, of course, but I do not recognize that these gentlemen from the maritime provinces are endowed with superior qualifications.
We have in the province of Quebec men who are just as able to earn big salaries and to do honour to their positions. I see no reason why, for the last forty years, the railway management has constantly ignored the province of Quebec. The superintendent of track-menders has always been a man from the province of New Brunswick, and still there are between St. Flavie and Campbellton 105 miles of track in the province of Quebec and only 11 miles in New Brunswick. It has always been so for the last forty years.
Why should we, in the province of Quebec, be treated as inferior men? It is time that we should have justice. I made that remark quite recently to the Minister of Railways. The foreman of the labourers was retiring and he recommended to take his place a Mr. Macdonald, of the county of Bonaven-ture. He was recommending a man who for 25 years had been chief foreman of labourers on the Intercolonial; a man who had managed working trains for 25 years and who therefore knows the whole line between Campbellton and St. Flavie better than any one else. He is known by everybody and speaks the two languages fluently. Therefore, there was no reason why he should not have been appointed. Still,*in spite of the foreman's recommendation, the appointment was given to a young man, aged 30, who also hails from New Brunswick. I object to .such proceeding. I protest against such a state of things. Why not choose people from the province of Quebec?

Mr. Chairman, as >a representative of the city of Quebec, I feel it my duty to make a few remarks on the administration of the Railway Department with regard to the terminals of the Transcontinental in Quebec. Those who are familiar with that question know that it is of the utmost importance for the city, district and province of Quebec in general. What the explanations and statements of the hon. Minister of Railways on this point amount to is simply this: that a double track shall be laid from Cap Rouge to the site of the Champlain Market, along the river. The minister said they intended to build a small station there, but he cannot tell us what it will cost nor when the work of building shall be commenced. He has no plans prepared as yet, and lie does not seem to know what he ought to do nor what he will do. Nevertheless it seems to me that t'he Liberal Government had cleared the way.
