The Government has completely abandoned its projects, as it has also practically given up using the general traffic from the Transcontinental line facing the river, from Cap Rouge to Champlain market. In fact, here is what the Postmaster General was saying on this subject on May 29, 1913:
We will have the Transcontinental at Quebec in a most beautiful manner. The Transcontinental will come over the viaduct, as I understand it at Cap Rouge, and then will come into Quebec by tbe valley of the Tiver St. Charles, coming down by the Canadian Northern railway connection. Then we will have the union station at the Palais and at the same time the Transcontinental commission and the Minister of Railways are extending the lines of the river front from Sillery to the Champlain market. From the Charm plain market there is a gap over which a railway is going to be built. So that the Trans-: continental now will go encircling the whole city of Quebec. These are the arrangements and it is no wonder that the people are so well satisfied with them.
However, the vagueness of the declarations of the Government on the use of the Champlain market site confirms that conclusion. Secondly, he is proposing to rent the right of way on the Canadian Northern and on the Canadian Pacific, so as to bring up the traffic of the Transcontinental from Cap Rouge, through the St. Charles valley, to the wharfs where are moored the ocean steamers.
Therefore, the Government is giving up the advantage to have its own track and puts itself at the mercy of the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific. More
than that, the Quebec Harbour Commissioners are even going to build the required line from the Champlain market site to the central station which it is proposed to erect at the Palais, and thence to -the wharfs where the steamers come alongside. I have the greatest confidence in the Quebec Harbour Commission, which is composed undoubtedly of men who have at heart the interest of our city and our harbour; but I cannot see why the Government should not itself build that line, which, after all, is the continuation of the terminal tracks.
According to that policy, the Government will have to make arrangements with that company and that commission, and to pay those rentals for the circulation of the Transcontinental. Would it not have been more advantageous to have used the thousands of dollars which are going to be paid annually to go on with the works at the Champlain market and farther up, which works would have been the property of t'he Government and of which it would have had the absolute control? [DOT] Such is the principle which has been affirmed in the report which I have just read.
Then, what justification has the Government given for having stopped those works since it has assumed power in September, 1911? None whatever. At that date, work had been started on the terminal tracks, and they were just about beginning the foundations of the shops and of the station. I am not naturally, at this moment, criticising the decisions which had been arrived at, as to the site where'those shops and that station were -to be erected. That is a settled question, and I accept that decision. And the result of all those delays, of all those interviews, of all those delegations, has been the policy which I have just exposed, that is to say the negligence of the Government to use its own terminal tracks and so putting itself at the mercy of the companies, which I have just mentioned.
I will frankly tell the Government what a great many people are thinking of all those changes which do not seem to be justified. It is that what the Government and the parties interested have in mind is to prevent practically the city of Quebec from becoming the terminus of the Transcontinental during the season of navigation. It must be admitted that those who have all that in mind are to a certain extent justified to think so by the alterations which have been authorized by the Government on the grades of the Transcontinental, from Cochrane to Quebec.
From the discussion which has taken place in this House, and also from the correspondence exchanged between Mr. Leonard, president of the Transcontinental Commission, and Mr. Chamberlain, president of the Grand Trunk, there comes out the implicit admittance that such altera-

tions of those grades will result in affecting considerably the hauling capacity of the trains. And the fact is so evident that Mr. Leonard declares that it would be then an easy thing to come back to the maximums and minimums of grades as established at first. Then, if there is an uncertainty as to the result of those changes, why has not the Government stood by the first decisions of the engineers on that question, and which were that the Transcontinental has been built from Cochrane to the Pacific ocean, and from Quebec to Moncton? Why have those alterations been authorized only from the section between Cochrane and Quebec?
The only justification given by the Government is that there will be a saving of money on the construction. But, surely, it cannot hope that serious people will believe that, under pretext of saving a few thousand dollars on an enterprise of 160 millions, it could be justifiable to compromise on that section the efficacity of the railway.
The Government has put $3,500,000 at the disposition of the Quebec Harbour Commissioners. That sum of money is destined to the works required, so that the city and the harbour of Quebec may be put in a position to handle t'he considerable traffic which will come by way of the Transcontinental.
But of what use can be those works if, through the alterations of the grades, that traffic in which Quebec is interested is now reduced tq a minimum?
We have there the actual situation. In short, nothing is determined and nothing is decided. The Government says they want to erect a small station at Champlain! market, and a central station at the Palais, but nobody knows when those works will be started, what will be those stations and what they will cost. They do not even know if the seven or eight railway companies, which would have interest in using the central station, are concurring in those views. The Government wants to use the line which will be built by the Harbour Commission, as I have already said, and also the line of the Canadian Northern and that of the Canadian Pacific, but there has been no arrangement made to that end with those companies; and if the Government cannot come to any arrangement with those companies, in what position will it be, and consequently in what situation will then be the city of Quebec, -as terminus of the Transcontinental?
The hon. Postmaster General has stated, the other day, that the citizens of Quebec were delighted with those arrangements. It may be that some people who are interested in the scheme have so declared their satisfaction. But I have reason to believe that the majority of the citizens are not so well satisfied, and that what they Mr. LACHANCE
desire is to see the Transcontinental entering Quebec on its own line, and to have communication established with the ocean navigation and the maritime trade by means of works which would be its own property, and of which it would have the absolute -control, independently of all other companies.

I would point out to the minister that he really has no right to have this vote passed at all. He had no business to buy the car without a vote of Parliament; and it is only by grace of the Opposition at this stage of the session that this vote is allowed. Why should the minister purchase cars in the United States? The hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy) is interested in a car company, and they are in a position to manufacture private cars quite as good as those manufactured for the Bangor & Aroostook road. If private cars are to be obtained, I would prefer for one, to vote the money to the minister to pay for a new car purchased in Canada than to go to a Yankee road for a second-hand car. When we come into power, we do not want second-hand cars. The minister should understand that he cannot depend on another occasion, to put over on the House the buying of second-hand cars in the United States.

It was necessary, not very long ago, to furnish a new car for the Governor General, Earl Grey. That ear was built at Amherst by Rhodes Curry & Company. Certainly, it did not cost $27,000. It, was built, I think at an expense of $20,000.
Furnished?

Ready for use, if I remember well. It may not have had the beds and that sort of thing, but these certainly would not cost $7,000. And that car was purchased' by tender and contract. Was this car bought from the Bangor & Aroostook road directly, or was there some individual intermediary?
Direct from the railway company-there was a change of president.

I do not wish to take up much time, but I want to make a proposition to the Minister of Railways with regard to this item. We know from discussion in this House earlier in the present sitting that the Canada Highways Act will not become law this year. So, it looks as if the provinces would be deprived of this $1,500,000. I assure the minister that it will be a great harship to practically all the provinces. I am not going into a discussion of who is right and who is wrong in the matter-we have threshed that out already. But as I view it, the provinces want to get this money. Speaking for my own province we need it, the worst way. If the minister can find worse roads in Canada, those roads will be found to be pretty bad. This $73,000 for New Brunswick would not be very much, but it would be something. It would be a great benefit to the people if we could use it for ordinary temporary work, not even for permanent work. Would not the minister be willing to change this vote to such an extent, that for this year at least this amount of money would go to the provinces just in the form of a subsidy? Such a course would not bind the minister to anything in the future, nor would it. create any dangerous precedent. The hon. minister may have time next year to repent of his rash act in refusing to bring down and put through proper legislation, and the people would have the benefit of this amount of money. This could easily be effected by striking out a few words which would make this appropriation a subsidy to the provinces.

I am afraid I cannot comply with the suggestion of the hon.
Mr. MACDONALD.
member for Carle ton. I am sorry that there is a disagreement with regard to this matter, but I have seen a good deal of road money expended and in many cases I do not think it was spent in the interest of the provinces or the country it was supposed to serve. I think the Dominion can take a stronger stand on this than the different provinces can. We have officials who are capable of laying down the specifications for permanent roads equal to anything in this country, and I think if we did nothing more than lay down a specification of that kind and carry it out we would do a great deal and show the people the benefit of making permanent roads. The first essential of good road building is drainage, and the people do not seem to realize that; they turn up the sod and let the water soak through it during the wet season. I hope that before the House prorogues the Senate will see the error of their ways.

I am sorry indeed that the minister takes such a pessimistic view of the matter. There will be greater disappointment all over Canada, especially in my province The Premier of Nova Scotia will be disappointed, because, when be has not been attending the Presbyterian congress at Toronto, he has been travelling through the country interviewing newspapers and saying what he will do with the $73,000 if the wicked Senate does not defeat the Bill. He wants that $73,000; he has ample opportunity for spending it, and if it were $730,000 he could squander it all in a few months. Possibly some little benefit might come from it as well. He is providing far provincial engineers and county engineers who will, perhaps, be able to carry on the work as efficiently as the minister could. I hope the minister will consider hi3 rather hastily formed decision, and decide to amend this resolution as I have suggested. He would not change the vote or its destination; he would simply change the condition under which it i* granted.
I intended to make a definite arrangement with the provinces as to the roads upon which this money should be expended.

That can he done under the arrangement I suggest. I was somewhat surprised upon looking at the public accounts this afternoon to find that in 1867 the total taxes collected from the people of Canada were $11,700,000, and that subsidies were paid to the provinces to the amount of $2,753,000, or 24 per cent. In 1911 and 1912 we collected $105,847,000, and only paid $10,281,000 in subsidies, or only 10 per cent. Having regard to the. increased levenue of last year, this percentage would probably be decreased by 2 per cent. This

is a wonderful shrinkage, yet, in proportion to the revenue of Canada, the provinces have not the money to-day that they had forty years ago. My hon. friend could very weli afford to increase the subsidy,_ and make this a grant to the provinces. He will at least have washed his hands of the matter and any blame will have to fall upon the wicked Senate. hereby recommend the dismissal of Frederick R. Irish, postmaster of Afton in the county of Antigonish as postmaster because the said Frederick R. Irish has been an active partisan. The following are the specific charges against the sa'id Frederick R. Irish:

Afton, April 19, 1913.
Post Office Inspector,
Halifax.
Dear Sir,-On the 4th instant I mailed my resignation as postmaster to the department at Ottawa to take effect on the 18th instant. Have not heard from them about it. I want to be relieved as soon as possible as my assistant is away at present and my business compels me to be absent a good part of the time. Please let me know when the transfer will be made as I do not wish to have an assistant appointed for such a short time.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) Fred. R. Irish,
Postmaster.

Who was appointed
as his successor?
William R. Sterns.

At this late hour I do not propose to take up the time of the House, but I wished to get this information. I found there was no other way in which I could get it except by bringing it to in the House this evening. It is true that Mr, Irish did resign. He resigned because there was a charge of partisanship preferred against him by W. C. Chisholm, the secretary of the club. W. C. Chisholm is now the Indian agent and I observe that he has ceased to sign his name to these charges. He was an active partisan all his life, and when these charges were -made he signed the documents. It is rather refreshing to find W. J. Rogers making charges of this kind while at the same time seeking office. As far as Mr. Irish is concerned he has been a Liberal all his life. The office has been in that family for upwards of fifty years. His is the most centrally located place there, and the people of the district protested emphatically against the removal of the office. But the office was removed a month ago from a location that suited the convenience of the people. When Mr. Irish found that Partisanship had run mad down there and that charges had been made against him he res'gned. As far as Fraser is concerned, I am not going into his case but I will say to the minister that he has in his department information that is absolutely at variance with the facts, but information that he seizes upon in order to find an excuse for the dismissals that he makes. Mr. Fraser is not and never has been a partisan. I wrote a letter to the Department of Marine and Fisheries in compliance with his request stating that Fraser had received notice that he would be dismissed unless he made this declaration, a declaration that no conscientious man would make, a declaration that must have been drafted either by a knave or an ignorant person. If the intention was to draw up the declaration so that a man to whom it was submitted could not make it then the author of it was a knave. If, on the other hand, we are to look at the affidavit in the form in which it is drafted we must come to the conclusion that the author of it did not know very much about drawing up affidavits because the declaration covers all times. It states: I never paid any money, I have not given any liquor, I have not carried any voters to the polls at any time whatever. He is asked to declare that he has never done so. If a man is a tax-paver and he pays his taxes to the tax-collector and the tax-collector happens to be a voter he cannot make that declaration because he has paid money to a voter. If he had treated his neighbour at Christmas time he could not make that declaration because he would be swearing to what was untrue. The declaration was drawn in a form so that no conscientious man could make it.
A good many Grits signed it.

Perhaps so, because it was represented to them it only referred to elections. Grits signed that declaration. and the moment it was received in the department the Postmaster General wrote them expressing surprise that they should . sign such a declaration and virtually charged them with perjury. I refer to the case of McDonald, postmaster at McArras Brook, who signed one of those declarations and the department wrote: We are surprised you would make a declaration of that kind; do you understand it amounts to an oath; we must ask for an investigation. The investigation was held, and Duchemin was there, and there was no evidence against the man, and he still holds his job. When Mr. Fraser received that declaration from the Postmaster General he at once said: What is the use of signing it, because if I sign it 1 wiii be dismissed as my neighbours were, and probably charged with perjury. A more shameful, dastardly method of dealing with respectable men than that in which the Postmaster General has been dealing with

honest citizens, was never known before. Such treatment as that deserves the condemnation of everybody. Senator Girroir asked that James Stewart, of Middleton, be dismissed because the office was taken away from John McDonald and given to James Stewart, some time after 1896. The facts are that James Stewart refused again and again to take the office until he was pressed by the people of the district to do so because his place was centrally located and better adapted for the purpose than John McDonald's, which was at the extreme end of the section. If the minister looked at his records in the department, he would have found that to be the case. In the case of Lachlin McNeil, postmaster, Senator Girroir asked that he be removed and the office given to Peter Perrault, because the office was taken away from Perrault and given to McNeil some years ago on account of partisanship. The minister looked at the files in his department and he found that Girriornis stated the facts that' Peter Perrault had resigned and removed from the section some time before McNeil had got the office, and Perrault's son got tired of keeping the office and asked that the office be taken away. The next thing was a charge of partisanship against Lachlin McNeil, and he was asked to make a declaration, but he declined to make it in that form, but he was ready to swear that he never was guilty of any kind of active partisanship in municipal, local or Dominion elections. And what do you think, but the minister dismissed McNeil for not signing the declaration? The minister drew up a declaration that no conscientious man could make, and when he found a man would not sign it he dismissed him.

And there is a petition to the Postmaster General signed by over a hundred of the residents of Bromptonville in favour o-f Mr. Bougie being kept in his position. But I do not see any letter in answer to this petition, even acknowledging its receipt. There was no complaint by anybody against Mr. Bougie. There were parties who wanted to have him dismissed, not for political reasons, but because they said: We have got to keep our friends together, and to do that we must cut the head off this old man. The contract was given to a retired gentleman who has a revenue of $30 or $40 a month and who is alone. I think the Postmaster General should tell me and tell this House, that when he investigates this matter, if he finds an injustice has been done, he will see that it is rectified. If he will make me that promise-iwhich he ought to make, because no justification can be shown for this dismissal, and there is no partisanship in the case-I shall be satisfied. Mr. Bougie is too old a man to take part in politics. He certainly has not taken part in politics for a number of years, if he ever did.

no charge of offensive partisanship is made against him. I hope the Postmaster General will see that justice is done.

I would call the attention of the Postmaster General also to the fact that some time ago I asked with regard to the carriage of the mails between Frangois Xavier de Brompton and Windsor Mills. Tenders were called for, and two tenders were put in for the same amount. Both tenderers happened to be Grits. Neither
of them was given the contract. The matter was delayed so that a Tory could get in a tender for a few dollars less, and the contract was awarded to him. I do not know whether that is the new policy in the department since the present Postmaster General took office, but I know that under the late regime, when I came here to discuss tenders for my friends and went to the Deputy Postmaster General of that time or to Mr. Anderson, I was told:	This is a
business department; if your friend is the lowest tenderer he will get the contract, otherwise he will not. That is the way we were treated for fifteen years or more in the Post Office Department. But with the advent to power of the present Government we have the introduction of the spoils system. I hope the Postmaster General will take note of this matter, and if in future he wants to run his department on business, principles that when tenders are called the lowest tenderer will be given the contract. Now, I desire to ask, is it the intention of the Postmaster General to increase the salaries of postmasters in the rural districts?

I am sure my hon.
friend wishes to be fair. This question has been put to me at least twenty times during this session. I have answered it, and am prepared to do so again; but why always the same question?

This is the first time I have put it. I would urge upon the minister that $35 a year for keeping a post office open from six in morning until nine at night is too little pay for so much work. The salary does not even pay to keep the room clean. And for a number of years past there has been a great deal more for these postmasters to do. Post offices are apt to be located where there is a cheese or butter factory, and people come in for their mail at all hours.
I believe that these postmasters deserve an increase of salary. I hope the Postmaster General will look into the matter and pay his officers a sufficient salary for the work they are doing, and for which they are now so poorly paid. Some time ago I moved for two or three returns, one of which was for a copy of all correspondence regarding the tenders for the carrying of mails between St. Francis Xavier de Brompton and Windsor'Mills. I will.

what is proposed there?
That is for repairs and extension to the present wharf.
How will this work be done, by day labour or by contract?

The repairs will be done
by day labour, and the extension by contract.
No knowledge of it. It may be in the flies of the department, but they do not remember it at the moment.
I would ask what it is proposed to do at McAra's Brook where $1,200 is to be expended?

Extending the present
boat landing.

Was anything done
last year?

There is no information
that anything was done last year.

Was anything done
the year before?
Mr. ROGERS.

MV. ROGERS : No information.
At South Lake, extension of the present pier, $3,000, in the estimates' of 1911-12 there is a vote for $12,000. Is this an estimate for practically the same work?
The proposed expenditure is based on the report of the district engineer that this work is necessary.

What is the item of
$27,000 for harbour improvement at Tra-cadie for?

Those improvements include a block and span wharf, 222 feet in length, with a creosoted superstructure 15 feet wide and having :% block 20 by 20 at the outer end, estimated cost $4,000. There are also protection works on the northern side 860 feet in length and 400 feet of brush and stone 7 feel wide and some other work
Is that work to be done at Bowerman Head or Barry's Beach?
There does not seem to be any mention of the name.

When was the report
made on which the estimate is founded r
In August, 1912.

Have you before you
the report made in the summer of 1911?
No.

Will the minister
give me a copy of the report made in 1911 when it was proposed to build a wharf at the west pier at an estimated cost of $12,700 and will the minister inform me why it is that the original grant was dropped and the new preposition undertaken?
I will supply all that information.

How does it happen
that the item in the estimates of last year to extend the breakwater at New Harbour has been dropped from the estimates of this year? It is a very important item and a very necessary work at this place. It is one of the exposed places on the coast and prior to the building of the breakwater the fishermen of that district endured great hardships. In fact they had to keep a watch on stormy nights so that if a sudden storm came on, their boats would not be lost. The late Government built a breakwater, spending $27,000, which made a very good little harbour for fishing boats. Immediately the place became prosperous and a thriving village grew up beside the breakwater. A large number of comfortable cottages were built and it is now one of the most thriving villages on the coast in that vicinity. So many young men got boats of
their own and the place grew so rapidly that there was not room behind the breakwater and there was a good deal of quarrelling as to who should get in on the approach of a storm. The Liberals used to complain that it was their breakwater and that they would get in and the Conservatives would try to drive them out. The late Government decided to extend the breakwater one hundred feet and an item for $20,000 was included in the first estimates brought down by this Government. I have been informed that tenders were asked for and a survey made and everything done preparatory to building an extension of the breakwater. I was very much surprised that the work did not go on. Under the late Government, during ten years out of the fourteen they were in power, the county of Guysborough does not appear in the estimates prior to 1896 simply because the county was represented by a Liberal. It looks as though the Government intended to starve out the county again .because nearly every item for improvements of that kind w'as struck out by his predecessor or himself. This item of New Harbour is most important, and I feel it is my duty to draw the attention of the minister to it. It ought to be restored to the estimates. That breakwater ought to be extended. I want to press upon him the importance of carrying out the plan of the late Government and of constructing an extension of that breakwater.

I wish to refer to the promises of the Minister of Public Works made to the electors of the county of Antigonish on the eve of the recent election, but as the hour is late I shall do so very briefly. There are a few facts which I wish to have placed on ' Hansard ' for the benefit of the minister and for his future consideration. According to the letter which the minister wrote to Senator Girroir, and which appeared in the Casket of January 9, 1913, the main and supplementary estimates neither of which had then been prepared would amount to $211,300, but according to the estimates, main and supplementary, that have been brought down I find that the total is only $100,100 or not quite half of what was promised. Some people might be uncharitable enough to say that that is a3 near as Tory promises come to realization, but let that pass. I desire to point out that there is not a single new item for Antigonish county. The items that are in these estimates are practically revotes, or items that were in the estimates for 19111912. I also wish to point out that in the letter which the Minister of Public Works sent to Senator Girroir, and which the latter circulated throughout the county there was an item of $90,000 for George-ville and another item for Auld's Cove,

amounting to $15,000, and yet neither of these items is to be found in this year's estimates. Perhaps the minister would be able to explain why they are not included, and why he has not implemented the promises which he made to Senator Girroir and which the senator made to the electors of Antigonish. It is very humiliating to some Conservatives in the district that these items have been omitted. To such an extent were the people misled that the Sunday before the election public announcement was made that the material was required and that men were required to go to work in the course of a very short time. I had occasion to discuss the matter of the minister's promise to Senator Girroir with one of the leading citizens there-I will not mention his name-and I toid him that the letter which had been published in a newspaper and which purported to show that the items had been placed in the estimates for Antigonish county for 1913-1914 was a fake. The gentleman with whom I discussed the matter said, nonsense. It is true that the list of items was headed ' list of items noted for Antigonish county ' but you will observe that the letter states distinctly that these amounts had been placed in the estimates for Antigonish county; the word ' noted ' merely means that the estimates have not yet been passed, and the minister could not use any other word. He said it was a sort of technical word but it meant that the minister and Senator Girroir had pledged themselves that these items would be in the estimates. This gentleman to whom I refer is an honest conscientious Conservative, a good loyal Scotchman, who will resent this if he has the blood in his veins that I think he has. He will not allow himself to be imposed upon in this manner by the Minister of Public Works or by Senator Girroir. As to the items, the first is that of Tracadie. We initiated this work. A survey was made in the summer of 1911 for a wharf at West Arm, estimated to cost $12,700. I am glad to see that the minister is going one better and that he proposes to spend $27,000 there. Then there is Blue Bock. A report dated January 31, 1911, was for ian extension, to cost $8,300, and $600 for repairs. Neglect to attend to the repairs makes $1,200 necessary instead of $600. The extension provided for in the estimates for 1911-12, under the late Administration, is not found in the main or supplementary estimates of this year. Then there is Delorey's Beach, that is not a new item. There was a report dated February 13, 1908, in regard to this work which was estimated to cost $20,000. The first block was built at a cost of about $5,000, and the intention was to spend $6,500 in 1911-12. The $6,500 was not spent, and the $14,700 is therefore now available. In regard to Malignant Cove, that is an Mr. CHISHOLM (Antigonish)
old work. A sum of $2,300 was in the estimates for 1911-12, but was not spent. The result is that it will now cost $4,000 to do the work. If the department had not neglected to attend to the work, it could have been completed for $2,300. Then McNair's Cove is an old work, the present estimate being virtually a revote of the amount which was in the estimates of 1911-12, when there was an item of $5,400. That item was dropped and there was only an expenditure of $1,100 for repairs, and now the present estimate is $5,500. South lake, Lakeville, is an old work which was estimated at $4,000 in the estimates of 1911-12; the present appropriation is $3,000. Ogden's Pond is an old work, and is merely for the purpose of repairing damage done in the summer of 1911-12. McAra's brook is an old work, as there was an item of $1,700 in the estimates of 1911-12. That sum was not spent, and it is in the estimates now. With the exception of the additional $14,300, the difference between $27,000 and $12,700 for Tracadie harbour improvements, which we had in the estimates for 1911-12, not a single dollar has been provided for Antigonish county, but what we had in the estimates as I have stated or arises out of neglect on the part of the Government to spend the money that was available at the proper time. All the remaining items are revotes. What i3 the matter with Georgeville and Auld's Cove? Why is it that these districts have been cut off? Why is it that nothing outside of some wharf repairs to the wharf is provided for at Bayfield? In a report dated April 1, 1911, the estimated cost of improvements at the place was $35,000. Bayfield is an important place. According to that report the exports for 1910 amounted to $25,950, and the imports to $4,000. There were twenty-five boats belonging to the place engaged in fishing, and thirty boats from the outside frequented the harbour during the fishing season. This is the point to which the farmers of Antigonish county and of Guysborough county shipped their products to Newfoundland. That harbour should have been provided for. In the estimates of 1911-12, we had the sum of $35,000, but the present Government has dropped that altogether. Then there is the Blue Bock extension. When the Minister of Public Works wrote the letter to Senator Girroir, and talked of the generosity and munificence of the Government he was merely drawing on his imagination. The fact is the present Government found estimates for Antigonish county in 1911-12 which they dropped. They revised these and now claim great credit for them. But as I have said there is virtually nothing new in the present estimates so far as Antigonish county is interested. Now they are reviving them and they are seeking

to get credit for it. They are doing nothing but what they should have done last year.
I know from the hon. gentleman's remarks that he is apparently pleased that the $90,000 for Georgetown has been dropped.
I am sorry.

If I felt that I could still further please the hon. member for Anti-gonish, I would have no hesitation, at his request, in removing the different items to which he has ref erred j entirely from the list of estimates.
Mr . CHISHOLM: Surely the minister would not be as petty as that ?

I would like to please my hon. friend.
New Brunswick-Bathurst harbour improvements, $50,000.
I presume this is to do the inside dredging at Bathurst harbour. Has the contract been signed yet ?
Not yet.

I would ask the minister to have the contract signed as quickly as possible and to push these works on with all the vigour possible, because there are immense interests depending on the completion of these improvements, which were commenced a few years ago by the late Government. The Bathurst Lumber Company have 40,000,000 feet of lumber to be shipped out of that harbour, and they are very greatly handicapped by reason of the fact that it has to be taken out on launches. This amount will not be sufficient to complete the whole work. Meanwhile, I hope the contractors will be able to give a sufficient depth of water to allow large ships to take out part cargoes before the close of the season. I congratulate the minister about having placed this amount in the estimates. I expected that he would have done so last year. Still, I am not attaching any blame to him, as he was not responsible for the action of the department last year. Have the scows arrived at Bathurst to assist the Resti-gouche which is engaged in dredging the outside bar ?	-

The tug has arrived and the scows are expected very shortly. Tenders have been called for the dredging and the work will be let in a short time.
Stonehaven-wharf, $1,200.
Is that for repairs?

Repairs to the wharf.
Prince Edward Island-Cardigan-extension and reconstruction of ferry wharf, $10,000.

Does
that mean a wharf on each side of the river?
This is for the reconstruction of the existing wharf.
It will be no good without a wharf on each side of the river, because this is intended to be a ferry.
You must not expect everything in one year.
I suppose it will he done by tender and contract ?

By contract.
Little Sands

breakwater, $13,500.
Is it intended to make a boat harbour?
A boat harbour for the fishermen.
Will the amount be sufficient to build a breakwater ?

The estimate is $22,500;
$11,500 for the wharf and $13,500 for the breakwater.
This is a very desirable piece of work. What depth of water is it expected to have?

Eight to ten feet.
North Lake-boat harbour, $24,000.
This is for the construction of two breakwaters forming a fishing boat harbour.
Has the department a report from the engineer on this?
Yes.
Does he recommend it?
Yes.

I had information from the engineer himself who made the survey some two years ago that he did not think a breakwater there would be practicable, and he recommended that it be constructed at Long Point, some distance from that place. The chief engineer was Mr. Hegan. Who made the survey upon which the report to the minister was founded?
Mr. Hyndman.

I think it was young Mr. Miller who made the survey. No doubt Mr. Hyndman may have signed it. A boat harbour will be very desirable on that shore, but it is important to select a suitable place for it. If there is a shifting sandbar, as Mr. Hegan says, and he has had a great deal of experience in work of this kind, it might be well to consider whether yjj can construct a harbour that will be permanent at that place. Another thing to be considered is whether the harbour might not interfere with the direction of the sand drifts. The farms in the neigh-

bourhood might be greatly injured. If that should happen in this case, and I know that the chief engineer has some doubts about it, the department would have to compensate the farmers whose lands would be injured. The department would be well advised to carefully consider whether this particular place, or Long Point, which the chief engineer recommended some few years ago, would be the better place.
We will have the matter carefully looked into.

Has any changes been
made in the status of the chief engineer at Charlottetown?
He is consulting engineer.
What does that mean?
The acting engineer would have the benefit of his advise.
Will Mr. Hegan have to take the responsibility?
No, but he will give the acting engineer all the information possible.

After the change of Government many of the supporters of the Administration seemed to be under the impression they would have an opportunity of getting a considerable rake-off on most of the expenditure made in Prince Edward Island, and Mr. Hegan was waited upon many times, but he would not approve of anything of the kind. He set his face steadily against it and these men went so far as to threaten him with dismissal. Under these circumstances I would like to know whether Mr. Hegan would have the power to resist that kind of thing in the future as he has done in the past, or whether it is because of his resistance that his responsibility will be taken away from him.

Would
you please name the men you refer to?
Mr. Hegan applied for a change; did my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) get that information from Mr. Hegan himself or is it second-hand?

That is hardly a fair
question; it is well known it was done. And although I do not think anything of the kind was done by the members supporting the Government in this House, and perhaps they would not approve of it, yet I think they knew it. I am not surprised that Mr. Hegan has asked for a change, because it was a difficult position for him to occupy. He had to put up a fight for the protection of the department, that must have been very unpleasant for him. I tell the minister that it is my opinion that if Mr. Hegan's power is taken away from him the department will suffer. So far as his politics are concerned, I heard him express himself in Mr. HUGHES (Kings, P.E.I.).
words that would indicate that he had Conservative leanings, but I do not think he has any party beyond the fact that he was appointed by Sir John Macdonald. The department would be well advised to strengthen Mr. Hegan's hands rather than take power from him. Mr. Hyndman is a good man, I think, but he knows what is going on and if he knows that his chief was kicked upstairs for trying to protect the department it is only natural to expect that Mr. Hyndman will not seek to borrow trouble by doing the same thing. The chief engineer was supposed to have charge of the dredging of the province, but since the Government came into power a superintendent of dredging was appointed and I do not know whether Mr. Hegan was over the superintendent or the superintendent was over the engineer, but I do know that a new captain was appointed on dredge No. 9, and the captain was doing private dredging for Matthew and McLean at Souris, and against the wishes of Mr. Hegan, and Mr. McLean of the firm of Matthew and McLean told Mr. Hegan he would not allow him to interfere. He called the captain to account for doing work without the authority of the officers of the department, and the captain of the dredge went on and did the work. I put a question on the Order Paper this session asking what dredging had been done for private firms, or parties in Prince Edward Island, and the answer was none, except half a day's dredging done for McDonald Brothers, Georgetown, and the department did not think it worth while to charge for that. I say that the department did private dredging for McLean at Souris and the captain knows it.
Does Mr. Hegan know it?

Yes, he had a dispute
about it, for Mr. Hegan objected to the captain doing it without authority from him or from the department. I understand that Mr. Poole of Lower Montague wanted dredging done, but the department would not do it unless it was paid for. I think everybody should be treated in the same way. These are the facts and I would ask the minister to have an enquiry made.
We will look into it and if the statement the hon. member makes is in accordance with the facts, we will fire everybody connected with it.
Hear, hear.

The
hon. member (Mr. Hughes) made the statement that Mr. Hegan was approached by leading Conservatives and asked about a rake-off on public works. I do not believe a word of that statement

and I do not believe Mr. Hughes could get Mr. Hegan to say so because it is not a fact, and the hon. member is drawing on his imagination. There is not a leading man of the Conservative party that would be guilty of such a thing. I challenge the hon. member to produce any statement from Mr. Hegan, to the effect that he was approached. I do not think the hon. gentleman can come here himself with clean skirts, because if report be true he built a warehouse on the public property of the Dominion of Canada and that warehouse is there still. While the Liberal party was in power, dredging was done near his own warehouse. The dredging that was stopped by the department was in a place in which there was a deposit of about eighteen inches of mud suitable for holding anchors. This was being removed by the order of some officials. The consequence was that the vessels could not anchor there. The captain of the dredge reported this to the department, and the department ordered that the dredging be stopped. The hon. member for Kings makes a statement to the contrary which he must know to be untrue.

I did
nothing of the kind, but the hon. member for Queens is making a statement which he knows to be untrue, or else he does not know anything about it. He says the dredging was done at my wharf in Souris. I have no wharf in Souris. There are only two wharfs there, the Government wharf and that of Matthew McLean.
Carried.

No it is not carried. The hon. gentleman is making a statement that is entirely untrue. If he wishes I will characterize it by a stronger term. If the department will bring Mr. Hegan to Ottawa and assure him that he will be protected. he will give the information. The superintendent of dredging will give the information, if it is wanted.
Public Works-chargeable to income-harbours and rivers-Quebec-Knowlton Landing-reconstruction of wharf. $8,000.
Is this Knowlton landing in the county of Brome on Lake Memphra-magog? .
Yes.
Has not the hon. gentleman made a mistake? $8,000 for a wharf there?
No. The notes before me show that this is for the reconstruction of a wharf, and the items, including round and square timber, stone filling, labour, &c., make a total of $8,000.

Does the minister know
the population of Knowlton landing?

I do not, but I do not
see that that affects the case; it is the business to be done.
Does the minister think it right to spend $8,000 on a wharf where there are only three or four families-$2,-000 per family?

That is nothing; the
late Government built a wharf where there were no families at all.

A timber wharf was built there by the late Government, but to spend $8,000 for a wharf at such a point-I could not let the item go through without calling attention to it. I do not want to move that it be struck out.

I have given the hon.
gentleman the information, and I assure him I will look into what he says.
St. Croix-extension of wharf and removal of boulders, $5,000.

Is that to be done by
contract or by day work?
By contract.

Both the extension of
the wharf and removal of boulders?
Yes.
Have the plans been prepared for the extension of the wharf?
Not yet.
Will the minister call for tenders for that work?
Yes.
This spring?
Yes.

I am very glad, for the locality greatly needs that wharf. It was commenced five years ago. This is a very important place, and the farmers only have this wharf to carry their products by boat to market at Quebec and Montreal.
Public Works-chargeable to income-harbours and rivers-British Columbia-Fraser river-North America-improvements, $200,000.
I move that the item be amended by striking out the words ' North Arm.'

Will not that be ' changing the destination of the vote?' It changes it from the North Arm to some other part of the river. I am not going to insist on it, but if I did, Mr. Chairman, you would have to rule it out of order.

12132i
To provide for making good the full sessional indemnity of members of the Senate -days lost through absence caused by illness during the present session-notwithstanding anything in chapter 10 of the Revised Statutes, an Act respecting the Senate and House of Commons, $11,840.00.
Does this cover the case of Dr Robertson of Prince Edward Island?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I cannot speak for the Senate, but in connection with the members of the House of Commons all those who have been sick are provided for. I presume the same .rule applies to the>
Senate.

My deskmate, Mr. Bickerdike, has been ill; will he be provided for?
Mr. STANFIELD. Yes.
Is provision made for those who have not been sick, but who have been away on business?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
No, only on public business.
Labour-grant to the international association for labour legislation, $500.
What does this item mean?

There is an association which has its headquarters in Switzerland, and which is engaged in collecting labour legislation throughout the world and making it public to the different nations. The United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, New Zealand and other countries contribute to the maintenance of this association. Many of them gave $1,000 this year, but we are giving only $500.
Mr. VERVIT.LE: Has the minister increased his staff during the past year, and if so, are there any practical men in his department, and from which counties do they come?

I will be able to give my hon. friend the particulars in that regard; there have been very few appointments. I think there is one additional clerk in the inside service, and two or three in the outside service.

The Minister of Inland Revenue called my attention to a statement which I made in this House a week or two ago. I stated that a Mr. Brown had been appointed as a preventive officer in Woodstock, New Brunswick, at a salary of $400. The minister tells me that is not true. I am very much surprised. I know the gentleman intimately, he is a friend and neighbour of mine, and I certainly believed that he was enjoying this little salary. However, the minister tells me he is not and I accept his statement.
Mr. GRAHAM.

Will the Minister
of Public Works tell us whether we will have any supplementary estimates later on? I ask with particular reference to the question as to whether there will be any compensation to members of the House. The minister is aware of the interest that has been taken by hon. members on both sides of the House in this question and I think he should make some statement as to what the (Government propose to do on the subject.

I have been very much
interested in that myself. I am not able to give my hon. friend a definite answer, but I shall give him an answer at eleven o'clock, the first .thing when we reassemble this morning.
If the Government decides that the bonus will not be given, then are there any other supplementaries to be tabled at eleven o'clock?

Not unless this item of
indemnity for the members is brought down. There will be no further supplementaries.

We have endeavoured
to do our best to expedite the passing of this large amount of supplementaries tonight in order that the House might be prorogued this afternoon as per arrangement. But I think the Government will agree that the passing of estimates in this way is not really just what it should be, and that another session they ought to endeavour to get the estimates down so that we may have a fairly reasonable time to discuss them. A good deal has been said about the rules of the House. I am going to give away a state .secret. One of the suggestions that I made to my colleagues when in the Government as to rules, and I think it would perhaps do as much as anything else to expedite business, was to have a date set after which no. legislation could be introduced by the Government except by the unanimous consent of the House, no railway subsidies could be introduced and no estimates could be brought down; so many weeks after the opening of the session this business must be on the table of the House unless there was some emergency which could be met by the unanimous consent of the House. Another suggestion I made was that there should be no supplementary estimates. The Minister of Public Works would be in terrible trouble for some time at least-

I would be very glad of
it.

I undertook to enforce
the rule in my own department to show that it could be done and there were no supplementaries in the Railway Department the last year I was in that depart-

ment. It involves a good deal of difficulty but it can be done. If that rule were laid down, that' everything should be in the main estimates except under exceptional circumstances where the unanimous consent of the House should be obtained, I think it would expedite business more than any other rule that could be devised and would prevent us being asked to put through such large amounts, practically without discussion.

There is some force in what my non. friend has said. The matter will be brought to the attention of the Government and they will give it consideration. I quite agree that the passage of estimates in the form we have been doing is not really the best we might hope for in this House, and we will endeavour at the next session to so arrange the business that the estimates will be brought down at a little earlier date.
Resolutions reported, read the first and the second time and concurred in.

Mr. Speaker read a communication from the Governor General's secretary, announcing that His Excellency the Administrator would proceed to the Senate Chamber to-morrow at 4 p.m. for the purpose of proroguing the present session of Parliament.
On motion of Mr. Rogers (Minister of Public Works), the House went into Committee of Ways and Means.

Resolved that towards making good the supply granted to His Majesty on account of certain expenses of the public service for the financial year ending 31st March, 1914, the sum of $23,470,316.65 be granted out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.

Motion agreed to.
Resolution reported, read the first and the second time, and concurred in.
Mr. ROGERS thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 249, to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the public service for the financial year ending 31st March, 1914.

That Bill No. 97, respecting the Canadian Northern Branch Lines Railway Company be withdrawn and the fees paid thereon, less the cost of printing and translation, be refunded
